abstract: The efficient realization, using current silicon technology, of Very Large Connection Networks (VLCN) with more than a billion connections requires that these networks exhibit a high degree of communication locality. Real neural networks exhibit significant locality, yet most connectionist/neural network models have little. In this paper, the connectivity requirements of a simple associative network are analyzed using communication theory. Several techniques based on communication theory are presented that improve the robust(cid:173) ness of the network in the face of sparse, local interconnect structures. Also discussed are some potential problems when information is distributed too widely.

paragraphs: This paper studies the communication requirements of a simple associative network. Its hardware motivation is that efficiently implementing networks with more than a billion connections in silicon requires substantial communication locality. Much of the information exchange must remain local, making the arrangement of connections a central part of the computational design.

The authors contrast the significant locality of biological neural networks with the limited locality in many connectionist models. They use communication theory to analyze what an associative network needs from its connections. This shifts attention toward how information moves through a network and whether the required communication fits a sparse, locally connected implementation.

The paper presents communication-theoretic techniques for improving robustness under those interconnection constraints. It also discusses problems that can arise when information is distributed too widely. The resulting design issue is how to preserve associative behavior while respecting limited communication paths. This makes representation and physical connectivity interdependent: spreading information across a network changes what its wiring must support.
summary.tldr: Communication theory is used to analyze associative-network wiring and improve robustness when connections must be sparse and local.

title: The Connectivity Analysis of Simple Association

paragraphs: This paper addresses slow training in multilayer perceptrons. The authors describe backpropagation as requiring many iterations on large or complex problems, with speech recognition motivating the concern. Their approach changes the mathematical framing of training so that a different estimation method can be applied.

They formulate training as identification of a nonlinear dynamic system. In this view, learning means determining system parameters from the available examples. The Extended Kalman Algorithm then provides a procedure for estimating those parameters. The paper describes the method and compares it with backpropagation on two-dimensional examples, making the comparison concrete at that scale.

The authors report that the Kalman approach usually converges in a few iterations, while also emphasizing its computational complexity. The relevant tradeoff is therefore between the number of iterations and the work required by the algorithm. The result suggests that a more elaborate update procedure can substantially reduce iteration counts, without making iteration count alone a complete measure of training cost.
summary.tldr: Treating perceptron training as nonlinear system identification enables Extended Kalman updates that usually converge in few, computationally complex iterations.

title: Training Multilayer Perceptrons with the Extended Kalman Algorithm

abstract: We have developed graphics to visualize static and dynamic infor(cid:173) mation in layered neural network learning systems. Emphasis was placed on creating new visuals that make use of spatial arrange(cid:173) ments, size information, animation and color. We applied these tools to the study of back-propagation learning of simple Boolean predicates, and have obtained new insights into the dynamics of the learning process.
originalAbstract: We have developed graphics to visualize static and dynamic infor(cid:173) mation in layered neural network learning systems. Emphasis was placed on creating new visuals that make use of spatial arrange(cid:173) ments, size information, animation and color. paragraphs: This paper develops graphical tools for examining layered neural networks as they learn. The tools cover both static information and dynamic behavior. A static view shows the system at a particular point, while a dynamic view makes change during learning part of what the researcher can inspect.

The visual designs use spatial arrangement, size, color, and animation. These provide several ways to present information that would otherwise need to be interpreted through numerical descriptions. Animation is especially relevant to the stated goal of understanding learning dynamics, because it lets a display communicate a process unfolding rather than only its final state.

The authors apply the tools to backpropagation networks learning simple Boolean predicates, which are rules producing true-or-false answers. They report gaining new insights into the learning process from these visualizations. The contribution is therefore an investigative method: graphical representations help researchers study how training proceeds. The reported outcome concerns understanding network behavior, rather than a change to the learning algorithm or a claim of improved prediction accuracy.
summary.tldr: Graphics using space, size, color, and animation reveal aspects of backpropagation learning dynamics on simple Boolean tasks.

title: Neural Network Visualization

abstract: Multi-layer perceptrons and trained classification trees are two very different techniques which have recently become popular. Given enough data and time, both methods are capable of performing arbi(cid:173) trary non-linear classification. We first consider the important differences between multi-layer perceptrons and classification trees and conclude that there is not enough theoretical basis for the clear(cid:173) cut superiority of one technique over the other. For this reason, we performed a number of empirical tests on three real-world problems in power system load forecasting, power system security prediction, and speaker-independent vowel identification. paragraphs: The paper compares multilayer perceptrons with trained classification trees. Both can represent arbitrary nonlinear classifications when enough data and time are available, but they organize their decisions differently. The authors first examine those differences and conclude that theory does not provide a sufficient basis for declaring either method clearly superior.

They therefore compare the methods empirically on three applications: power system load forecasting, power system security prediction, and vowel identification across speakers. These tasks provide concrete settings in which to assess the alternatives. The comparison includes piecewise-linear trees, so the tree side is not restricted to its simplest possible decision structure.

Across the reported tests, the multilayer perceptron performs at least as well as the trained classification trees and sometimes better. This supplies evidence favoring the perceptron for the applications examined, while the authors' initial argument explains why practical testing was necessary. The contribution is a consistent empirical comparison across several problems in the absence of a clear theoretical ranking.
summary.tldr: Multilayer perceptrons match or outperform trained classification trees across three tested real-world applications.

title: Performance Comparisons Between Backpropagation Networks and Classification Trees on Three Real-World Applications

abstract: We report learning measurements from a system composed of a cascadable learning chip, data generators and analyzers for training pattern presentation, and an X-windows based software interface. The 32 neuron learning chip has 496 adaptive synapses and can perform Boltzmann and mean-field learning using separate noise and gain controls. We have used this system to do learning experiments on the parity and replication problem. The system settling time limits the learning speed to about 100,000 patterns per second roughly independent of system size.
originalAbstract: We report learning measurements from a system composed of a cascadable learning chip, data generators and analyzers for training pattern presentation, and an X-windows based software interface. The 32 neuron learning chip has 496 adaptive synapses and can perform Boltzmann and mean-field learning using separate noise and gain controls. We have used this system to do learning experiments on the parity and replication problem. The system settling time limits the learning speed to about 100,000 patterns per second roughly independent of system size.

paragraphs: The paper reports measurements of learning in a hardware neural microsystem. Its central component is a cascadable chip containing 32 neurons and 496 adaptive synapses. The complete experimental system also includes equipment for generating and analyzing training patterns, together with an X-windows software interface for operating the setup.

Separate controls for noise and gain allow the chip to perform both Boltzmann learning and mean-field learning. The researchers use the system for experiments on parity and replication problems. These experiments place learning directly in the implemented hardware, allowing its practical operating behavior to be measured as part of the complete system.

The principal speed constraint is the time required for the system to settle. This limits learning to approximately 100,000 patterns per second, a rate reported as roughly independent of system size. That finding identifies settling dynamics as the relevant bottleneck and gives a concrete measure of the system's training throughput. It also connects the behavior of individual learning components to the performance of a cascadable implementation.
summary.tldr: A cascadable neural learning chip achieves about 100,000 training patterns per second, with speed limited by system settling time.

title: Experimental Evaluation of Learning in a Neural Microsystem

abstract: In this paper we discuss the asymptotic properties of the most com(cid:173) monly used variant of the backpropagation algorithm in which net(cid:173) work weights are trained by means of a local gradient descent on ex(cid:173) amples drawn randomly from a fixed training set, and the learning rate TJ of the gradient updates is held constant (simple backpropa(cid:173) gation). Using stochastic approximation results, we show that for TJ ~ 0 this training process approaches a batch training and pro(cid:173) vide results on the rate of convergence. Further, we show that for small TJ one can approximate simple back propagation by the sum of a batch training process and a Gaussian diffusion which is the unique solution to a linear stochastic differential equation. Using this approximation we indicate the reasons why simple backprop(cid:173) agation is less likely to get stuck in local minima than the batch training process and demonstrate this empirically on a number of examples.

Using this approximation we indicate the reasons why simple backprop(cid:173) agation is less likely to get stuck in local minima than the batch training process and demonstrate this empirically on a number of examples.

paragraphs: This paper studies backpropagation when training examples are sampled randomly from a fixed dataset and the learning rate stays constant. Although each update follows a local gradient, the randomly selected example makes the sequence of updates stochastic. The authors examine how this training process relates to batch training, which uses the dataset collectively.

Using stochastic approximation theory, they show that the process approaches batch training as the learning rate tends to zero and provide convergence-rate results. For a small learning rate, they describe training as a batch trajectory plus Gaussian diffusion. The diffusion component is specified by a linear stochastic differential equation, giving a mathematical account of fluctuations around the batch process.

This approximation helps explain why randomly sampled backpropagation is less likely than batch training to remain trapped in a local minimum. The authors also demonstrate this behavior empirically on several examples. The explanation is grounded in the small-learning-rate approximation: random updates introduce fluctuations alongside the systematic movement described by batch training.
summary.tldr: A diffusion approximation explains how randomness in constant-rate backpropagation can reduce trapping in local minima compared with batch training.

title: Diffusion Approximations for the Constant Learning Rate Backpropagation Algorithm and Resistence to Local Minima

abstract: With a point matching distance measure which is invariant under translation, rotation and permutation, we learn 2-D point-set ob(cid:173) jects, by clustering noisy point-set images. Unlike traditional clus(cid:173) tering methods which use distance measures that operate on feature vectors - a representation common to most problem domains - this object-based clustering technique employs a distance measure spe(cid:173) cific to a type of object within a problem domain. Formulating the clustering problem as two nested objective functions, we derive optimization dynamics similar to the Expectation-Maximization algorithm used in mixture models.
originalAbstract: With a point matching distance measure which is invariant under translation, rotation and permutation, we learn 2-D point-set ob(cid:173) jects, by clustering noisy point-set images. Unlike traditional clus(cid:173) tering methods which use distance measures that operate on feature vectors - a representation common to most problem domains - this object-based clustering technique employs a distance measure spe(cid:173) cific to a type of object within a problem domain. Formulating the clustering problem as two nested objective functions, we derive optimization dynamics similar to the Expectation-Maximization algorithm used in mixture models.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn two-dimensional objects by clustering noisy images represented as sets of points. The key choice is the meaning of distance between two examples. The authors use a point-matching distance designed for these objects, so clustering depends on their spatial arrangement rather than a generic comparison of feature vectors.

The distance is invariant to translation, rotation, and permutation. Moving or rotating a point set, or changing the order in which its points are listed, therefore does not change the comparison in the way those transformations would under an unsuitable representation. This builds relevant knowledge about object identity directly into the similarity measure used for learning.

The authors express the learning problem through two nested objective functions and derive optimization dynamics resembling the Expectation-Maximization algorithm for mixture models. The approach connects object matching with clustering in a common optimization formulation. Its significance is that the learner's notion of similarity reflects the structure of the objects themselves, making the distance measure an active part of the modeling approach.
summary.tldr: Object-specific point matching lets clustering learn noisy shapes while ignoring translation, rotation, and point ordering.

title: Clustering with a Domain-Specific Distance Measure

abstract: Sridhar Mahadevan Department of Computer Science Michigan State University East Lansing, MI 48824 mahadeva@cse.msu.edu A key challenge for reinforcement learning is scaling up to large partially observable domains. In this paper, we show how a hier(cid:173) archy of behaviors can be used to create and select among variable length short-term memories appropriate for a task. At higher lev(cid:173) els in the hierarchy, the agent abstracts over lower-level details and looks back over a variable number of high-level decisions in time. We formalize this idea in a framework called Hierarchical Suffix Memory (HSM). HSM uses a memory-based SMDP learning method to rapidly propagate delayed reward across long decision sequences. We describe a detailed experimental study comparing memory vs. hierarchy using the HSM framework on a realistic corridor navigation task.
originalAbstract: Sridhar Mahadevan Department of Computer Science Michigan State University East Lansing, MI 48824 mahadeva@cse.msu.edu A key challenge for reinforcement learning is scaling up to large partially observable domains. In this paper, we show how a hier(cid:173) archy of behaviors can be used to create and select among variable length short-term memories appropriate for a task. At higher lev(cid:173) els in the hierarchy, the agent abstracts over lower-level details and looks back over a variable number of high-level decisions in time. We formalize this idea in a framework called Hierarchical Suffix Memory (HSM). HSM uses a memory-based SMDP learning method to rapidly propagate delayed reward across long decision sequences. We describe a detailed experimental study comparing memory vs. hierarchy using the HSM framework on a realistic corridor navigation task.

paragraphs: In a partially observable environment, an agent may need recent history to decide what to do because its current observation does not fully describe the situation. This paper addresses scaling reinforcement learning in such environments by linking memory to a hierarchy of behaviors. Different levels can retain different amounts of task-relevant history.

The framework, Hierarchical Suffix Memory, creates and selects variable-length short-term memories. Higher levels abstract away lower-level details and look back over a variable number of high-level decisions. This changes both what the agent remembers and the temporal units used to represent that memory, allowing history to be expressed through more abstract decisions.

HSM uses a memory-based semi-Markov decision-process learning method to propagate delayed rewards rapidly across long decision sequences. The paper also describes a detailed experimental comparison of memory and hierarchy on a realistic corridor-navigation task. The stated contribution is the framework and its study of these two resources together; the abstract does not report a particular winner or numerical performance advantage.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Suffix Memory combines behavior hierarchies with variable-length memories to support reinforcement learning under partial observability.

title: Hierarchical Memory-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We describe a neurally-inspired, unsupervised learning algorithm that builds a non-linear generative model for pairs of face images from the same individual. Individuals are then recognized by finding the highest relative probability pair among all pairs that consist of a test image and an image whose identity is known. Our method compares favorably with other methods in the literature. The generative model consists of a single layer of rate-coded, non-linear feature detectors and it has the property that, given a data vector, the true posterior probability distribution over the feature detector activities can be inferred rapidly without iteration or approximation. The weights of the feature detectors are learned by com(cid:173) paring the correlations of pixel intensities and feature activations in two phases: When the network is observing real data and when it is observing reconstructions of real data generated from the feature activations.

paragraphs: This paper approaches face recognition by learning a generative model of pairs of images showing the same person. To identify a test image, the method pairs it with images of known identity and chooses the pair with the highest relative probability. Recognition therefore depends on how well a candidate pair fits the learned model.

The model contains one layer of nonlinear, rate-coded feature detectors. Given an observed data vector, the exact posterior distribution over their activities can be inferred quickly, without iterative computation or approximation. This property makes the hidden-feature inference step particularly direct within the proposed architecture.

Learning compares pixel–feature correlations in two phases: one while observing real images, and another while observing reconstructions generated from feature activity. The difference between these phases supplies the basis for adjusting detector weights. The authors describe the learning algorithm as unsupervised and report favorable comparisons with methods in the literature. The contribution combines pair-based recognition with a generative model whose feature inference is exact and rapid.
summary.tldr: A generative model recognizes faces by scoring same-person image pairs and permits rapid, exact inference of hidden feature activities.

title: Rate-coded Restricted Boltzmann Machines for Face Recognition

abstract: Psychologists call behavior intrinsically motivated when it is engaged in for its own sake rather than as a step toward solving a specific problem of clear practical value. But what we learn during intrinsically motivated behavior is essential for our development as competent autonomous entities able to efficiently solve a wide range of practical problems as they arise. In this paper we present initial results from a computational study of intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning aimed at allowing artificial agents to construct and extend hierarchies of reusable skills that are needed for competent autonomy.
originalAbstract: Psychologists call behavior intrinsically motivated when it is engaged in for its own sake rather than as a step toward solving a specific problem of clear practical value. But what we learn during intrinsically motivated behavior is essential for our development as competent autonomous entities able to efficiently solve a wide range of practical problems as they arise. In this paper we present initial results from a computational study of intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning aimed at allowing artificial agents to construct and extend hierarchies of reusable skills that are needed for competent autonomy.

paragraphs: The paper explores learning driven by activity pursued for its own sake. The psychological motivation is that behavior without an immediate practical objective can still develop abilities that become useful later. This raises a computational question: how can an artificial agent learn capabilities before it faces a specific problem requiring them?

The authors investigate intrinsically motivated reinforcement learning as a way for agents to construct and extend hierarchies of reusable skills. Reusability is central to the goal because a learned capability could support more than one future task. Organizing skills hierarchically gives the study a focus on structured competence that an agent can continue to develop.

The paper reports initial results from this computational investigation. Its intended destination is competent autonomy: agents able to address a broad range of practical problems efficiently as those problems arise. The results are presented as an early step toward that objective, with the emphasis on developing reusable skills through intrinsic motivation.
summary.tldr: An initial computational study explores intrinsic motivation as a way for reinforcement-learning agents to build hierarchies of reusable skills.

title: Intrinsically Motivated Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose consensus propagation, an asynchronous distributed protocol for averaging numbers across a network. We establish convergence, characterize the convergence rate for regular graphs, and demonstrate that the protocol exhibits better scaling properties than pairwise averaging, an alternative that has received much recent attention. Consensus propagation can be viewed as a special case of belief propagation, and our results contribute to the belief propagation literature. In particular, beyond singly-connected graphs, there are very few classes of relevant problems for which belief propagation is known to converge.
originalAbstract: We propose consensus propagation, an asynchronous distributed protocol for averaging numbers across a network. We establish convergence, characterize the convergence rate for regular graphs, and demonstrate that the protocol exhibits better scaling properties than pairwise averaging, an alternative that has received much recent attention. Consensus propagation can be viewed as a special case of belief propagation, and our results contribute to the belief propagation literature. In particular, beyond singly-connected graphs, there are very few classes of relevant problems for which belief propagation is known to converge.

paragraphs: Consensus propagation addresses the problem of averaging numbers distributed across a network. The authors propose an asynchronous distributed protocol, allowing the computation to proceed without requiring every part of the network to update in lockstep. The goal is agreement on an average through a networked procedure.

The paper establishes convergence and characterizes the convergence rate for regular graphs. It also demonstrates better scaling properties than pairwise averaging, another approach to the same problem. The distinction between these findings matters: convergence is established, while the stated rate characterization specifically concerns regular graphs. The scaling comparison explains why the protocol is of computational interest.

The method can also be understood as a special case of belief propagation. This gives the averaging result a second role as evidence about when belief propagation converges. The authors emphasize that relevant convergence results beyond singly connected graphs are scarce. Their contribution therefore joins a distributed averaging algorithm with a convergence result for a particular class of belief propagation problems.
summary.tldr: Consensus propagation provides convergent asynchronous network averaging and demonstrates better scaling than pairwise averaging.

title: Consensus Propagation

abstract: Techniques such as probabilistic topic models and latent-semantic indexing have been shown to be broadly useful at automatically extracting the topical or semantic content of documents, or more generally for dimension-reduction of sparse count data. These types of models and algorithms can be viewed as generating an abstraction from the words in a document to a lower-dimensional latent variable representation that captures what the document is generally about beyond the specific words it contains. In this paper we propose a new probabilistic model that tempers this approach by representing each document as a combination of (a) a background distribution over common words, (b) a mixture distribution over general topics, and (c) a distribution over words that are treated as being specific to that document. We illustrate how this model can be used for information retrieval by matching documents both at a general topic level and at a specific word level, providing an advantage over techniques that only match documents at a general level (such as topic models or latent-sematic indexing) or that only match documents at the specific word level (such as TF-IDF).

These types of models and algorithms can be viewed as generating an abstraction from the words in a document to a lower-dimensional latent variable representation that captures what the document is generally about beyond the specific words it contains. In this paper we propose a new probabilistic model that tempers this approach by representing each document as a combination of (a) a background distribution over common words, (b) a mixture distribution over general topics, and (c) a distribution over words that are treated as being specific to that document. We illustrate how this model can be used for information retrieval by matching documents both at a general topic level and at a specific word level, providing an advantage over techniques that only match documents at a general level (such as topic models or latent-sematic indexing) or that only match documents at the specific word level (such as TF-IDF).

paragraphs: A document can resemble another because they discuss the same broad subject, because they share particular words, or both. Topic models capture general subject matter by reducing a document to a smaller latent representation. This paper argues for retaining document-specific vocabulary alongside that abstraction when representing documents for retrieval.

The proposed probabilistic model separates a document into three components. One distribution accounts for common background words, a mixture of topics represents general content, and another distribution captures words treated as specific to that document. This gives shared vocabulary, broad themes, and document-specific wording distinct places in the same model.

The authors illustrate retrieval that matches documents at both the topic level and the specific-word level. They report an advantage over methods that use only general representations, such as topic models and latent-semantic indexing, or only word-level matching, such as TF-IDF. The stated benefit comes from combining these two kinds of evidence so that broad semantic similarity and particular wording can both contribute to a match.
summary.tldr: A three-part document model combines background words, general topics, and document-specific vocabulary to improve retrieval matching.

title: Modeling General and Specific Aspects of Documents with a Probabilistic Topic Model

abstract: We present a method for learning max-weight matching predictors in bipartite graphs. The method consists of performing maximum a posteriori estimation in exponential families with sufficient statistics that encode permutations and data features. Although inference is in general hard, we show that for one very relevant application - document ranking - exact inference is efficient. For general model instances, an appropriate sampler is readily available. Contrary to existing max-margin matching models, our approach is statistically consistent and, in addition, experiments with increasing sample sizes indicate superior improvement over such models. We apply the method to graph matching in computer vision as well as to a standard benchmark dataset for learning document ranking, in which we obtain state-of-the-art results, in particular improving on max-margin variants. The drawback of this method with respect to max-margin alternatives is its runtime for large graphs, which is high comparatively.

paragraphs: The paper learns predictors that choose maximum-weight matchings in bipartite graphs. Its probabilistic model uses an exponential family whose sufficient statistics encode both permutations and observed features. Learning proceeds through maximum a posteriori estimation, connecting the matching problem to a statistical model of possible assignments.

Inference is generally difficult, but the authors identify document ranking as an important application where exact inference is efficient. For general instances, they describe an available sampling approach. This distinction matters because the computational demands depend on the structure of the application, even within the same modeling framework.

The authors establish statistical consistency for their approach and report that its performance improves more favorably with growing sample size than existing max-margin matching models. Applications include computer-vision matching and a standard document-ranking benchmark, where they obtain leading results and improve on max-margin variants. The stated tradeoff is runtime: on large graphs, the method is comparatively expensive relative to max-margin alternatives.
summary.tldr: A statistically consistent probabilistic matching model achieves strong ranking results, with efficient exact ranking inference but comparatively high runtime on large graphs.

title: Exponential Family Graph Matching and Ranking

abstract: The Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle selects the model that has the shortest code for data plus model. We show that for a countable class of models, MDL predictions are close to the true distribution in a strong sense. The result is completely general. No independence, ergodicity, stationarity, identifiability, or other assumption on the model class need to be made. More formally, we show that for any countable class of models, the distributions selected by MDL (or MAP) asymptotically predict (merge with) the true measure in the class in total variation distance. Implications for non-i.i.d. domains like time-series forecasting, discriminative learning, and reinforcement learning are discussed.
originalAbstract: The Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle selects the model that has the shortest code for data plus model. We show that for a countable class of models, MDL predictions are close to the true distribution in a strong sense. The result is completely general. No independence, ergodicity, stationarity, identifiability, or other assumption on the model class need to be made. More formally, we show that for any countable class of models, the distributions selected by MDL (or MAP) asymptotically predict (merge with) the true measure in the class in total variation distance. Implications for non-i.i.d. domains like time-series forecasting, discriminative learning, and reinforcement learning are discussed.

paragraphs: Minimum Description Length chooses a model by balancing the code needed to describe the model against the code needed to describe the data under it. This paper investigates the predictive consequences of that selection rule. Its central result concerns a countable collection of candidate models that contains the true data-generating probability measure.

Under that setting, the predictions of models selected by MDL, or by MAP, asymptotically merge with the true measure in total variation distance. Total variation measures discrepancies across events, so this is a strong form of predictive agreement. The conclusion concerns predictions becoming accurate over time, without requiring that model selection settle on a uniquely identifiable explanation.

The theorem does not require independence, stationarity, ergodicity, or identifiability assumptions on the model class. That breadth makes it relevant to settings where observations have dependencies or their distribution changes over time. The paper discusses implications for time-series forecasting, discriminative learning, and reinforcement learning. The essential qualifications are that the candidate class is countable, includes the true measure, and the predictive guarantee is asymptotic.
summary.tldr: For a countable model class containing the truth, MDL or MAP predictions converge to the true measure in total variation without independence or stationarity assumptions.

title: Discrete MDL Predicts in Total Variation

abstract: The reinforcement learning community has explored many approaches to obtain- ing value estimates and models to guide decision making; these approaches, how- ever, do not usually provide a measure of confidence in the estimate. Accurate estimates of an agent’s confidence are useful for many applications, such as bi- asing exploration and automatically adjusting parameters to reduce dependence on parameter-tuning. Computing confidence intervals on reinforcement learning value estimates, however, is challenging because data generated by the agent- environment interaction rarely satisfies traditional assumptions. Samples of value- estimates are dependent, likely non-normally distributed and often limited, partic- ularly in early learning when confidence estimates are pivotal. In this work, we investigate how to compute robust confidences for value estimates in continuous Markov decision processes. We illustrate how to use bootstrapping to compute confidence intervals online under a changing policy (previously not possible) and prove validity under a few reasonable assumptions. We demonstrate the applica- bility of our confidence estimation algorithms with experiments on exploration, parameter estimation and tracking.

Computing confidence intervals on reinforcement learning value estimates, however, is challenging because data generated by the agent- environment interaction rarely satisfies traditional assumptions. Samples of value- estimates are dependent, likely non-normally distributed and often limited, partic- ularly in early learning when confidence estimates are pivotal. In this work, we investigate how to compute robust confidences for value estimates in continuous Markov decision processes. We illustrate how to use bootstrapping to compute confidence intervals online under a changing policy (previously not possible) and prove validity under a few reasonable assumptions. paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent needs estimates of future value to guide its decisions, but an estimate alone does not indicate how much confidence to place in it. Confidence information can help guide exploration and adjust parameters automatically. This paper studies how to obtain such information for value estimates in continuous-state Markov decision processes.

The statistical difficulty is that data from ongoing interaction rarely fit traditional assumptions. Value estimates are dependent, may have non-normal distributions, and can be based on very few observations early in learning. Moreover, the agent's policy changes as it learns. These features make conventional confidence-interval reasoning difficult precisely when uncertainty information can be especially useful.

The authors show how bootstrapping can compute confidence intervals online while the policy changes, and prove validity under a set of assumptions. They demonstrate applications to exploration, parameter estimation, and tracking. The contribution is a way to accompany evolving value estimates with statistically supported uncertainty estimates, connecting confidence assessment to practical decisions during learning.
summary.tldr: The paper develops bootstrap confidence intervals for online reinforcement learning with changing policies and proves their validity under assumptions.

title: Interval Estimation for Reinforcement-Learning Algorithms in Continuous-State Domains

abstract: Many machine learning and signal processing problems can be formulated as linearly constrained convex programs, which could be efficiently solved by the alternating direction method (ADM). However, usually the subproblems in ADM are easily solvable only when the linear mappings in the constraints are identities. To address this issue, we propose a linearized ADM (LADM) method by linearizing the quadratic penalty term and adding a proximal term when solving the subproblems. For fast convergence, we also allow the penalty to change adaptively according a novel update rule. We prove the global convergence of LADM with adaptive penalty (LADMAP). As an example, we apply LADMAP to solve low-rank representation (LRR), which is an important subspace clustering technique yet suffers from high computation cost. By combining LADMAP with a skinny SVD representation technique, we are able to reduce the complexity $O(n^3)$ of the original ADM based method to $O(rn^2)$, where $r$ and $n$ are the rank and size of the representation matrix, respectively, hence making LRR possible for large scale applications. Numerical experiments verify that for LRR our LADMAP based methods are much faster than state-of-the-art algorithms.

paragraphs: Many learning and signal-processing tasks become convex optimization problems with linear constraints. The alternating direction method can solve these efficiently, but its component subproblems are often easy only when the constraint mappings are identities. This paper modifies the method to handle the difficulty introduced by more general linear mappings.

The proposed algorithm linearizes the quadratic penalty term and adds a proximal term when solving each subproblem. It also adapts the penalty through a new update rule intended to accelerate convergence. The authors prove global convergence of this combined method, called LADMAP, establishing a theoretical foundation for the algorithmic changes.

The paper applies LADMAP to low-rank representation, a computationally demanding subspace-clustering technique. Combined with a skinny singular value decomposition representation, it reduces complexity from O(n³) to O(rn²), where n is the representation matrix size and r its rank. Numerical experiments report substantially faster performance than state-of-the-art LRR algorithms, supporting the method's use in larger-scale applications.
summary.tldr: LADMAP combines linearized updates and adaptive penalties with proven convergence and faster low-rank representation computation.

title: Linearized Alternating Direction Method with Adaptive Penalty for Low-Rank Representation

abstract: Subspace learning seeks a low dimensional representation of data that enables accurate reconstruction. However, in many applications, data is obtained from multiple sources rather than a single source (e.g. an object might be viewed by cameras at different angles, or a document might consist of text and images). The conditional independence of separate sources imposes constraints on their shared latent representation, which, if respected, can improve the quality of the learned low dimensional representation. In this paper, we present a convex formulation of multi-view subspace learning that enforces conditional independence while reducing dimensionality. For this formulation, we develop an efficient algorithm that recovers an optimal data reconstruction by exploiting an implicit convex regularizer, then recovers the corresponding latent representation and reconstruction model, jointly and optimally. Experiments illustrate that the proposed method produces high quality results.

paragraphs: Subspace learning compresses data into a low-dimensional representation while preserving the ability to reconstruct it accurately. When observations come from multiple sources, such as different camera angles or text paired with images, the representation must account for relationships across those sources. The paper focuses on conditional independence constraints imposed on their shared latent representation.

The authors formulate multi-view subspace learning as a convex problem that enforces these constraints while reducing dimensionality. Respecting the structure of the separate views can improve the learned representation. Their algorithm exploits an implicit convex regularizer to obtain an optimal reconstruction, making the structural constraint part of the optimization rather than an informal modeling preference.

The procedure then jointly and optimally recovers the corresponding latent representation and reconstruction model. These optimality claims concern the proposed formulation. Experiments illustrate high-quality results, supporting the usefulness of combining reconstruction, dimensionality reduction, and conditional independence in a single framework. The contribution is both a structured way to combine views and an efficient algorithm for solving that formulation.
summary.tldr: A convex formulation learns compact representations from multiple data sources while enforcing conditional independence and optimizing reconstruction.

title: Convex Multi-view Subspace Learning

abstract: We show a principled way of deriving online learning algorithms from a minimax analysis. Various upper bounds on the minimax value, previously thought to be non-constructive, are shown to yield algorithms. This allows us to seamlessly recover known methods and to derive new ones, also capturing such ''unorthodox'' methods as Follow the Perturbed Leader and the R^2 forecaster. Understanding the inherent complexity of the learning problem thus leads to the development of algorithms. To illustrate our approach, we present several new algorithms, including a family of randomized methods that use the idea of a ''random play out''. New versions of the Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader algorithms are presented, as well as methods based on the Littlestone's dimension, efficient methods for matrix completion with trace norm, and algorithms for the problems of transductive learning and prediction with static experts.

paragraphs: The paper presents a way to turn minimax analysis into online learning algorithms. A minimax value describes a learning problem through its worst-case difficulty. Upper bounds on that value can seem to offer only theoretical reassurance, but the authors show that various such bounds also contain enough structure to construct actual learning procedures.

Their approach recovers known algorithms and produces new ones within the same framework. It accommodates methods such as Follow the Perturbed Leader and the R² forecaster. A new family of randomized algorithms uses random play out, illustrating how randomization can enter an algorithm derived from an analysis of the problem's value.

The examples include new Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader variants, methods based on Littlestone's dimension, efficient trace-norm matrix completion methods, and algorithms for transductive learning and prediction with static experts. The main contribution is the connection between understanding a problem's inherent complexity and designing a learner. Bounds previously regarded as nonconstructive become tools for generating methods across several online-learning settings.
summary.tldr: Upper bounds from minimax analysis can construct online learning algorithms, recovering established methods and generating new randomized ones.

title: Relax and Randomize : From Value to Algorithms

abstract: A new methodology is developed for joint analysis of a matrix and accompanying documents, with the documents associated with the matrix rows/columns. The documents are modeled with a focused topic model, inferring latent binary features (topics) for each document. A new matrix decomposition is developed, with latent binary features associated with the rows/columns, and with imposition of a low-rank constraint. The matrix decomposition and topic model are coupled by sharing the latent binary feature vectors associated with each. The model is applied to roll-call data, with the associated documents defined by the legislation. State-of-the-art results are manifested for prediction of votes on a new piece of legislation, based only on the observed text legislation. The coupling of the text and legislation is also demonstrated to yield insight into the properties of the matrix decomposition for roll-call data.

paragraphs: Matrices often come with documents describing their rows or columns. This paper develops a model that analyzes both sources together. A focused topic model represents each document through hidden binary features indicating topics, while a new matrix decomposition assigns binary features to rows or columns and imposes a low-rank constraint.

The two models are connected by sharing their binary feature vectors. This gives the text analysis and matrix decomposition a common representation, so the documents participate directly in how the matrix is modeled. The low-rank constraint adds structure to the matrix component, while the shared topic features establish the link between textual content and matrix patterns.

The authors apply the method to roll-call voting data, using legislation as the associated text. They report state-of-the-art prediction of votes on new legislation using only its observed text. This is a meaningful use of the coupling: text can support predictions for legislation whose votes are not yet available. The authors also show that the connection to legislative text helps explain properties of the learned matrix decomposition.
summary.tldr: Shared binary topic features connect documents to a low-rank matrix model, enabling vote prediction for new legislation from its text.

title: Joint Modeling of a Matrix with Associated Text via Latent Binary Features

abstract: Keypoint matching between pairs of images using popular descriptors like SIFT or a faster variant called SURF is at the heart of many computer vision algorithms including recognition, mosaicing, and structure from motion. For real-time mobile applications, very fast but less accurate descriptors like BRIEF and related methods use a random sampling of pairwise comparisons of pixel intensities in an image patch. Here, we introduce Locally Uniform Comparison Image Descriptor (LUCID), a simple description method based on permutation distances between the ordering of intensities of RGB values between two patches. LUCID is computable in linear time with respect to patch size and does not require floating point computation. An analysis reveals an underlying issue that limits the potential of BRIEF and related approaches compared to LUCID. Experiments demonstrate that LUCID is faster than BRIEF, and its accuracy is directly comparable to SURF while being more than an order of magnitude faster.

paragraphs: Matching keypoints across images requires a compact description of each surrounding image patch. Such descriptors support recognition, image mosaicing, and structure from motion, but their computation can be costly for real-time mobile use. This paper introduces LUCID, a simple descriptor intended to combine inexpensive computation with strong matching accuracy.

LUCID compares the ordering of RGB intensity values in two patches using permutation distances. Its computation grows linearly with patch size and does not require floating point arithmetic. This differs from BRIEF and related methods, which describe patches through randomly sampled pairwise intensity comparisons. The authors also provide an analysis identifying an issue that limits those methods relative to LUCID.

In the reported experiments, LUCID is faster than BRIEF. Its accuracy is directly comparable to SURF while its speed exceeds SURF by more than an order of magnitude. These results make the intensity-ordering representation practically significant: the descriptor achieves a favorable combination of speed and accuracy in the evaluations, rather than requiring accuracy to be sacrificed simply to obtain cheap computation.
summary.tldr: LUCID compares patch intensity orderings, achieving SURF-comparable accuracy at more than ten times its speed in the reported experiments.

title: Locally Uniform Comparison Image Descriptor

abstract: The problem of matching not just two, but m different sets of objects to each other arises in a variety of contexts, including finding the correspondence between feature points across multiple images in computer vision. At present it is usually solved by matching the sets pairwise, in series. In contrast, we propose a new method, permutation synchronization, which finds all the matchings jointly, in one shot, via a relaxation to eigenvector decomposition. The resulting algorithm is both computationally efficient, and, as we demonstrate with theoretical arguments as well as experimental results, much more stable to noise than previous methods.
originalAbstract: The problem of matching not just two, but m different sets of objects to each other arises in a variety of contexts, including finding the correspondence between feature points across multiple images in computer vision. At present it is usually solved by matching the sets pairwise, in series. In contrast, we propose a new method, permutation synchronization, which finds all the matchings jointly, in one shot, via a relaxation to eigenvector decomposition. The resulting algorithm is both computationally efficient, and, as we demonstrate with theoretical arguments as well as experimental results, much more stable to noise than previous methods.

paragraphs: Matching objects across several sets arises when, for example, corresponding feature points must be identified across multiple images. A common approach solves a sequence of pairwise matching problems. This paper treats the collection of matchings as a joint problem, aiming to determine the correspondences among all sets together.

The proposed method is permutation synchronization. It represents the matching task through permutations and uses a relaxation that leads to an eigenvector decomposition. That converts the joint formulation into a computationally efficient procedure, allowing information from the collection of sets to participate in one combined matching calculation.

The authors support the method with both theoretical arguments and experiments, reporting substantially greater stability to noise than previous methods. This is the central benefit beyond computational efficiency: the joint solution makes multi-set correspondence more robust in the reported analysis and evaluations. The paper therefore contributes both a different formulation of matching and an efficient route for solving its relaxed form, with evidence that the joint treatment improves noise tolerance.
summary.tldr: Permutation synchronization jointly matches multiple object sets through an eigenvector relaxation, with theoretical and experimental support for improved noise stability.

title: Solving the multi-way matching problem by permutation synchronization

abstract: We demonstrate that there is significant redundancy in the parameterization of several deep learning models. Given only a few weight values for each feature it is possible to accurately predict the remaining values. Moreover, we show that not only can the parameter values be predicted, but many of them need not be learned at all. We train several different architectures by learning only a small number of weights and predicting the rest. In the best case we are able to predict more than 95% of the weights of a network without any drop in accuracy.
originalAbstract: We demonstrate that there is significant redundancy in the parameterization of several deep learning models. Given only a few weight values for each feature it is possible to accurately predict the remaining values. Moreover, we show that not only can the parameter values be predicted, but many of them need not be learned at all. We train several different architectures by learning only a small number of weights and predicting the rest. In the best case we are able to predict more than 95% of the weights of a network without any drop in accuracy.

paragraphs: A deep learning model can contain many weight values, but this paper shows that those values need not all carry independent information. Across several models, the authors find substantial redundancy in the parameterization. Knowing only a few weights associated with a feature can be enough to accurately predict its remaining weights.

The paper takes this observation beyond predicting parameters that have already been learned. The authors train several architectures by learning only a small number of weights and predicting the others. This changes which parameters must be learned directly during training while still supplying values for the rest of the network.

In the strongest reported case, more than 95 percent of the network's weights are predicted without a drop in accuracy. That figure describes the best case, rather than a guarantee for every architecture. The broader finding is that several tested models contain enough parameter redundancy for prediction to replace much of direct weight learning while retaining useful predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Several deep models can learn only a small share of their weights and predict the rest, exceeding 95 percent predicted weights in the best case without accuracy loss.

title: Predicting Parameters in Deep Learning

abstract: Given a convergent sequence of graphs, there exists a limit object called the graphon from which random graphs are generated. This nonparametric perspective of random graphs opens the door to study graphs beyond the traditional parametric models, but at the same time also poses the challenging question of how to estimate the graphon underlying observed graphs. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient algorithm to estimate a graphon from a set of observed graphs generated from it. We show that, by approximating the graphon with stochastic block models, the graphon can be consistently estimated, that is, the estimation error vanishes as the size of the graph approaches infinity.

paragraphs: A graphon is a limiting object associated with a convergent sequence of graphs and can generate random graphs. It provides a nonparametric way to describe network structure beyond a fixed parametric model. This paper addresses the estimation problem that comes with that flexibility: recovering the underlying graphon from observed graphs.

The authors propose a computationally efficient algorithm based on approximating the graphon with stochastic block models. The block-model representation supplies a structured approximation to an otherwise more general object. This connects a tractable modeling approach to the broader goal of estimating a nonparametric source of random graphs.

The main theoretical result is consistency: the graphon can be estimated so that the estimation error tends to zero as graph size tends to infinity. The observations in the stated problem are a set of graphs generated from the underlying graphon. The result establishes a large-graph recovery guarantee for the approximation strategy. Its significance is that computationally manageable block models can serve as a route toward recovering this more flexible underlying network description.
summary.tldr: An efficient stochastic-blockmodel approximation consistently estimates a graphon as the size of generated graphs grows.

title: Stochastic blockmodel approximation of a graphon: Theory and consistent estimation

abstract: We analyze skip-gram with negative-sampling (SGNS), a word embedding method introduced by Mikolov et al., and show that it is implicitly factorizing a word-context matrix, whose cells are the pointwise mutual information (PMI) of the respective word and context pairs, shifted by a global constant. We find that another embedding method, NCE, is implicitly factorizing a similar matrix, where each cell is the (shifted) log conditional probability of a word given its context. We show that using a sparse Shifted Positive PMI word-context matrix to represent words improves results on two word similarity tasks and one of two analogy tasks. When dense low-dimensional vectors are preferred, exact factorization with SVD can achieve solutions that are at least as good as SGNS's solutions for word similarity tasks. On analogy questions SGNS remains superior to SVD. We conjecture that this stems from the weighted nature of SGNS's factorization.

We find that another embedding method, NCE, is implicitly factorizing a similar matrix, where each cell is the (shifted) log conditional probability of a word given its context. paragraphs: The paper explains word embedding methods through the matrices they implicitly factorize. For skip-gram with negative sampling, the matrix contains word-context pointwise mutual information values shifted by a global constant. For noise-contrastive estimation, it contains shifted log probabilities of a word conditional on its context. This connects neural embedding objectives to explicit statistical representations.

The authors then examine representations built from these insights. A sparse matrix of shifted positive PMI values improves results on two word similarity tasks and one of two analogy tasks. When compact, dense vectors are needed, singular value decomposition can produce solutions at least as good as those from skip-gram with negative sampling on the word similarity tasks.

The task distinction is important: skip-gram with negative sampling remains better than SVD on analogy questions. The authors conjecture that its weighted factorization explains this advantage; they do not establish that explanation as a finding. The paper therefore offers both an interpretation of embedding objectives and evidence that the choice of factorization or representation has different consequences across evaluation tasks.
summary.tldr: SGNS implicitly factorizes shifted PMI, connecting neural embeddings to matrix methods whose relative performance differs between similarity and analogy tasks.

title: Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization

abstract: The goal of hierarchical clustering is to construct a cluster tree, which can be viewed as the modal structure of a density. For this purpose, we use a convex optimization program that can efficiently estimate a family of hierarchical dense sets in high-dimensional distributions. We further extend existing graph-based methods to approximate the cluster tree of a distribution. By avoiding direct density estimation, our method is able to handle high-dimensional data more efficiently than existing density-based approaches. We present empirical results that demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing ones.
originalAbstract: The goal of hierarchical clustering is to construct a cluster tree, which can be viewed as the modal structure of a density. For this purpose, we use a convex optimization program that can efficiently estimate a family of hierarchical dense sets in high-dimensional distributions. We further extend existing graph-based methods to approximate the cluster tree of a distribution. By avoiding direct density estimation, our method is able to handle high-dimensional data more efficiently than existing density-based approaches. We present empirical results that demonstrate the superiority of our method over existing ones.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering aims to describe groups at multiple levels of detail through a cluster tree. This paper takes a density-based view of that tree: its organization reflects the modes, or concentrations, of the underlying distribution. The computational challenge is to recover that organization efficiently when observations have many dimensions.

The proposed method uses convex optimization to estimate a family of hierarchical dense sets. These sets provide information about where the distribution concentrates without requiring a direct estimate of its entire density. The authors also extend graph-based methods to turn that information into an approximation of the distribution's cluster tree.

The approach matters because the desired output is the hierarchy of clusters, so estimating dense regions can target that output more directly. The abstract reports better efficiency on high-dimensional data than existing density-based approaches, along with empirical results favoring the proposed method over existing alternatives. Together, these findings support using hierarchical dense-set estimation as a practical route to cluster trees in the settings examined.
summary.tldr: Convex estimation of hierarchical dense sets supports efficient cluster-tree approximation without directly estimating the full density.

title: Approximating Hierarchical MV-sets for Hierarchical Clustering

abstract: In classical reinforcement learning agents accept arbitrary short term loss for long term gain when exploring their environment. This is infeasible for safety critical applications such as robotics, where even a single unsafe action may cause system failure or harm the environment. In this paper, we address the problem of safely exploring finite Markov decision processes (MDP). We define safety in terms of an a priori unknown safety constraint that depends on states and actions and satisfies certain regularity conditions expressed via a Gaussian process prior. We develop a novel algorithm, SAFEMDP, for this task and prove that it completely explores the safely reachable part of the MDP without violating the safety constraint. To achieve this, it cautiously explores safe states and actions in order to gain statistical confidence about the safety of unvisited state-action pairs from noisy observations collected while navigating the environment. Moreover, the algorithm explicitly considers reachability when exploring the MDP, ensuring that it does not get stuck in any state with no safe way out. We demonstrate our method on digital terrain models for the task of exploring an unknown map with a rover.

paragraphs: Exploration can be unacceptable when a single unsafe action risks failure or environmental harm. This paper studies exploration in finite Markov decision processes with an initially unknown safety constraint depending on states and actions. The constraint has regularity properties represented through a Gaussian process prior.

The proposed SAFEMDP algorithm gathers noisy observations while cautiously visiting safe states and taking safe actions. It uses those observations to build statistical confidence about state-action pairs it has not visited. It also considers reachability explicitly, including whether a state has a safe way out, so exploration does not trap the agent.

Under the stated safety framework and regularity conditions, the authors prove that SAFEMDP completely explores the safely reachable portion of the process without breaking the constraint. The scope is the safely reachable region, with the guarantee relying on the modeling assumptions. A rover exploring an unknown map represented by digital terrain models demonstrates the approach, linking uncertainty about local safety with the need to preserve safe movement through the environment.
summary.tldr: Under its regularity assumptions, SAFEMDP explores the safely reachable region while learning unknown constraints and preserving safe escape routes.

title: Safe Exploration in Finite Markov Decision Processes with Gaussian Processes

abstract: Deep kernel learning combines the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods with the inductive biases of deep learning architectures. We propose a novel deep kernel learning model and stochastic variational inference procedure which generalizes deep kernel learning approaches to enable classification, multi-task learning, additive covariance structures, and stochastic gradient training. Specifically, we apply additive base kernels to subsets of output features from deep neural architectures, and jointly learn the parameters of the base kernels and deep network through a Gaussian process marginal likelihood objective. Within this framework, we derive an efficient form of stochastic variational inference which leverages local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and structure exploiting algebra. We show improved performance over stand alone deep networks, SVMs, and state of the art scalable Gaussian processes on several classification benchmarks, including an airline delay dataset containing 6 million training points, CIFAR, and ImageNet.
originalAbstract: Deep kernel learning combines the non-parametric flexibility of kernel methods with the inductive biases of deep learning architectures. We propose a novel deep kernel learning model and stochastic variational inference procedure which generalizes deep kernel learning approaches to enable classification, multi-task learning, additive covariance structures, and stochastic gradient training. Specifically, we apply additive base kernels to subsets of output features from deep neural architectures, and jointly learn the parameters of the base kernels and deep network through a Gaussian process marginal likelihood objective. Within this framework, we derive an efficient form of stochastic variational inference which leverages local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and structure exploiting algebra. We show improved performance over stand alone deep networks, SVMs, and state of the art scalable Gaussian processes on several classification benchmarks, including an airline delay dataset containing 6 million training points, CIFAR, and ImageNet.

paragraphs: The paper combines deep networks with kernel methods, aiming to retain the representation biases of neural architectures and the nonparametric flexibility of kernels. It extends deep kernel learning to support classification, multitask learning, additive covariance structures, and stochastic gradient training. These capabilities broaden both the tasks and the training procedures available within the framework.

The model applies additive base kernels to subsets of features produced by a deep network. Kernel parameters and network parameters are learned jointly through a Gaussian process marginal-likelihood objective. Its stochastic variational inference procedure uses local kernel interpolation, inducing points, and algebra that exploits structure to make the combined model computationally manageable.

Experiments report improved performance over standalone deep networks, support vector machines, and state-of-the-art scalable Gaussian processes on several classification benchmarks. These include an airline-delay dataset with six million training examples, CIFAR, and ImageNet. The findings support both the predictive value and the demonstrated scale of the combined approach, while the inference contribution explains how the richer model can be trained stochastically.
summary.tldr: Jointly trained deep features and additive Gaussian process kernels support scalable stochastic learning and improve results on several classification benchmarks.

title: Stochastic Variational Deep Kernel Learning

abstract: We study the effectiveness of neural sequence models for premise selection in automated theorem proving, a key bottleneck for progress in formalized mathematics. We propose a two stage approach for this task that yields good results for the premise selection task on the Mizar corpus while avoiding the hand-engineered features of existing state-of-the-art models. To our knowledge, this is the first time deep learning has been applied theorem proving on a large scale.
originalAbstract: We study the effectiveness of neural sequence models for premise selection in automated theorem proving, a key bottleneck for progress in formalized mathematics. We propose a two stage approach for this task that yields good results for the premise selection task on the Mizar corpus while avoiding the hand-engineered features of existing state-of-the-art models. To our knowledge, this is the first time deep learning has been applied theorem proving on a large scale.

paragraphs: Automated theorem proving depends on selecting useful premises from the mathematical material available to it. The paper focuses on this selection task, which the authors describe as a major bottleneck for formalized mathematics. Its central question is whether neural sequence models can learn to identify relevant premises effectively.

The proposed approach has two stages and uses deep sequence modeling without the hand-engineered features employed by existing state-of-the-art models. This makes learned representations central to the selection process. The contribution concerns an important component of theorem proving: choosing mathematical information that can support a proof attempt, rather than claiming that premise selection alone completes the proof.

The authors report good premise-selection results on the Mizar corpus and, to their knowledge, the first large-scale application of deep learning to theorem proving. These findings support the usefulness of sequence models for this particular bottleneck. The broader significance is a demonstrated route toward learning premise-selection behavior from formal mathematical material without requiring the same manually designed feature representations.
summary.tldr: DeepMath uses a two-stage neural sequence approach to select theorem-proving premises, reporting good Mizar results without hand-engineered features.

title: DeepMath - Deep Sequence Models for Premise Selection

abstract: Asynchronous-parallel algorithms have the potential to vastly speed up algorithms by eliminating costly synchronization. However, our understanding of these algorithms is limited because the current convergence theory of asynchronous block coordinate descent algorithms is based on somewhat unrealistic assumptions. In particular, the age of the shared optimization variables being used to update blocks is assumed to be independent of the block being updated. Additionally, it is assumed that the updates are applied to randomly chosen blocks. In this paper, we argue that these assumptions either fail to hold or will imply less efficient implementations. We then prove the convergence of asynchronous-parallel block coordinate descent under more realistic assumptions, in particular, always without the independence assumption. The analysis permits both the deterministic (essentially) cyclic and random rules for block choices. Because a bound on the asynchronous delays may or may not be available, we establish convergence for both bounded delays and unbounded delays. The analysis also covers nonconvex, weakly convex, and strongly convex functions. The convergence theory involves a Lyapunov function that directly incorporates both objective progress and delays. A continuous-time ODE is provided to motivate the construction at a high level.

paragraphs: Asynchronous block coordinate descent lets parallel workers update parts of an optimization problem without waiting for one another. That can avoid costly synchronization, but workers may act on outdated shared variables. The paper examines convergence theory whose assumptions about those outdated values and update choices can conflict with practical implementations.

In particular, earlier analyses assume that the age of a worker’s information is independent of the block it updates, and that blocks are selected randomly. The authors remove the independence requirement throughout their analysis. They also accommodate both random selection and essentially cyclic deterministic selection, bringing the theory closer to a broader range of update schedules.

The convergence results cover settings with bounded or unbounded delays and include nonconvex, weakly convex, and strongly convex objectives under the analyzed assumptions. A Lyapunov function tracks both progress on the objective and the effects of delays. A continuous-time differential equation motivates this construction, helping explain how stale information can be incorporated directly into a convergence argument.
summary.tldr: The paper proves asynchronous coordinate descent convergence under broader update schedules and delay assumptions that better reflect practical implementations.

title: Asynchronous Coordinate Descent under More Realistic Assumptions

abstract: Recent progress in deep learning for audio synthesis opens the way to models that directly produce the waveform, shifting away from the traditional paradigm of relying on vocoders or MIDI synthesizers for speech or music generation. Despite their successes, current state-of-the-art neural audio synthesizers such as WaveNet and SampleRNN suffer from prohibitive training and inference times because they are based on autoregressive models that generate audio samples one at a time at a rate of 16kHz. In this work, we study the more computationally efficient alternative of generating the waveform frame-by-frame with large strides. We present a lightweight neural audio synthesizer for the original task of generating musical notes given desired instrument, pitch and velocity. Our model is trained end-to-end to generate notes from nearly 1000 instruments with a single decoder, thanks to a new loss function that minimizes the distances between the log spectrograms of the generated and target waveforms. On the generalization task of synthesizing notes for pairs of pitch and instrument not seen during training, SING produces audio with significantly improved perceptual quality compared to a state-of-the-art autoencoder based on WaveNet as measured by a Mean Opinion Score (MOS), and is about 32 times faster for training and 2, 500 times faster for inference.

paragraphs: SING generates musical note waveforms from a requested instrument, pitch, and velocity. The paper targets the high computational cost of neural audio models that produce one sample at a time. Its alternative generates audio frame by frame with large strides, reducing the sequential work involved in synthesizing a note.

The model is lightweight and trained end to end, using one decoder for nearly 1,000 instruments. A new loss compares the log spectrograms of generated and target waveforms. This gives training a way to measure discrepancies in the spectral representations of the sounds while the model directly produces the waveform.

The evaluation tests pitch-and-instrument combinations absent from training. Compared with a state-of-the-art WaveNet-based autoencoder, SING achieves significantly better perceptual quality as measured by Mean Opinion Score. It is also reported to train about 32 times faster and perform inference about 2,500 times faster. These findings show that the frame-based approach can combine substantial speed gains with improved perceived quality on the stated generalization task.
summary.tldr: SING synthesizes musical notes frame by frame, improving perceptual quality and greatly reducing computation in the reported WaveNet-autoencoder comparison.

title: SING: Symbol-to-Instrument Neural Generator

abstract: Semantic scene completion predicts volumetric occupancy and object category of a 3D scene, which helps intelligent agents to understand and interact with the surroundings. In this work, we propose a disentangled framework, sequentially carrying out 2D semantic segmentation, 2D-3D reprojection and 3D semantic scene completion. This three-stage framework has three advantages: (1) explicit semantic segmentation significantly boosts performance; (2) flexible fusion ways of sensor data bring good extensibility; (3) progress in any subtask will promote the holistic performance. Experimental results show that regardless of inputing a single depth or RGB-D, our framework can generate high-quality semantic scene completion, and outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on both synthetic and real datasets.
