paragraphs: Semantic scene completion predicts both which parts of a three-dimensional volume are occupied and which object categories occupy them. These predictions provide information that an intelligent agent can use to understand its surroundings. This paper organizes the task into a sequence of distinct stages, making intermediate semantic interpretation an explicit part of the process.

The framework first performs two-dimensional semantic segmentation, then reprojects that information into three dimensions, and finally completes the three-dimensional semantic scene. The authors identify explicit segmentation as a significant source of improved performance. The separation also allows flexible combinations of sensor data and creates opportunities for improvements in individual subtasks to benefit the overall system.

Experiments show high-quality completion from either a single depth input or RGB-D input. The framework outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on both synthetic and real datasets. These findings support the proposed decomposition as an effective architecture for the tested scene-completion settings, while the modular stages explain how it can accommodate sensor fusion and advances in its component tasks.
summary.tldr: Separating segmentation, reprojection, and 3D completion improves semantic scene reconstruction from depth or RGB-D inputs.

title: See and Think: Disentangling Semantic Scene Completion

abstract: We consider the case of derivative-free algorithms for non-convex optimization, also known as zero order algorithms, that use only function evaluations rather than gradients. For a wide variety of gradient approximators based on finite differences, we establish asymptotic convergence to second order stationary points using a carefully tailored application of the Stable Manifold Theorem. Regarding efficiency, we introduce a noisy zero-order method that converges to second order stationary points, i.e avoids saddle points. Our algorithm uses only $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1 / \epsilon^2)$ approximate gradient calculations and, thus, it matches the converge rate guarantees of their exact gradient counterparts up to constants. In contrast to previous work, our convergence rate analysis avoids imposing additional dimension dependent slowdowns in the number of iterations required for non-convex zero order optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies non-convex optimization when an algorithm can evaluate an objective but cannot directly obtain its gradients. Such derivative-free methods can estimate gradients from finite differences. The central question is whether these estimates allow algorithms to avoid saddle points efficiently, rather than merely reach places where first-order changes are small.

For a broad range of finite-difference gradient approximators, the authors establish asymptotic convergence to second-order stationary points. Their argument uses a tailored application of the Stable Manifold Theorem. They also introduce a noisy zero-order algorithm with a convergence-rate guarantee, extending the contribution from eventual behavior to the amount of optimization work required.

The noisy method requires approximately an inverse-square number of approximate gradient calculations in the target accuracy, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its guarantee matches the corresponding exact-gradient rate up to constants as stated in the abstract. The analysis avoids additional dimension-dependent penalties in iteration count. This distinction concerns iterations and approximate gradient calculations; it does not claim that every gradient approximation has dimension-independent evaluation cost.
summary.tldr: The paper proves saddle-avoidance guarantees for finite-difference methods and introduces a noisy algorithm with efficient iteration bounds.

title: Efficiently avoiding saddle points with zero order methods: No gradients required

abstract: We prove that $\Omega(s\log p)$ samples suffice to learn a sparse Gaussian directed acyclic graph (DAG) from data, where $s$ is the maximum Markov blanket size. This improves upon recent results that require $\Omega(s^{4}\log p)$ samples in the equal variance case. To prove this, we analyze a popular score-based estimator that has been the subject of extensive empirical inquiry in recent years and is known to achieve state-of-the-art results. Furthermore, the approach we study does not require strong assumptions such as faithfulness that existing theory for score-based learning crucially relies on. The resulting estimator is based around a difficult nonconvex optimization problem, and its analysis may be of independent interest given recent interest in nonconvex optimization in machine learning. Our analysis overcomes the drawbacks of existing theoretical analyses, which either fail to guarantee structure consistency in high-dimensions (i.e. learning the correct graph with high probability), or rely on restrictive assumptions. In contrast, we give explicit finite-sample bounds that are valid in the important $p\gg n$ regime.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph from data means recovering a network of directed statistical relationships without cycles. This paper analyzes a score-based estimator for sparse Gaussian graphs, with particular attention to settings where the number of variables exceeds the number of observations. The goal is structure consistency: recovering the correct graph with high probability.

The authors establish a sufficient sample bound with dependence proportional to s log p, where p counts variables and s is the maximum Markov blanket size. This improves on the cited s-to-the-fourth log p requirement in the equal-variance case. The result concerns how much data suffices for recovery; it does not state that this amount is necessary in every setting.

The analysis also avoids strong assumptions such as faithfulness that earlier score-based theory relied on. It provides explicit finite-sample bounds despite the estimator involving a difficult nonconvex optimization problem. The main advance is a statistical guarantee for a widely studied estimator, including the high-dimensional regime, rather than a claim that solving its optimization problem has become easy.
summary.tldr: The paper proves improved sufficient sample bounds for recovering sparse Gaussian DAGs with a score-based estimator, including high-dimensional settings.

title: Globally optimal score-based learning of directed acyclic graphs in high-dimensions

abstract: Blind image denoising is an important yet very challenging problem in computer vision due to the complicated acquisition process of real images. In this work we propose a new variational inference method, which integrates both noise estimation and image denoising into a unique Bayesian framework, for blind image denoising. Specifically, an approximate posterior, parameterized by deep neural networks, is presented by taking the intrinsic clean image and noise variances as latent variables conditioned on the input noisy image. This posterior provides explicit parametric forms for all its involved hyper-parameters, and thus can be easily implemented for blind image denoising with automatic noise estimation for the test noisy image. On one hand, as other data-driven deep learning methods, our method, namely variational denoising network (VDN), can perform denoising efficiently due to its explicit form of posterior expression. On the other hand, VDN inherits the advantages of traditional model-driven approaches, especially the good generalization capability of generative models. VDN has good interpretability and can be flexibly utilized to estimate and remove complicated non-i.i.d. noise collected in real scenarios. Comprehensive experiments are performed to substantiate the superiority of our method in blind image denoising.

paragraphs: Blind image denoising requires recovering a clean image while also dealing with noise whose properties are not supplied in advance. Real image acquisition can produce complicated noise, making that joint problem difficult. The Variational Denoising Network places noise estimation and image restoration within a single Bayesian framework rather than treating them as unrelated operations.

The method uses deep neural networks to parameterize an approximate posterior conditioned on the noisy input. Both the clean image and noise variances are latent variables to be inferred. Explicit parameterizations make the posterior practical to compute and allow the network to estimate noise automatically for a test image. This formulation gives the learned predictions an interpretation in terms of image content and noise.

The authors combine the efficiency of data-driven neural prediction with the generalization advantages they attribute to generative modeling. The model can estimate and remove complicated noise that is not independent and identically distributed. Comprehensive experiments support its reported superiority in blind denoising, illustrating the value of jointly modeling what the image contains and how its observations are corrupted.
summary.tldr: VDN jointly infers clean images and noise variances through a neural Bayesian model, enabling efficient blind denoising of complicated real-world noise.

title: Variational Denoising Network: Toward Blind Noise Modeling and Removal

abstract: Class probabilities predicted by most multiclass classifiers are uncalibrated, often tending towards over-confidence. With neural networks, calibration can be improved by temperature scaling, a method to learn a single corrective multiplicative factor for inputs to the last softmax layer. On non-neural models the existing methods apply binary calibration in a pairwise or one-vs-rest fashion. We propose a natively multiclass calibration method applicable to classifiers from any model class, derived from Dirichlet distributions and generalising the beta calibration method from binary classification. It is easily implemented with neural nets since it is equivalent to log-transforming the uncalibrated probabilities, followed by one linear layer and softmax. Experiments demonstrate improved probabilistic predictions according to multiple measures (confidence-ECE, classwise-ECE, log-loss, Brier score) across a wide range of datasets and classifiers. Parameters of the learned Dirichlet calibration map provide insights to the biases in the uncalibrated model.

paragraphs: A classifier can predict a class while assigning probabilities that are too confident. Calibration addresses the reliability of those probabilities. This paper proposes a correction designed directly for multiclass predictions, applicable to classifiers from any model class. It extends beyond temperature scaling, which learns a single corrective factor for the inputs to a neural network's final softmax layer.

The method, Dirichlet calibration, is derived from Dirichlet distributions and generalizes beta calibration from binary classification. Its implementation is straightforward: take logarithms of the predicted probabilities, apply a linear layer, and then apply softmax. This provides a multiclass correction without constructing it from separate pairwise or one-versus-rest binary calibration problems.

Experiments report improved probability predictions across a broad range of datasets and classifiers, measured using confidence-ECE, classwise-ECE, log-loss, and Brier score. The learned calibration parameters also offer information about biases in the original predictions. The method thus provides both a practical probability correction and a way to examine how a classifier's confidence needs adjustment.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet calibration provides a directly multiclass probability correction that improves calibration across diverse classifiers and datasets.

title: Beyond temperature scaling: Obtaining well-calibrated multi-class probabilities with Dirichlet calibration

abstract: In this paper, we propose one novel model for point cloud semantic segmentation,which exploits both the local and global structures within the point cloud based onthe contextual point representations. Specifically, we enrich each point represen-tation by performing one novel gated fusion on the point itself and its contextualpoints. Afterwards, based on the enriched representation, we propose one novelgraph pointnet module, relying on the graph attention block to dynamically com-pose and update each point representation within the local point cloud structure.Finally, we resort to the spatial-wise and channel-wise attention strategies to exploitthe point cloud global structure and thereby yield the resulting semantic label foreach point. Extensive results on the public point cloud databases, namely theS3DIS and ScanNet datasets, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model,outperforming the state-of-the-art approaches. Our code for this paper is available at https://github.com/fly519/ELGS.

paragraphs: Point-cloud semantic segmentation assigns a semantic label to each point in a three-dimensional collection. This paper builds point representations that incorporate both nearby structure and information from the wider point cloud. Its central idea is that a point's representation should be enriched by context before the model makes its final labeling decision.

The model first applies gated fusion to combine a point's own information with information from contextual points. A graph PointNet module then uses graph attention to compose and update representations within local structures. Finally, spatial-wise and channel-wise attention incorporate global structure, bringing broader context into the representations used to produce semantic labels.

Experiments on S3DIS and ScanNet report performance above state-of-the-art approaches. These results support the proposed combination of contextual fusion, local graph processing, and global attention. The architecture gives each of these stages a specific role: enriching individual points, modeling local relationships, and using information across the point cloud to support the final segmentation.
summary.tldr: Contextual fusion, local graph attention, and global attention improve point-cloud semantic segmentation on S3DIS and ScanNet.

title: Exploiting Local and Global Structure for Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation with Contextual Point Representations

abstract: Neural network models of memory and error correction famously include the Hopfield network, which can directly store---and error-correct through its dynamics---arbitrary N-bit patterns, but only for ~N such patterns. On the other end of the spectrum, Shannon's coding theory established that it is possible to represent exponentially many states (~e^N) using N symbols in such a way that an optimal decoder could correct all noise upto a threshold. We prove that it is possible to construct an associative content-addressable network that combines the properties of strong error correcting codes and Hopfield networks: it simultaneously possesses exponentially many stable states, these states are robust enough, with large enough basins of attraction that they can be correctly recovered despite errors in a finite fraction of all nodes, and the errors are intrinsically corrected by the network’s own dynamics. The network is a two-layer Boltzmann machine with simple neural dynamics, low dynamic-range (binary) pairwise synaptic connections, and sparse expander graph connectivity. Thus, quasi-random sparse structures---characteristic of important error-correcting codes---may provide for high-performance computation in artificial neural networks and the brain.

paragraphs: This paper connects associative memory with error-correcting codes. Hopfield networks can store patterns and repair corrupted versions through their own dynamics, but the abstract describes their capacity for arbitrary N-bit patterns as roughly proportional to N. Coding theory permits exponentially many represented states with strong error correction, provided an appropriate decoder is available.

The authors prove that a constructed network can combine exponential storage capacity with intrinsic correction. It has exponentially many stable states, each with a sufficiently large basin of attraction to recover from errors affecting a finite fraction of nodes. Recovery is performed by the network's dynamics, bringing the stored representation and its decoding mechanism into the same system.

The construction uses a two-layer Boltzmann machine, binary pairwise connections, and sparse expander connectivity. Its significance is an existence result showing that sparse, structured neural systems can support both high capacity and robust retrieval. The suggested relevance of such quasi-random connectivity to artificial networks and the brain remains a possibility, rather than a demonstrated biological conclusion.
summary.tldr: A sparse neural construction provably combines exponentially many stable memories with error correction performed by its own dynamics.

title: Bipartite expander Hopfield networks as self-decoding high-capacity error correcting codes

abstract: We study the problem of learning a series of tasks in a fully online Meta-Learning setting. The goal is to exploit similarities among the tasks to incrementally adapt an inner online algorithm in order to incur a low averaged cumulative error over the tasks. We focus on a family of inner algorithms based on a parametrized variant of online Mirror Descent. The inner algorithm is incrementally adapted by an online Mirror Descent meta-algorithm using the corresponding within-task minimum regularized empirical risk as the meta-loss. In order to keep the process fully online, we approximate the meta-subgradients by the online inner algorithm. An upper bound on the approximation error allows us to derive a cumulative error bound for the proposed method. Our analysis can also be converted to the statistical setting by online-to-batch arguments. We instantiate two examples of the framework in which the meta-parameter is either a common bias vector or feature map. Finally, preliminary numerical experiments confirm our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a sequence of tasks when both task learning and learning across tasks must happen online. The goal is to exploit similarities among tasks so that an inner learning algorithm improves incrementally, reducing average cumulative error across the sequence. Neither level of the process is treated as a purely offline stage.

The inner algorithms use a parameterized form of online mirror descent. An outer mirror-descent algorithm adapts their shared parameter using a meta-loss based on each task's minimum regularized empirical risk. To keep this outer update online, the method approximates the required meta-subgradients using information from the inner online algorithm.

The authors bound the approximation error and use that result to derive a cumulative-error guarantee. They also translate the analysis into a statistical setting through online-to-batch arguments. Examples learn either a shared bias vector or a feature map, and preliminary numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The framework connects incremental learning within tasks with incremental adaptation across them.
summary.tldr: Nested online mirror-descent algorithms adapt a shared learning strategy across tasks while preserving a fully online process.

title: Online-Within-Online Meta-Learning

abstract: We are interested in a framework of online learning with kernels for low-dimensional, but large-scale and potentially adversarial datasets. We study the computational and theoretical performance of online variations of kernel Ridge regression. Despite its simplicity, the algorithm we study is the first to achieve the optimal regret for a wide range of kernels with a per-round complexity of order $n^\alpha$ with $\alpha < 2$. The algorithm we consider is based on approximating the kernel with the linear span of basis functions. Our contributions are twofold: 1) For the Gaussian kernel, we propose to build the basis beforehand (independently of the data) through Taylor expansion. For $d$-dimensional inputs, we provide a (close to) optimal regret of order $O((\log n)^{d+1})$ with per-round time complexity and space complexity $O((\log n)^{2d})$. This makes the algorithm a suitable choice as soon as $n \gg e^d$ which is likely to happen in a scenario with small dimensional and large-scale dataset; 2) For general kernels with low effective dimension, the basis functions are updated sequentially, adapting to the data, by sampling Nyström points. In this case, our algorithm improves the computational trade-off known for online kernel regression.

The algorithm we consider is based on approximating the kernel with the linear span of basis functions. Our contributions are twofold: 1) For the Gaussian kernel, we propose to build the basis beforehand (independently of the data) through Taylor expansion. For $d$-dimensional inputs, we provide a (close to) optimal regret of order $O((\log n)^{d+1})$ with per-round time complexity and space complexity $O((\log n)^{2d})$. This makes the algorithm a suitable choice as soon as $n \gg e^d$ which is likely to happen in a scenario with small dimensional and large-scale dataset; 2) For general kernels with low effective dimension, the basis functions are updated sequentially, adapting to the data, by sampling Nyström points. In this case, our algorithm improves the computational trade-off known for online kernel regression.

paragraphs: Online kernel regression must repeatedly update predictions as data arrive, which can become computationally expensive for long sequences. This paper studies low-dimensional, large-scale datasets that may be adversarial. Its approach approximates the kernel using a span of basis functions, aiming to retain strong regret guarantees while reducing the work required at each round.

For Gaussian kernels, the basis is constructed before seeing data through a Taylor expansion. With n observations and d input dimensions, the authors obtain nearly optimal regret of order (log n)^(d+1), with per-round time and space of order (log n)^(2d). The stated favorable regime is n much larger than e^d, making the dependence on dimension central to its usefulness.

For more general kernels with low effective dimension, the method instead updates its basis sequentially by sampling Nyström points. This lets the approximation adapt to observed data. The paper reports an improved computational trade-off for online kernel regression and optimal regret for a wide range of kernels with per-round complexity below quadratic in n.
summary.tldr: Basis approximations make online kernel regression cheaper while retaining optimal or nearly optimal regret under the stated kernel and dimensionality conditions.

title: Efficient online learning with kernels for adversarial large scale problems

abstract: We present a flexible framework for learning predictive models that approximately satisfy the equalized odds notion of fairness. This is achieved by introducing a general discrepancy functional that rigorously quantifies violations of this criterion. This differentiable functional is used as a penalty driving the model parameters towards equalized odds. To rigorously evaluate fitted models, we develop a formal hypothesis test to detect whether a prediction rule violates this property, the first such test in the literature. Both the model fitting and hypothesis testing leverage a resampled version of the sensitive attribute obeying equalized odds, by construction. We demonstrate the applicability and validity of the proposed framework both in regression and multi-class classification problems, reporting improved performance over state-of-the-art methods. Lastly, we show how to incorporate techniques for equitable uncertainty quantification---unbiased for each group under study---to communicate the results of the data analysis in exact terms.

paragraphs: This paper develops a framework for training predictive models that approximately meet the equalized odds fairness criterion. It addresses both how to encourage the criterion during learning and how to evaluate a fitted model afterward. These are distinct tasks: a training objective can encourage fairness, while a statistical test assesses evidence of a violation.

The authors introduce a differentiable discrepancy measure that quantifies departures from equalized odds. Adding this measure as a penalty steers model parameters toward the criterion. Both training and testing use a resampled version of the sensitive attribute that satisfies equalized odds by construction, providing a common basis for the two procedures.

The evaluation component is a formal hypothesis test for violations, described as the first such test in the literature. Demonstrations cover regression and multiclass classification and report improved performance over existing leading methods. The framework also incorporates uncertainty quantification that is unbiased for each studied group, allowing reported analytical results to include group-equitable uncertainty information.
summary.tldr: Resampling sensitive attributes supports both a differentiable equalized odds training penalty and a formal test for fairness violations.

title: Achieving Equalized Odds by Resampling Sensitive Attributes

abstract: Learning object-centric representations of complex scenes is a promising step towards enabling efficient abstract reasoning from low-level perceptual features. Yet, most deep learning approaches learn distributed representations that do not capture the compositional properties of natural scenes. In this paper, we present the Slot Attention module, an architectural component that interfaces with perceptual representations such as the output of a convolutional neural network and produces a set of task-dependent abstract representations which we call slots. These slots are exchangeable and can bind to any object in the input by specializing through a competitive procedure over multiple rounds of attention. We empirically demonstrate that Slot Attention can extract object-centric representations that enable generalization to unseen compositions when trained on unsupervised object discovery and supervised property prediction tasks.

paragraphs: A scene contains distinct objects, but a neural network’s internal representation does not necessarily preserve that organization. This can make it harder to represent how familiar objects combine in new ways. Slot Attention is an architectural component that converts perceptual features, such as the output of a convolutional network, into a set of abstract representations called slots.

The slots are exchangeable: each can become associated with any object in the input. They specialize through several rounds of competitive attention, allowing the representations to organize around different parts of the scene. Their content is task-dependent, so the module provides a way to build object-oriented representations within a broader learning system.

The authors test Slot Attention on unsupervised object discovery and supervised property prediction. In these experiments, it extracts object-centric representations that support generalization to previously unseen compositions. The finding matters because compositional organization is built into the resulting representation: the system can represent objects as separate units whose combinations may change across scenes.
summary.tldr: Slot Attention turns perceptual features into exchangeable object-centered representations that empirically support generalization to unseen compositions.

title: Object-Centric Learning with Slot Attention

abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) are ubiquitous in modern 2D interfaces due to their ability to scale to different resolutions. However, despite the success of deep learning-based models applied to rasterized images, the problem of vector graphics representation learning and generation remains largely unexplored. In this work, we propose a novel hierarchical generative network, called DeepSVG, for complex SVG icons generation and interpolation. Our architecture effectively disentangles high-level shapes from the low-level commands that encode the shape itself. The network directly predicts a set of shapes in a non-autoregressive fashion. We introduce the task of complex SVG icons generation by releasing a new large-scale dataset along with an open-source library for SVG manipulation. We demonstrate that our network learns to accurately reconstruct diverse vector graphics, and can serve as a powerful animation tool by performing interpolations and other latent space operations. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexandre01/deepsvg.

paragraphs: Vector graphics describe images through shapes and drawing commands, allowing them to scale across display resolutions. DeepSVG learns representations of this structured format and uses them to generate and interpolate complex SVG icons. The paper addresses a form of image modeling that had received less attention than learning from raster images.

Its hierarchical network separates the high-level organization of shapes from the low-level commands that describe each shape. The network predicts a set of shapes directly in a non-autoregressive manner. This organization gives the model a way to handle both the composition of an icon and the detailed instructions defining its constituent shapes.

The authors introduce a large-scale dataset for complex SVG icon generation and an open-source library for manipulating SVGs. They demonstrate accurate reconstruction of diverse vector graphics and show how interpolation and other operations in the learned latent space can support animation. The results connect representation learning with practical graphics manipulation: a learned representation can serve as a space in which vector designs are transformed.
summary.tldr: DeepSVG separates shapes from drawing commands to learn vector representations that support icon generation, reconstruction, and animation.

title: DeepSVG: A Hierarchical Generative Network for Vector Graphics Animation

abstract: In recent years it was proved that simple modifications of the classical Frank-Wolfe algorithm (aka conditional gradient algorithm) for smooth convex minimization over convex and compact polytopes, converge with linear rate, assuming the objective function has the quadratic growth property. However, the rate of these methods depends explicitly on the dimension of the problem which cannot explain their empirical success for large scale problems. In this paper we first demonstrate that already for very simple problems and even when the optimal solution lies on a low-dimensional face of the polytope, such dependence on the dimension cannot be avoided in worst case. We then revisit the addition of a strict complementarity assumption already considered in Wolfe's classical book \cite{Wolfe1970}, and prove that under this condition, the Frank-Wolfe method with away-steps and line-search converges linearly with rate that depends explicitly only on the dimension of the optimal face, hence providing a significant improvement in case the optimal solution is sparse. We motivate this strict complementarity condition by proving that it implies sparsity-robustness of optimal solutions to noise.

paragraphs: Variants of Frank-Wolfe can converge at a linear rate when minimizing smooth convex functions over polytopes under a quadratic growth assumption. However, established rates explicitly depend on the dimension of the entire problem. This paper asks whether a solution lying on a much smaller face of the feasible polytope can justify a better guarantee.

The authors first show that a low-dimensional optimal face alone is insufficient: even simple problems can require dependence on the full dimension in the worst case. They then add a strict complementarity assumption. Under this condition, Frank-Wolfe with away-steps and line search converges linearly at a rate whose explicit dimensional dependence involves only the optimal face.

This can substantially improve the bound when the solution is sparse, because its relevant face may be much smaller than the full problem. The paper also shows that strict complementarity implies robustness of solution sparsity to noise. That result motivates the extra assumption and explains why sparse structure can support faster guarantees when it is accompanied by the required stability property.
summary.tldr: With strict complementarity, away-step Frank-Wolfe has a linear convergence rate whose explicit dimensional dependence is on the optimal face.

title: Revisiting Frank-Wolfe for Polytopes: Strict Complementarity and Sparsity

abstract: Counterfactual explanations are emerging as an attractive option for providing recourse to individuals adversely impacted by algorithmic decisions. As they are deployed in critical applications (e.g. law enforcement, financial lending), it becomes important to ensure that we clearly understand the vulnerabilties of these methods and find ways to address them. However, there is little understanding of the vulnerabilities and shortcomings of counterfactual explanations. In this work, we introduce the first framework that describes the vulnerabilities of counterfactual explanations and shows how they can be manipulated. More specifically, we show counterfactual explanations may converge to drastically different counterfactuals under a small perturbation indicating they are not robust. Leveraging this insight, we introduce a novel objective to train seemingly fair models where counterfactual explanations find much lower cost recourse under a slight perturbation. We describe how these models can unfairly provide low-cost recourse for specific subgroups in the data while appearing fair to auditors. We perform experiments on loan and violent crime prediction data sets where certain subgroups achieve up to 20x lower cost recourse under the perturbation. These results raise concerns regarding the dependability of current counterfactual explanation techniques, which we hope will inspire investigations in robust counterfactual explanations.

paragraphs: Counterfactual explanations describe changes that could lead to a different algorithmic decision, making them attractive for offering recourse after an unfavorable outcome. This paper examines whether those explanations can be trusted when small perturbations change what recourse they recommend. It introduces a framework for characterizing and manipulating these vulnerabilities.

The authors show that a small perturbation can cause an explanation method to converge to a drastically different counterfactual. Building on this sensitivity, they design a training objective that produces models which appear fair while allowing much cheaper recourse under a slight perturbation. Such models can selectively favor particular subgroups while still appearing fair to auditors.

Experiments on loan and violent-crime prediction datasets find that certain subgroups obtain recourse at up to twenty times lower cost under the perturbation. This is a demonstrated vulnerability in the studied settings, rather than a claim that every counterfactual explanation behaves this way. The findings show why apparent fairness in an explanation-based audit may fail to reveal unequal access to favorable outcomes.
summary.tldr: Small perturbations can manipulate counterfactual explanations, allowing models to offer selected subgroups much cheaper recourse while appearing fair to auditors.

title: Counterfactual Explanations Can Be Manipulated

abstract: This paper considers the problem of estimating the unknown intervention targets in a causal directed acyclic graph from observational and interventional data. The focus is on soft interventions in linear structural equation models (SEMs). Current approaches to causal structure learning either work with known intervention targets or use hypothesis testing to discover the unknown intervention targets even for linear SEMs. This severely limits their scalability and sample complexity. This paper proposes a scalable and efficient algorithm that consistently identifies all intervention targets. The pivotal idea is to estimate the intervention sites from the difference between the precision matrices associated with the observational and interventional datasets. It involves repeatedly estimating such sites in different subsets of variables. The proposed algorithm can be used to also update a given observational Markov equivalence class into the interventional Markov equivalence class. Consistency, Markov equivalency, and sample complexity are established analytically. Finally, simulation results on both real and synthetic data demonstrate the gains of the proposed approach for scalable causal structure recovery. Implementation of the algorithm and the code to reproduce the simulation results are available at \url{https://github.com/bvarici/intervention-estimation}.

paragraphs: Causal learning can use data collected before and after an intervention, but the variables directly affected by the intervention may be unknown. This paper studies how to identify those targets in linear structural equation models with soft interventions. Existing approaches that require known targets or discover them through hypothesis testing can face substantial scaling and sample-efficiency difficulties.

The proposed algorithm estimates intervention sites from differences between the precision matrices of observational and interventional data. Precision matrices are inverse covariance matrices, so the method uses changes in statistical relationships among variables. It repeatedly performs this estimation on different variable subsets. This provides a route to target discovery that is organized around matrix differences.

The authors analytically establish consistency, sample complexity, and results concerning Markov equivalence. The algorithm can also refine an observational equivalence class of causal graphs into an interventional equivalence class. Simulations using real and synthetic data demonstrate gains for scalable causal structure recovery. Together, the findings support using the estimated intervention targets both as useful outputs and as information for narrowing the possible causal structures.
summary.tldr: Differences between observational and interventional precision matrices enable scalable identification of soft-intervention targets in linear causal models.

title: Scalable Intervention Target Estimation in Linear Models

abstract: For an image query, unsupervised contrastive learning labels crops of the same image as positives, and other image crops as negatives. Although intuitive, such a native label assignment strategy cannot reveal the underlying semantic similarity between a query and its positives and negatives, and impairs performance, since some negatives are semantically similar to the query or even share the same semantic class as the query. In this work, we first prove that for contrastive learning, inaccurate label assignment heavily impairs its generalization for semantic instance discrimination, while accurate labels benefit its generalization. Inspired by this theory, we propose a novel self-labeling refinement approach for contrastive learning. It improves the label quality via two complementary modules: (i) self-labeling refinery (SLR) to generate accurate labels and (ii) momentum mixup (MM) to enhance similarity between query and its positive. SLR uses a positive of a query to estimate semantic similarity between a query and its positive and negatives, and combines estimated similarity with vanilla label assignment in contrastive learning to iteratively generate more accurate and informative soft labels. We theoretically show that our SLR can exactly recover the true semantic labels of label-corrupted data, and supervises networks to achieve zero prediction error on classification tasks. MM randomly combines queries and positives to increase semantic similarity between the generated virtual queries and their positives so as to improves label accuracy. Experimental results on CIFAR10, ImageNet, VOC and COCO show the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Contrastive image learning usually treats two crops of one image as a positive pair and crops from different images as negative pairs. That assignment can conflict with meaning: a different image may depict the same semantic class. The paper theoretically links inaccurate assignments to worse generalization for semantic instance discrimination, motivating a way to refine the training labels.

Its self-labeling refinery uses a query's positive example to estimate semantic similarity to both positive and negative examples. It combines these estimates with the original assignments to iteratively produce informative soft labels. A complementary momentum mixup module randomly combines queries and positives, making the resulting virtual queries more semantically similar to their associated positives.

The authors give theoretical results in which the refinery exactly recovers semantic labels from corrupted labels and supports zero classification prediction error. These are theoretical claims, rather than a claim of universally perfect empirical classification. Experiments on CIFAR10, ImageNet, VOC, and COCO demonstrate the method's effectiveness, supporting the value of improving the semantic meaning of contrastive supervision.
summary.tldr: Refining contrastive labels using estimated semantic similarity and mixed examples improves the supervision used to learn image representations.

title: A Theory-Driven Self-Labeling Refinement Method for Contrastive Representation Learning

abstract: Although the fairness community has recognized the importance of data, researchers in the area primarily rely on UCI Adult when it comes to tabular data. Derived from a 1994 US Census survey, this dataset has appeared in hundreds of research papers where it served as the basis for the development and comparison of many algorithmic fairness interventions. We reconstruct a superset of the UCI Adult data from available US Census sources and reveal idiosyncrasies of the UCI Adult dataset that limit its external validity. Our primary contribution is a suite of new datasets derived from US Census surveys that extend the existing data ecosystem for research on fair machine learning. We create prediction tasks relating to income, employment, health, transportation, and housing. The data span multiple years and all states of the United States, allowing researchers to study temporal shift and geographic variation. We highlight a broad initial sweep of new empirical insights relating to trade-offs between fairness criteria, performance of algorithmic interventions, and the role of distribution shift based on our new datasets. Our findings inform ongoing debates, challenge some existing narratives, and point to future research directions.

The authors reconstruct a superset of that dataset from available US Census sources and identify peculiarities that limit how broadly conclusions drawn from it can apply. This motivates expanding the evidence used to evaluate fairness methods.

The paper’s main contribution is a suite of Census-derived datasets with prediction tasks covering income, employment, health, transportation, and housing. The data include multiple years and every US state. That coverage lets researchers examine whether findings persist across time and geography, rather than treating one dataset as representative of many deployment settings.

An initial empirical investigation explores tradeoffs among fairness criteria, the performance of algorithmic interventions, and distribution shift. The authors report findings that challenge some existing narratives and suggest new research directions. The value of the contribution is both practical and methodological: it supplies additional benchmarks and makes variation across populations and time an explicit part of evaluating claims about fair machine learning.
summary.tldr: New Census-derived datasets broaden fairness research beyond UCI Adult and enable studies of geographic variation, temporal shift, and intervention performance.

title: Retiring Adult: New Datasets for Fair Machine Learning

abstract: Recent advances in self-supervised learning have dramatically improved the state of the art on a wide variety of tasks. However, research in language model pre-training has mostly focused on natural languages, and it is unclear whether models like BERT and its variants provide the best pre-training when applied to other modalities, such as source code. In this paper, we introduce a new pre-training objective, DOBF, that leverages the structural aspect of programming languages and pre-trains a model to recover the original version of obfuscated source code. We show that models pre-trained with DOBF significantly outperform existing approaches on multiple downstream tasks, providing relative improvements of up to 12.2% in unsupervised code translation, and 5.3% in natural language code search. Incidentally, we found that our pre-trained model is able to deobfuscate fully obfuscated source files, and to suggest descriptive variable names.

paragraphs: DOBF explores a pretraining task designed around source code's structure. The paper starts from the observation that much language-model pretraining research concerns natural language, leaving open whether those objectives are best suited to programming languages. It proposes training a model to reconstruct the original source code from an obfuscated version, making deobfuscation the learning objective.

The approach uses a property specific to the material being modeled: programming languages have structural information that can support recovery of obscured code. The recovered original program supplies the training target. This makes DOBF a way to learn code representations through a task directly tied to recovering meaningful source rather than simply transferring a natural-language pretraining recipe.

Models pretrained with DOBF significantly outperform existing approaches on multiple downstream tasks. Reported relative improvements reach 12.2% for unsupervised code translation and 5.3% for natural-language code search. The authors also find that the pretrained model can deobfuscate fully obfuscated source files and suggest descriptive variable names, showing a direct use for the learned capability.
summary.tldr: DOBF pretrains code models by reconstructing obfuscated programs, improving downstream code translation and search while enabling useful deobfuscation.

title: DOBF: A Deobfuscation Pre-Training Objective for Programming Languages

abstract: The interdependence between nodes in graphs is key to improve class prediction on nodes, utilized in approaches like Label Probagation (LP) or in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). Nonetheless, uncertainty estimation for non-independent node-level predictions is under-explored. In this work, we explore uncertainty quantification for node classification in three ways: (1) We derive three axioms explicitly characterizing the expected predictive uncertainty behavior in homophilic attributed graphs.(2) We propose a new model Graph Posterior Network (GPN) which explicitly performs Bayesian posterior updates for predictions on interdependent nodes. GPN provably obeys the proposed axioms. (3) We extensively evaluate GPN and a strong set of baselines on semi-supervised node classification including detection of anomalous features, and detection of left-out classes. GPN outperforms existing approaches for uncertainty estimation in the experiments.

paragraphs: Connections between graph nodes provide useful information for predicting their classes. Those same connections also make predictions dependent, complicating the question of how uncertain each prediction should be. This paper focuses on uncertainty for node classification, where methods that exploit graph structure need an account of confidence as well as class predictions.

The authors first formulate three axioms describing expected uncertainty behavior in homophilic attributed graphs, where connected nodes tend to be similar and nodes carry features. They then introduce Graph Posterior Network, which explicitly performs Bayesian posterior updates for interdependent node predictions. The model is proved to satisfy the proposed axioms, linking its uncertainty behavior to stated formal requirements.

The empirical evaluation covers semi-supervised node classification, including the detection of anomalous features and classes omitted from training. GPN outperforms existing uncertainty estimation approaches in those experiments. The contribution combines a formal description of desirable behavior with a model designed to meet it and practical evaluation. Its theoretical claims remain tied to the proposed axioms and graph setting, while the experimental results address the tested uncertainty tasks.
summary.tldr: Graph Posterior Network uses Bayesian updates to estimate node uncertainty, satisfies proposed graph-specific axioms, and improves uncertainty estimation in experiments.

title: Graph Posterior Network: Bayesian Predictive Uncertainty for Node Classification

abstract: We investigate the problem of minimizing the excess generalization error with respect to the best expert prediction in a finite family in the stochastic setting, under limited access to information. We consider that the learner has only access to a limited number of expert advices per training round, as well as for prediction. Assuming that the loss function is Lipschitz and strongly convex, we show that if we are allowed to see the advice of only one expert per round in the training phase, or to use the advice of only one expert for prediction in the test phase, the worst-case excess risk is ${\Omega}(1/\sqrt{T})$ with probability lower bounded by a constant. However, if we are allowed to see at least two actively chosen expert advices per training round and use at least two experts for prediction, the fast rate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ can be achieved. We design novel algorithms achieving this rate in this setting, and in the setting where the learner have a budget constraint on the total number of observed experts advices, and give precise instance-dependent bounds on the number of training rounds needed to achieve a given generalization error precision.

We consider that the learner has only access to a limited number of expert advices per training round, as well as for prediction. Assuming that the loss function is Lipschitz and strongly convex, we show that if we are allowed to see the advice of only one expert per round in the training phase, or to use the advice of only one expert for prediction in the test phase, the worst-case excess risk is ${\Omega}(1/\sqrt{T})$ with probability lower bounded by a constant. However, if we are allowed to see at least two actively chosen expert advices per training round and use at least two experts for prediction, the fast rate $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ can be achieved. We design novel algorithms achieving this rate in this setting, and in the setting where the learner have a budget constraint on the total number of observed experts advices, and give precise instance-dependent bounds on the number of training rounds needed to achieve a given generalization error precision.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning from a finite collection of expert predictors when access to their advice is limited. The learner aims to approach the generalization performance of the best expert, but can consult only a restricted number during training and prediction. The analysis assumes a stochastic setting and a loss that is both Lipschitz and strongly convex.

Under these assumptions, access to just one expert per training round, or use of just one expert at prediction time, creates a worst-case barrier. The excess risk is at least on the order of 1/√T with probability bounded below by a constant, where T is the number of rounds. Allowing at least two actively chosen experts during each training round and at least two for prediction makes an O(1/T) rate achievable.

The authors construct algorithms attaining that faster rate, including a version with a total budget on observed advice. They also derive instance-dependent bounds on the rounds needed for a desired error level. The result identifies a consequential access threshold under the stated loss assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under the stated loss assumptions, consulting and combining at least two experts enables faster learning rates than one-expert access permits in the worst case.

title: Fast rates for prediction with limited expert advice

abstract: We consider the problem of online linear regression in the stochastic setting. We derive high probability regret bounds for online $\textit{ridge}$ regression and the $\textit{forward}$ algorithm. This enables us to compare online regression algorithms more accurately and eliminate assumptions of bounded observations and predictions. Our study advocates for the use of the forward algorithm in lieu of ridge due to its enhanced bounds and robustness to the regularization parameter. Moreover, we explain how to integrate it in algorithms involving linear function approximation to remove a boundedness assumption without deteriorating theoretical bounds. We showcase this modification in linear bandit settings where it yields improved regret bounds. Last, we provide numerical experiments to illustrate our results and endorse our intuitions.

paragraphs: Online linear regression makes predictions as data arrive over time. This paper studies the stochastic setting and compares online ridge regression with the forward algorithm through high-probability regret bounds. Regret measures the cumulative cost of the learner's predictions relative to a comparison predictor, making the bounds a way to assess learning performance over time.

The analysis removes assumptions that observations and predictions are bounded. It also gives a more precise comparison between the two algorithms. The authors advocate the forward algorithm because of its stronger bounds and robustness to the choice of regularization parameter, connecting the theoretical comparison to a practical algorithm-selection issue.

The paper further explains how to incorporate the forward algorithm into methods that use linear function approximation. This substitution can remove a boundedness assumption without worsening theoretical bounds. In linear bandit applications, the modification yields improved regret guarantees. Numerical experiments illustrate the analysis and support the authors' intuitions, complementing the theoretical argument for using the forward algorithm in the studied settings.
summary.tldr: New stochastic regret bounds favor the forward algorithm over online ridge regression and support improvements in linear bandit methods.

title: Stochastic Online Linear Regression: the Forward Algorithm to Replace Ridge

abstract: Various recent proposals increase the distinguishing power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) by propagating features between k-tuples of vertices. The distinguishing power of these “higher-order” GNNs is known to be bounded by the k-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (WL) test, yet their O(n^k) memory requirements limit their applicability. Other proposals infuse GNNs with local higher-order graph structural information from the start, hereby inheriting the desirable O(n) memory requirement from GNNs at the cost of a one-time, possibly non-linear, preprocessing step. We propose local graph parameter enabled GNNs as a framework for studying the latter kind of approaches and precisely characterize their distinguishing power, in terms of a variant of the WL test, and in terms of the graph structural properties that they can take into account. Local graph parameters can be added to any GNN architecture, and are cheap to compute. In terms of expressive power, our proposal lies in the middle of GNNs and their higher-order counterparts. Further, we propose several techniques to aide in choosing the right local graph parameters. Our results connect GNNs with deep results in finite model theory and finite variable logics. Our experimental evaluation shows that adding local graph parameters often has a positive effect for a variety of GNNs, datasets and graph learning tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can gain distinguishing power by passing information among groups of vertices, but representing all k-vertex tuples requires O(n^k) memory. Another approach supplies local structural information before learning begins. This retains the O(n) memory requirement of ordinary graph neural networks, while introducing a one-time preprocessing step that can be nonlinear.

The paper develops local graph parameter enabled GNNs as a framework for understanding this second approach. It characterizes exactly which graphs these models can distinguish through a variant of the Weisfeiler-Leman test and through the structural properties they can capture. Their expressive power falls between ordinary GNNs and higher-order alternatives, giving a precise account of the capabilities gained from local information.

The proposed local parameters are cheap to compute and can be added to any GNN architecture. The authors also provide techniques for selecting useful parameters and connect the framework to finite model theory and logic. Experiments across architectures, datasets, and graph tasks show that adding these parameters often improves performance, supporting their practical value alongside the expressiveness analysis.
summary.tldr: Local structural parameters give GNNs a theoretically characterized increase in expressive power while preserving linear model memory requirements.

title: Graph Neural Networks with Local Graph Parameters

abstract: Recently, a series of algorithms have been explored for GAN compression, which aims to reduce tremendous computational overhead and memory usages when deploying GANs on resource-constrained edge devices. However, most of the existing GAN compression work only focuses on how to compress the generator, while fails to take the discriminator into account. In this work, we revisit the role of discriminator in GAN compression and design a novel generator-discriminator cooperative compression scheme for GAN compression, termed GCC. Within GCC, a selective activation discriminator automatically selects and activates convolutional channels according to a local capacity constraint and a global coordination constraint, which help maintain the Nash equilibrium with the lightweight generator during the adversarial training and avoid mode collapse. The original generator and discriminator are also optimized from scratch, to play as a teacher model to progressively refine the pruned generator and the selective activation discriminator. A novel online collaborative distillation scheme is designed to take full advantage of the intermediate feature of the teacher generator and discriminator to further boost the performance of the lightweight generator. Extensive experiments on various GAN-based generation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of GCC. Among them, GCC contributes to reducing 80% computational costs while maintains comparable performance in image translation tasks.

paragraphs: Compressing generative adversarial networks can reduce the computation and memory needed for deployment on resource-constrained devices. This paper argues that concentrating on the generator overlooks the discriminator's role during training. GCC coordinates both components so that a lightweight generator can be trained with a suitably adjusted adversarial partner.

Its discriminator selectively activates convolutional channels according to local capacity and global coordination constraints. These constraints help maintain equilibrium with the smaller generator and avoid mode collapse. The original generator and discriminator are also trained from scratch as teacher models, progressively refining the pruned generator and selectively activated discriminator.

An online collaborative distillation procedure transfers intermediate features from both teacher components to improve the lightweight generator. Experiments across several GAN generation tasks support the scheme's effectiveness and generalization. In image translation, the reported result is an 80% reduction in computational cost while retaining comparable performance. The findings emphasize that compression quality can depend on coordinating adversarial training and teacher guidance, not solely on reducing generator size.
summary.tldr: GCC coordinates generator compression, discriminator capacity, and teacher distillation, reporting 80% lower computation with comparable image-translation performance.

title: Revisiting Discriminator in GAN Compression: A Generator-discriminator Cooperative Compression Scheme

abstract: We consider the problem of allocating divisible items among multiple agents, and consider the setting where any agent is allowed to introduce {\emph diversity constraints} on the items they are allocated. We motivate this via settings where the items themselves correspond to user ad slots or task workers with attributes such as race and gender on which the principal seeks to achieve demographic parity. We consider the following question: When an agent expresses diversity constraints into an allocation rule, is the allocation of other agents hurt significantly? If this happens, the cost of introducing such constraints is disproportionately borne by agents who do not benefit from diversity. We codify this via two desiderata capturing {\em robustness}. These are {\emph no negative externality} -- other agents are not hurt -- and {\emph monotonicity} -- the agent enforcing the constraint does not see a large increase in value. We show in a formal sense that the Nash Welfare rule that maximizes product of agent values is {\emph uniquely} positioned to be robust when diversity constraints are introduced, while almost all other natural allocation rules fail this criterion. We also show that the guarantees achieved by Nash Welfare are nearly optimal within a widely studied class of allocation rules. We finally perform an empirical simulation on real-world data that models ad allocations to show that this gap between Nash Welfare and other rules persists in the wild.

paragraphs: When divisible resources are allocated among several agents, one agent may request a demographically balanced allocation. Such constraints can arise when resources represent advertising slots or workers with demographic attributes. The paper asks whether adding a diversity constraint changes other agents' allocations so much that they disproportionately bear its cost.

The authors formalize robustness through two requirements. No negative externality concerns avoiding harm to other agents. Monotonicity concerns preventing a large increase in the value received by the agent imposing the constraint. Together, these criteria examine how an allocation rule redistributes value when someone changes the constraints on their own allocation.

The analysis identifies Nash Welfare, which maximizes the product of agents' values, as uniquely positioned to achieve robustness in the paper's formal sense. Almost all other natural rules fail the criterion, and Nash Welfare's guarantees are nearly optimal within a widely studied class of rules. A simulation of advertising allocation using real-world data also shows the gap persisting empirically. This supports the rule's robustness under the studied framework, rather than establishing that every diversity constraint is costless.
summary.tldr: Nash Welfare has distinctive, nearly optimal robustness guarantees when agents add diversity constraints to divisible-resource allocations.

title: Robust Allocations with Diversity Constraints

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of domain generalization in semantic segmentation, which aims to learn a robust model using only labeled synthetic (source) data. The model is expected to perform well on unseen real (target) domains. Our study finds that the image style variation can largely influence the model's performance and the style features can be well represented by the channel-wise mean and standard deviation of images. Inspired by this, we propose a novel adversarial style augmentation (AdvStyle) approach, which can dynamically generate hard stylized images during training and thus can effectively prevent the model from overfitting on the source domain. Specifically, AdvStyle regards the style feature as a learnable parameter and updates it by adversarial training. The learned adversarial style feature is used to construct an adversarial image for robust model training. AdvStyle is easy to implement and can be readily applied to different models. Experiments on two synthetic-to-real semantic segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that AdvStyle can significantly improve the model performance on unseen real domains and show that we can achieve the state of the art. Moreover, AdvStyle can be employed to domain generalized image classification and produces a clear improvement on the considered datasets.

paragraphs: A segmentation model trained on labeled synthetic scenes must recognize image regions in real scenes whose appearance it has never encountered. This paper studies that synthetic-to-real generalization problem. The authors find that image style strongly affects performance and that channel-wise means and standard deviations can represent style features well.

Their method, AdvStyle, treats these style features as parameters that can be changed during training. Adversarial updates produce difficult styles, which are then used to construct training images. The model therefore practices on challenging appearance variations generated dynamically, helping prevent it from fitting too closely to the style of its synthetic source data.

Experiments on two synthetic-to-real segmentation benchmarks report significant improvements on unseen real domains and state-of-the-art performance. The authors also apply the approach to domain-generalized image classification and find improvements on the datasets considered. Because the augmentation operates through style features, the paper presents it as straightforward to implement and applicable to different models. The findings support style variation as a useful target for improving generalization.
summary.tldr: AdvStyle generates challenging image styles during training to improve synthetic-to-real segmentation and generalization to unseen domains.

title: Adversarial Style Augmentation for Domain Generalized Urban-Scene Segmentation

abstract: The Adam optimization algorithm has proven remarkably effective for optimization problems across machine learning and even traditional tasks in geometry processing. At the same time, the development of equivariant methods, which preserve their output under the action of rotation or some other transformation, has proven to be important for geometry problems across these domains. In this work, we observe that Adam — when treated as a function that maps initial conditions to optimized results — is not rotation equivariant for vector-valued parameters due to per-coordinate moment updates. This leads to significant artifacts and biases in practice. We propose to resolve this deficiency with VectorAdam, a simple modification which makes Adam rotation-equivariant by accounting for the vector structure of optimization variables. We demonstrate this approach on problems in machine learning and traditional geometric optimization, showing that equivariant VectorAdam resolves the artifacts and biases of traditional Adam when applied to vector-valued data, with equivalent or even improved rates of convergence.

paragraphs: When optimization variables represent geometric vectors, rotating the starting problem should ideally rotate the optimized result in the corresponding way. This paper shows that standard Adam does not have that property. Its separate moment updates for individual coordinates can make optimization depend on the coordinate axes, producing noticeable artifacts and biases in geometric applications.

VectorAdam modifies Adam to account for the vector structure of its variables. This makes the optimizer rotation-equivariant when viewed as a mapping from initial conditions to optimized results. The change addresses the optimization procedure itself: even if geometric data are naturally organized as vectors, the update rule must also respect that organization to preserve the desired rotational behavior.

The authors demonstrate VectorAdam on both machine learning and traditional geometry optimization problems. In these experiments, it resolves the artifacts and biases associated with applying conventional Adam to vector-valued data, while matching or improving convergence rates. The results show that respecting geometric structure in an optimizer can improve its behavior without requiring slower convergence in the reported applications.
summary.tldr: VectorAdam makes Adam respect rotations of vector-valued parameters, removing reported geometric artifacts while matching or improving convergence.

title: VectorAdam for Rotation Equivariant Geometry Optimization

abstract: Controlling the behavior of language models (LMs) without re-training is a major open problem in natural language generation. While recent works have demonstrated successes on controlling simple sentence attributes (e.g., sentiment), there has been little progress on complex, fine-grained controls (e.g., syntactic structure). To address this challenge, we develop a new non-autoregressive language model based on continuous diffusions that we call Diffusion-LM. Building upon the recent successes of diffusion models in continuous domains, Diffusion-LM iteratively denoises a sequence of Gaussian vectors into word vectors, yielding a sequence of intermediate latent variables. The continuous, hierarchical nature of these intermediate variables enables a simple gradient-based algorithm to perform complex, controllable generation tasks. We demonstrate successful control of Diffusion-LM for six challenging fine-grained control tasks, significantly outperforming prior work.

To address this challenge, we develop a new non-autoregressive language model based on continuous diffusions that we call Diffusion-LM. Building upon the recent successes of diffusion models in continuous domains, Diffusion-LM iteratively denoises a sequence of Gaussian vectors into word vectors, yielding a sequence of intermediate latent variables. paragraphs: Controlling generated text becomes difficult when the requested property involves detailed structure rather than a broad attribute such as sentiment. This paper targets that problem with Diffusion-LM, a language model designed to make fine-grained control possible through its intermediate representations. The motivation is to steer generation without retraining a language model for each desired behavior.

Diffusion-LM generates text through a non-autoregressive process that repeatedly removes noise from a sequence of Gaussian vectors until it obtains word vectors. This produces a hierarchy of intermediate continuous variables. Because these variables are continuous, a gradient-based algorithm can adjust them during generation to pursue a control objective, making the intermediate generation process an explicit place to apply guidance.

The authors demonstrate successful control on six challenging fine-grained tasks and report substantial improvements over previous work. The findings support the value of a diffusion-based representation for controlling language generation. In particular, the model's sequence of intermediate states provides opportunities to guide complex properties, including the kind of syntactic control that motivates the paper.
summary.tldr: Diffusion-LM uses continuous denoising states to enable gradient-guided text generation with successful fine-grained control on six tasks.

title: Diffusion-LM Improves Controllable Text Generation

abstract: Video-Language Pretraining (VLP), which aims to learn transferable representation to advance a wide range of video-text downstream tasks, has recently received increasing attention. Best performing works rely on large-scale, 3rd-person video-text datasets, such as HowTo100M. In this work, we exploit the recently released Ego4D dataset to pioneer Egocentric VLP along three directions. (i) We create EgoClip, a 1st-person video-text pretraining dataset comprising 3.8M clip-text pairs well-chosen from Ego4D, covering a large variety of human daily activities. (ii) We propose a novel pretraining objective, dubbed EgoNCE, which adapts video-text contrastive learning to the egocentric domain by mining egocentric-aware positive and negative samples. (iii) We introduce EgoMCQ, a development benchmark that is close to EgoClip and hence can support effective validation and fast exploration of our design decisions in EgoClip and EgoNCE. Furthermore, we demonstrate strong performance on five egocentric downstream tasks across three datasets: video-text retrieval on EPIC-KITCHENS-100; action recognition on Charades-Ego; natural language query, moment query, and object state change classification on Ego4D challenge benchmarks. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/showlab/EgoVLP.

paragraphs: Video-language pretraining learns representations that can transfer to tasks involving both video and text. This paper focuses on first-person video, whereas the strongest prior systems described in the abstract rely on large third-person datasets. It develops data, a training objective, and a development benchmark specifically for the egocentric setting.

EgoClip contains 3.8 million clip-text pairs selected from Ego4D and covers varied everyday human activities. The proposed EgoNCE objective adapts contrastive video-text learning by choosing positive and negative samples with the egocentric domain in mind. EgoMCQ provides a nearby development benchmark, helping the authors validate and explore decisions about the dataset and training objective efficiently.

The resulting pretraining shows strong performance on five downstream tasks across three datasets. These include video-text retrieval on EPIC-KITCHENS-100, action recognition on Charades-Ego, and natural-language queries, moment queries, and object-state-change classification on Ego4D benchmarks. Together, these results support the usefulness of first-person-specific pretraining across several kinds of egocentric understanding, from matching descriptions to video through recognizing actions and changes in objects.
summary.tldr: EgoClip, EgoNCE, and EgoMCQ support first-person video-language pretraining with strong results across five downstream tasks.

title: Egocentric Video-Language Pretraining

abstract: In this paper we propose a general framework to perform statistical online inference in a class of constant step size stochastic approximation (SA) problems, including the well-known stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and Q-learning. Regarding a constant step size SA procedure as a time-homogeneous Markov chain, we establish a functional central limit theorem (FCLT) for it under weaker conditions, and then construct confidence intervals for parameters via random scaling. To leverage the FCLT results in the Markov chain setting, an alternative condition that is more applicable for SA problems is established. We conduct experiments to perform inference with both random scaling and other traditional inference methods, and finds that the former has a more accurate and robust performance.

Regarding a constant step size SA procedure as a time-homogeneous Markov chain, we establish a functional central limit theorem (FCLT) for it under weaker conditions, and then construct confidence intervals for parameters via random scaling. To leverage the FCLT results in the Markov chain setting, an alternative condition that is more applicable for SA problems is established. We conduct experiments to perform inference with both random scaling and other traditional inference methods, and finds that the former has a more accurate and robust performance.

paragraphs: Stochastic approximation updates an estimate using noisy information arriving over time. Producing an estimate is only part of the statistical problem: researchers also need confidence intervals that express its uncertainty. This paper develops an online inference framework for a class of these procedures with a constant step size, including stochastic gradient descent and Q-learning.

The authors treat the sequence of updates as a time-homogeneous Markov chain, meaning that the rule governing transitions stays fixed over time. They establish a functional central limit theorem under weaker conditions and provide an alternative condition suited to stochastic approximation. This theorem describes the large-scale fluctuations of the update process and supplies the basis for statistical inference.

The framework constructs confidence intervals through random scaling, using the observed stochastic process to scale uncertainty. In the reported experiments, this approach gives more accurate and robust inference than the traditional methods considered. The contribution connects constant-step optimization and learning procedures with a principled way to quantify uncertainty while those procedures operate.
summary.tldr: A Markov-chain framework enables online confidence intervals for constant-step stochastic approximation, with random scaling improving inference in the reported experiments.

title: A Statistical Online Inference Approach in Averaged Stochastic Approximation

abstract: We study the excess capacity of deep networks in the context of supervised classification. That is, given a capacity measure of the underlying hypothesis class - in our case, empirical Rademacher complexity - to what extent can we (a priori) constrain this class while retaining an empirical error on a par with the unconstrained regime? To assess excess capacity in modern architectures (such as residual networks), we extend and unify prior Rademacher complexity bounds to accommodate function composition and addition, as well as the structure of convolutions. The capacity-driving terms in our bounds are the Lipschitz constants of the layers and a (2,1) group norm distance to the initializations of the convolution weights. Experiments on benchmark datasets of varying task difficulty indicate that (1) there is a substantial amount of excess capacity per task, and (2) capacity can be kept at a surprisingly similar level across tasks. Overall, this suggests a notion of compressibility with respect to weight norms, complementary to classic compression via weight pruning. Source code is available at https://github.com/rkwitt/excess_capacity.
