paragraphs: This paper asks how much a neural network's available function class can be constrained in advance while retaining training error comparable to an unconstrained model. It calls the removable portion excess capacity and measures capacity through empirical Rademacher complexity. The question concerns supervised classification and includes modern architectures such as residual networks.

To support that investigation, the authors extend and unify complexity bounds to handle composed functions, added functions, and convolutional structure. The main capacity-related quantities are layer Lipschitz constants and a group-norm measure of how far convolutional weights move from initialization. These quantities provide a way to constrain capacity through properties of the weights.

Experiments across benchmark tasks of different difficulty indicate substantial excess capacity for each task. They also suggest that capacity can be held at surprisingly similar levels across tasks while retaining comparable empirical error. The authors interpret this as a form of compressibility through weight norms, complementary to pruning. The findings concern the studied capacity measure and empirical performance, making the choice of measurement central to their interpretation.
summary.tldr: Complexity bounds and experiments suggest networks can retain comparable training error under substantial constraints on weight-based capacity.

title: On Measuring Excess Capacity in Neural Networks

abstract: We study two problems related to recovering causal graphs from interventional data: (i) $\textit{verification}$, where the task is to check if a purported causal graph is correct, and (ii) $\textit{search}$, where the task is to recover the correct causal graph. For both, we wish to minimize the number of interventions performed. For the first problem, we give a characterization of a minimal sized set of atomic interventions that is necessary and sufficient to check the correctness of a claimed causal graph. Our characterization uses the notion of $\textit{covered edges}$, which enables us to obtain simple proofs and also easily reason about earlier known results. We also generalize our results to the settings of bounded size interventions and node-dependent interventional costs. For all the above settings, we provide the first known provable algorithms for efficiently computing (near)-optimal verifying sets on general graphs. For the second problem, we give a simple adaptive algorithm based on graph separators that produces an atomic intervention set which fully orients any essential graph while using $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ times the optimal number of interventions needed to $\textit{verify}$ (verifying size) the underlying DAG on $n$ vertices. This approximation is tight as $\textit{any}$ search algorithm on an essential line graph has worst case approximation ratio of $\Omega(\log n)$ with respect to the verifying size. With bounded size interventions, each of size $\leq k$, our algorithm gives an $\mathcal{O}(\log n \cdot \log k)$ factor approximation. Our result is the first known algorithm that gives a non-trivial approximation guarantee to the verifying size on general unweighted graphs and with bounded size interventions.

For the first problem, we give a characterization of a minimal sized set of atomic interventions that is necessary and sufficient to check the correctness of a claimed causal graph. Our characterization uses the notion of $\textit{covered edges}$, which enables us to obtain simple proofs and also easily reason about earlier known results. We also generalize our results to the settings of bounded size interventions and node-dependent interventional costs. For all the above settings, we provide the first known provable algorithms for efficiently computing (near)-optimal verifying sets on general graphs. For the second problem, we give a simple adaptive algorithm based on graph separators that produces an atomic intervention set which fully orients any essential graph while using $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ times the optimal number of interventions needed to $\textit{verify}$ (verifying size) the underlying DAG on $n$ vertices. This approximation is tight as $\textit{any}$ search algorithm on an essential line graph has worst case approximation ratio of $\Omega(\log n)$ with respect to the verifying size. With bounded size interventions, each of size $\leq k$, our algorithm gives an $\mathcal{O}(\log n \cdot \log k)$ factor approximation. Our result is the first known algorithm that gives a non-trivial approximation guarantee to the verifying size on general unweighted graphs and with bounded size interventions.

paragraphs: The paper distinguishes two intervention problems in causal discovery: verifying a proposed causal graph and searching for the correct graph. Both aim to minimize interventions, but verification begins with a candidate answer. The authors use the minimum cost of verification as a reference for understanding the harder search problem.

For verification, they characterize a smallest set of atomic interventions that is necessary and sufficient to check a claimed graph. The characterization uses covered edges and extends to interventions of bounded size and costs that depend on the targeted node. They provide efficient algorithms with provable optimality or near-optimality guarantees for computing verifying sets on general graphs.

For search, an adaptive algorithm based on graph separators fully orients an essential graph using O(log n) times the underlying graph’s optimal atomic verifying size. A worst-case lower bound for essential line graphs shows this logarithmic comparison is tight. When interventions can affect at most k nodes, the approximation becomes O(log n · log k). These guarantees quantify search effort relative to verification, rather than treating the two tasks as interchangeable.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes efficient causal-graph verification and bounds adaptive search costs relative to optimal verification.

title: Verification and search algorithms for causal DAGs

abstract: In response to subtle adversarial examples flipping classifications of neural network models, recent research has promoted certified robustness as a solution. There, invariance of predictions to all norm-bounded attacks is achieved through randomised smoothing of network inputs. Today's state-of-the-art certifications make optimal use of the class output scores at the input instance under test: no better radius of certification (under the $L_2$ norm) is possible given only these score. However, it is an open question as to whether such lower bounds can be improved using local information around the instance under test. In this work, we demonstrate how today's ``optimal'' certificates can be improved by exploiting both the transitivity of certifications, and the geometry of the input space, giving rise to what we term Geometrically-Informed Certified Robustness. By considering the smallest distance to points on the boundary of a set of certifications this approach improves certifications for more than $80 \%$ of Tiny-Imagenet instances, yielding an on average $5\%$ increase in the associated certification. When incorporating training time processes that enhance the certified radius, our technique shows even more promising results, with a uniform $4$ percentage point increase in the achieved certified radius.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing can certify that a model's prediction remains unchanged throughout a bounded neighborhood of an input. Existing certificates are optimal when restricted to the class scores at that input. This paper asks whether information from surrounding locations can enlarge the certified region without contradicting that restricted optimality result.

The proposed approach combines the transitivity of certifications with the geometry of input space. It considers a set of certified regions and measures the smallest distance to points on their boundary. Using relationships among those regions provides local information beyond the class scores at the single input being tested.

On Tiny-Imagenet, the approach improves certifications for more than 80% of instances and yields an average increase of 5% in the associated certification. The authors also report a uniform four-percentage-point increase in achieved certified radius when combining the technique with training processes that enhance the radius. These findings show that certificates optimal under one information restriction can still improve when additional geometric information is available.
summary.tldr: Combining nearby certificates through geometry and transitivity improves randomized-smoothing robustness guarantees beyond single-input score information.

title: Double Bubble, Toil and Trouble: Enhancing Certified Robustness through Transitivity

abstract: Aiming towards a holistic understanding of multiple downstream tasks simultaneously, there is a need for extracting features with better transferability. Though many latest self-supervised pre-training methods have achieved impressive performance on various vision tasks under the prevailing pretrain-finetune paradigm, their generalization capacity to multi-task learning scenarios is yet to be explored. In this paper, we extensively investigate the transfer performance of various types of self-supervised methods, e.g., MoCo and SimCLR, on three downstream tasks, including semantic segmentation, drivable area segmentation, and traffic object detection, on the large-scale driving dataset BDD100K. We surprisingly find that their performances are sub-optimal or even lag far behind the single-task baseline, which may be due to the distinctions of training objectives and architectural design lied in the pretrain-finetune paradigm. To overcome this dilemma as well as avoid redesigning the resource-intensive pre-training stage, we propose a simple yet effective pretrain-adapt-finetune paradigm for general multi-task training, where the off-the-shelf pretrained models can be effectively adapted without increasing the training overhead. During the adapt stage, we utilize learnable multi-scale adapters to dynamically adjust the pretrained model weights supervised by multi-task objectives while leaving the pretrained knowledge untouched. Furthermore, we regard the vision-language pre-training model CLIP as a strong complement to the pretrain-adapt-finetune paradigm and propose a novel adapter named LV-Adapter, which incorporates language priors in the multi-task model via task-specific prompting and alignment between visual and textual features. Our experiments demonstrate that the adapt stage significantly improves the overall performance of those off-the-shelf pretrained models and the contextual features generated by LV-Adapter are of general benefits for downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Features learned through self-supervised pretraining do not necessarily transfer well when one model must handle several driving tasks together. The authors examine semantic segmentation, drivable-area segmentation, and traffic-object detection on BDD100K. They find that several pretrained approaches perform poorly in this setting, sometimes substantially below a single-task baseline. Differences in objectives and architecture are suggested as possible causes.

The proposed solution inserts an adaptation stage between pretraining and fine-tuning. Learnable adapters operating at multiple scales adjust how pretrained weights serve the joint tasks while preserving the pretrained knowledge. This lets existing pretrained models be adapted without redesigning their expensive pretraining stage; the authors also report that it avoids increasing training overhead.

The paper further introduces LV-Adapter, which brings language information from CLIP into the model through task-specific prompts and alignment of visual and textual features. Experiments show significant overall improvements from adaptation across the pretrained models examined. They also indicate that the contextual features produced by LV-Adapter benefit the downstream tasks, supporting adaptation as a useful bridge between pretraining and joint task learning.
summary.tldr: An intermediate adaptation stage improves pretrained models for joint driving tasks, with a CLIP-based adapter adding useful language-informed features.

title: Effective Adaptation in Multi-Task Co-Training for Unified Autonomous Driving

abstract: Tree ensembles can be well-suited for black-box optimization tasks such as algorithm tuning and neural architecture search, as they achieve good predictive performance with little or no manual tuning, naturally handle discrete feature spaces, and are relatively insensitive to outliers in the training data. Two well-known challenges in using tree ensembles for black-box optimization are (i) effectively quantifying model uncertainty for exploration and (ii) optimizing over the piece-wise constant acquisition function. To address both points simultaneously, we propose using the kernel interpretation of tree ensembles as a Gaussian Process prior to obtain model variance estimates, and we develop a compatible optimization formulation for the acquisition function. The latter further allows us to seamlessly integrate known constraints to improve sampling efficiency by considering domain-knowledge in engineering settings and modeling search space symmetries, e.g., hierarchical relationships in neural architecture search. Our framework performs as well as state-of-the-art methods for unconstrained black-box optimization over continuous/discrete features and outperforms competing methods for problems combining mixed-variable feature spaces and known input constraints.

paragraphs: Tree ensembles are attractive for black-box optimization because they handle discrete features, often need little manual tuning, and are relatively insensitive to outliers. However, using them to choose new evaluations raises two difficulties: estimating uncertainty for exploration and optimizing an acquisition function that is constant within pieces of the search space.

This paper addresses both difficulties through a Gaussian-process interpretation of tree-ensemble kernels. The resulting prior supplies model variance estimates, while a compatible optimization formulation handles the acquisition function. The formulation also incorporates known input constraints, allowing domain knowledge to influence which evaluations are selected.

These constraints can express engineering requirements and search-space structure, including symmetries and hierarchical relationships in neural architecture search. Experiments show performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on unconstrained problems with continuous or discrete features. On problems combining mixed-variable spaces with known constraints, the framework outperforms competing methods. The contribution links the predictive strengths of tree ensembles with uncertainty-aware search and an explicit mechanism for respecting known structure.
summary.tldr: Tree-ensemble kernels support uncertainty-aware Bayesian optimization with mixed features and known constraints.

title: Tree ensemble kernels for Bayesian optimization with known constraints over mixed-feature spaces

abstract: Pretraining on large unlabeled datasets has been proven to improve the down-stream task performance on many computer vision tasks, such as 2D object detection and video classification. However, for large-scale 3D scenes, such as outdoor LiDAR point clouds, pretraining is not widely used. Due to the special data characteristics of large 3D point clouds, 2D pretraining frameworks tend to not generalize well. In this paper, we propose a new self-supervised pretraining method that targets large-scale 3D scenes. We pretrain commonly used point-based and voxel-based model architectures and show the transfer learning performance on 3D object detection and also semantic segmentation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on both dense 3D indoor point clouds and also sparse outdoor lidar point clouds.

paragraphs: Pretraining on unlabeled data has improved many vision tasks, but it is less widely used for large three-dimensional scenes. This paper focuses on point clouds, including outdoor LiDAR data. Their distinctive structure means that pretraining frameworks developed for two-dimensional images do not readily transfer to these large 3D inputs.

The authors propose a self-supervised pretraining method specifically for large-scale 3D scenes. They apply it to commonly used point-based and voxel-based architectures, covering two ways of representing and processing the data. The learned representations are then transferred to 3D object detection and semantic segmentation, testing their usefulness for locating objects and assigning semantic categories.

The study demonstrates effectiveness on both dense indoor point clouds and sparse outdoor LiDAR point clouds. That coverage matters because the proposed pretraining is evaluated across substantially different scene and sampling characteristics. The main contribution is evidence that pretraining designed around large 3D data can benefit downstream understanding across both architectural families and both kinds of point-cloud environments.
summary.tldr: Self-supervised pretraining tailored to large 3D point clouds benefits detection and segmentation across indoor and outdoor settings.

title: Self-Supervised Pretraining for Large-Scale Point Clouds

abstract: We investigate the parameterization of deep neural networks that by design satisfy the continuity equation, a fundamental conservation law. This is enabled by the observation that any solution of the continuity equation can be represented as a divergence-free vector field. We hence propose building divergence-free neural networks through the concept of differential forms, and with the aid of automatic differentiation, realize two practical constructions. As a result, we can parameterize pairs of densities and vector fields that always satisfy the continuity equation by construction, foregoing the need for extra penalty methods or expensive numerical simulation. Furthermore, we prove these models are universal and so can be used to represent any divergence-free vector field. Finally, we experimentally validate our approaches by computing neural network-based solutions to fluid equations, solving for the Hodge decomposition, and learning dynamical optimal transport maps.

paragraphs: The continuity equation expresses a fundamental conservation relationship between a density and its flow. This paper asks how to build neural representations that satisfy that relationship automatically. The goal is to encode conservation in the model’s construction, avoiding the need to enforce it through additional penalties or expensive numerical simulation.

The key observation is that solutions of the continuity equation can be expressed as divergence-free vector fields. The authors use differential forms to design neural networks with this property and implement two practical constructions with automatic differentiation. These networks parameterize density and vector-field pairs whose relationship satisfies the continuity equation by construction.

The paper also proves universality for the proposed models, establishing their ability to represent divergence-free vector fields rather than only a narrowly chosen family. Experiments validate the constructions through neural solutions of fluid equations, Hodge decomposition, and dynamical optimal transport maps. The contribution brings together an exact structural conservation property, expressive representation, and demonstrations across several related computational tasks.
summary.tldr: Divergence-free neural constructions enforce the continuity equation by design and have a universality guarantee.

title: Neural Conservation Laws: A Divergence-Free Perspective

abstract: Deceptive agents are a challenge for the safety, trustworthiness, and cooperation of AI systems. We focus on the problem that agents might deceive in order to achieve their goals (for instance, in our experiments with language models, the goal of being evaluated as truthful).There are a number of existing definitions of deception in the literature on game theory and symbolic AI, but there is no overarching theory of deception for learning agents in games. We introduce a formaldefinition of deception in structural causal games, grounded in the philosophyliterature, and applicable to real-world machine learning systems.Several examples and results illustrate that our formal definition aligns with the philosophical and commonsense meaning of deception.Our main technical result is to provide graphical criteria for deception. We show, experimentally, that these results can be used to mitigate deception in reinforcement learning agents and language models.

paragraphs: An AI agent may have an incentive to deceive if doing so helps it achieve its objective. The paper highlights an especially revealing example: language models pursuing the goal of being judged truthful can still exhibit deception. Studying that behavior requires a definition that applies to learning agents and captures more than whether an isolated statement is false.

The authors formulate deception within structural causal games, grounding their definition in philosophical work. This supplies a common mathematical setting for reasoning about agents, their objectives, and causal relationships. Examples and formal results are used to show that the definition agrees with philosophical and everyday understandings of deception.

The main technical contribution is a set of graphical criteria for deception. These criteria make the causal structure useful for identifying circumstances relevant to deceptive behavior. Experiments show that the resulting insights can mitigate deception in both reinforcement learning agents and language models. The contribution connects a formal account of the behavior with demonstrated mitigation, without claiming that deception is universally eliminated.
summary.tldr: The paper defines deception in causal games and derives graphical criteria used experimentally to reduce deceptive AI behavior.

title: Honesty Is the Best Policy: Defining and Mitigating AI Deception

abstract: This work proposes a Momentum-Enabled Kronecker-Factor-Based Optimizer Using Rank-1 updates, called MKOR, that improves the training time and convergence properties of deep neural networks (DNNs). Second-order techniques, while enjoying higher convergence rates vs first-order counterparts, have cubic complexity with respect to either the model size and/or the training batch size. Hence they exhibit poor scalability and performance in transformer models, e.g. large language models (LLMs), because the batch sizes in these models scale by the attention mechanism sequence length, leading to large model size and batch sizes. MKOR's complexity is quadratic with respect to the model size, alleviating the computation bottlenecks in second-order methods. Because of their high computation complexity, state-of-the-art implementations of second-order methods can only afford to update the second order information infrequently, and thus do not fully exploit the promise of better convergence from these updates. By reducing the communication complexity of the second-order updates as well as achieving a linear communication complexity, MKOR increases the frequency of second order updates. We also propose a hybrid version of MKOR (called MKOR-H) that mid-training falls backs to a first order optimizer if the second order updates no longer accelerate convergence. Our experiments show that MKOR outperforms state -of-the-art first order methods, e.g. the LAMB optimizer, and best implementations of second-order methods, i.e. KAISA/KFAC, up to 2.57x and 1.85x respectively on BERT-Large-Uncased on 64 GPUs.

paragraphs: Second-order optimizers can offer faster convergence, but their computational demands make them difficult to scale to large neural networks. The paper highlights cubic costs in model size or batch size, a particular problem for transformers. Those costs also force implementations to refresh second-order information infrequently, limiting how much benefit it can provide during training.

MKOR combines momentum, Kronecker factors, and rank-one updates to reduce these burdens. Its computational complexity is quadratic in model size, and its communication complexity is linear. Lower update costs allow second-order information to be refreshed more frequently. A hybrid variant, MKOR-H, switches to a first-order optimizer during training if second-order updates stop accelerating convergence.

On BERT-Large-Uncased using 64 GPUs, the reported improvements reach 2.57 times relative to LAMB and 1.85 times relative to KAISA/KFAC. These results support the paper's emphasis on training efficiency: more informative optimization updates become useful at scale when their computation and communication overheads are sufficiently reduced, with the hybrid variant adapting when their benefit diminishes.
summary.tldr: MKOR reduces second-order optimization costs with momentum and rank-one updates, delivering reported training improvements on BERT-Large.

title: MKOR: Momentum-Enabled Kronecker-Factor-Based Optimizer Using Rank-1 Updates

abstract: This paper investigates posterior sampling algorithms for competitive reinforcement learning (RL) in the context of general function approximations. Focusing on zero-sum Markov games (MGs) under two critical settings, namely self-play and adversarial learning, we first propose the self-play and adversarial generalized eluder coefficient (GEC) as complexity measures for function approximation, capturing the exploration-exploitation trade-off in MGs. Based on self-play GEC, we propose a model-based self-play posterior sampling method to control both players to learn Nash equilibrium, which can successfully handle the partial observability of states. Furthermore, we identify a set of partially observable MG models fitting MG learning with the adversarial policies of the opponent. Incorporating the adversarial GEC, we propose a model-based posterior sampling method for learning adversarial MG with potential partial observability. We further provide low regret bounds for proposed algorithms that can scale sublinearly with the proposed GEC and the number of episodes $T$. To the best of our knowledge, we for the first time develop generic model-based posterior sampling algorithms for competitive RL that can be applied to a majority of tractable zero-sum MG classes in both fully observable and partially observable MGs with self-play and adversarial learning.

paragraphs: Competitive reinforcement learning must balance learning about the environment with acting effectively against another player. This paper studies posterior sampling in zero-sum Markov games with general function approximation. It considers both self-play, where the learning procedure controls both players, and adversarial learning, where it faces an opponent’s policies.

The authors introduce separate generalized eluder coefficients for these two settings. These complexity measures capture the exploration-exploitation difficulty associated with function approximation. Using the self-play coefficient, they develop a model-based posterior-sampling algorithm for learning a Nash equilibrium that also handles partially observed states. For adversarial learning, they identify suitable partially observable model classes and construct a corresponding sampling method.

The proposed algorithms receive low-regret guarantees that can scale sublinearly with both the relevant coefficient and the number of episodes. The authors present the framework as applicable to a majority of tractable zero-sum Markov-game classes under full or partial observation. Its contribution is a common theoretical treatment of posterior sampling across these distinct competitive-learning situations.
summary.tldr: Generalized eluder coefficients support posterior-sampling algorithms and regret guarantees for self-play and adversarial zero-sum games, including partial observation.

title: Posterior Sampling for Competitive RL: Function Approximation and Partial Observation

abstract: We study a new class of Markov games, \textit{(multi-player) zero-sum Markov Games} with {\it Networked separable interactions} (zero-sum NMGs), to model the local interaction structure in non-cooperative multi-agent sequential decision-making. We define a zero-sum NMG as a model where {the payoffs of the auxiliary games associated with each state are zero-sum and} have some separable (i.e., polymatrix) structure across the neighbors over some interaction network. We first identify the necessary and sufficient conditions under which an MG can be presented as a zero-sum NMG, and show that the set of Markov coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) collapses to the set of Markov Nash equilibrium (NE) in these games, in that the {product of} per-state marginalization of the former for all players yields the latter. Furthermore, we show that finding approximate Markov \emph{stationary} CCE in infinite-horizon discounted zero-sum NMGs is \texttt{PPAD}-hard, unless the underlying network has a ``star topology''. Then, we propose fictitious-play-type dynamics, the classical learning dynamics in normal-form games, for zero-sum NMGs, and establish convergence guarantees to Markov stationary NE under a star-shaped network structure. Finally, in light of the hardness result, we focus on computing a Markov \emph{non-stationary} NE and provide finite-iteration guarantees for a series of value-iteration-based algorithms. We also provide numerical experiments to corroborate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential games in which multiple competing players interact through a network. At each state, the associated game has zero-sum payoffs and a separable structure across neighboring players. The framework captures local interactions while retaining a structured form of competition.

The authors characterize exactly when a Markov game admits this representation. They also establish a relationship between equilibrium concepts: taking each player's per-state marginal from a Markov coarse correlated equilibrium and forming their product yields a Markov Nash equilibrium. Despite this relationship, finding approximate stationary coarse correlated equilibria in infinite-horizon discounted games is PPAD-hard unless the network has a star topology.

For star-shaped networks, the paper develops fictitious-play-style learning dynamics and proves convergence to stationary Nash equilibria. It also studies non-stationary equilibria, providing finite-iteration guarantees for value-iteration-based algorithms. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings. The results distinguish the consequences of network structure and whether strategies must remain stationary, showing why these choices matter for equilibrium computation.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes equilibria and computational difficulty in networked zero-sum Markov games, with stronger stationary guarantees for star networks.

title: Multi-Player Zero-Sum Markov Games with Networked Separable Interactions

abstract: We study the connection between gradient-based meta-learning and convex optimisation. We observe that gradient descent with momentum is a special case of meta-gradients, and building on recent results in optimisation, we prove convergence rates for meta learning in the single task setting. While a meta-learned update rule can yield faster convergence up to constant factor, it is not sufficient for acceleration. Instead, some form of optimism is required. We show that optimism in meta-learning can be captured through the recently proposed Bootstrapped Meta-Gradient (Flennerhag et. al., 2022) method, providing deeper insight into its underlying mechanics.

paragraphs: Gradient-based meta-learning can learn how an optimization process updates its parameters. This paper connects that idea to convex optimization, beginning with the observation that gradient descent with momentum is a special case of meta-gradients. That connection allows familiar optimization tools to clarify what learning an update rule can accomplish.

Building on optimization results, the authors prove convergence rates for meta-learning in a single-task setting. They distinguish a constant-factor speed improvement from acceleration of the convergence rate. A meta-learned update rule can provide the former, but learning such a rule alone is insufficient for the latter in the analysis.

The missing ingredient is some form of optimism, which the paper shows can be captured through the Bootstrapped Meta-Gradient method. This gives a theoretical interpretation of that method's mechanics and explains why the structure of the meta-learning procedure matters. The result concerns the analyzed single-task setting and separates faster execution of a convergence pattern from a stronger improvement in how convergence scales.
summary.tldr: A single-task convergence analysis shows that meta-learned updates can offer constant-factor gains, while acceleration requires an additional form of optimism.

title: Optimistic Meta-Gradients

abstract: Deep learning methods have gained popularity in high energy physics for fast modeling of particle showers in detectors. Detailed simulation frameworks such as the gold standard \textsc{Geant4} are computationally intensive, and current deep generative architectures work on discretized, lower resolution versions of the detailed simulation. The development of models that work at higher spatial resolutions is currently hindered by the complexity of the full simulation data, and by the lack of simpler, more interpretable benchmarks. Our contribution is \textsc{SUPA}, the SUrrogate PArticle propagation simulator, an algorithm and software package for generating data by simulating simplified particle propagation, scattering and shower development in matter. The generation is extremely fast and easy to use compared to \textsc{Geant4}, but still exhibits the key characteristics and challenges of the detailed simulation. The proposed simulator generates thousands of particle showers per second on a desktop machine, a speed up of up to 6 orders of magnitudes over \textsc{Geant4}, and stores detailed geometric information about the shower propagation. \textsc{\textsc{SUPA}} provides much greater flexibility for setting initial conditions and defining multiple benchmarks for the development of models. Moreover, interpreting particle showers as point clouds creates a connection to geometric machine learning and provides challenging and fundamentally new datasets for the field.

paragraphs: Developing generative models of particle showers is difficult when the training data comes from expensive, highly complex simulations. SUPA supplies a simpler diagnostic environment for this work. It simulates particle propagation, scattering, and shower development while retaining key characteristics and challenges of detailed detector simulation.

The contribution includes both an algorithm and a software package. SUPA generates thousands of showers per second on a desktop machine, with a reported speedup of up to six orders of magnitude over Geant4. It also records detailed geometric information and allows flexible initial conditions, supporting the construction of multiple controlled benchmarks.

The simplification is central to its role: researchers gain an interpretable environment for developing models, including those aimed at higher spatial resolution. Representing showers as point clouds also connects particle-physics simulation with geometric machine learning. The paper thus offers fast benchmark data with adjustable conditions and rich geometry, giving model development a more accessible experimental setting than full detailed simulation.
summary.tldr: SUPA rapidly generates simplified particle showers with detailed geometry for interpretable machine-learning benchmarks.

title: SUPA: A Lightweight Diagnostic Simulator for Machine Learning in Particle Physics

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new functional point of view on bilevel optimization problems for machine learning, where the inner objective is minimized over a function space. These types of problems are most often solved by using methods developed in the parametric setting, where the inner objective is strongly convex with respect to the parameters of the prediction function. The functional point of view does not rely on this assumption and notably allows using over-parameterized neural networks as the inner prediction function. We propose scalable and efficient algorithms for the functional bilevel optimization problem and illustrate the benefits of our approach on instrumental regression and reinforcement learning tasks.

These types of problems are most often solved by using methods developed in the parametric setting, where the inner objective is strongly convex with respect to the parameters of the prediction function. The functional point of view does not rely on this assumption and notably allows using over-parameterized neural networks as the inner prediction function. We propose scalable and efficient algorithms for the functional bilevel optimization problem and illustrate the benefits of our approach on instrumental regression and reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves one optimization problem whose solution depends on another, inner optimization problem. In the machine-learning setting considered here, the inner problem chooses a prediction function. The paper changes the viewpoint used to solve this nested problem by treating the inner choice directly as an optimization over a function space.

Common approaches instead work with the parameters used to represent the prediction function. The methods described in the abstract rely on strong convexity of the inner objective with respect to those parameters. The proposed functional perspective does not require that particular assumption, making room for over-parameterized neural networks as inner prediction models.

The authors develop scalable, efficient algorithms around this formulation and illustrate their benefits on instrumental regression and reinforcement-learning tasks. The contribution is both conceptual and algorithmic: it changes the object being optimized and provides methods for working with that change. Its significance is the ability to address nested learning problems without relying on parameter-level strong convexity of the inner objective.
summary.tldr: A function-space formulation of bilevel optimization supports over-parameterized inner neural networks without requiring parameter-level strong convexity.

title: Functional Bilevel Optimization for Machine Learning

abstract: Dynamical systems theory (DST) is fundamental for many areas of science and engineering. It can provide deep insights into the behavior of systems evolving in time, as typically described by differential or recursive equations. A common approach to facilitate mathematical tractability and interpretability of DS models involves decomposing nonlinear DS into multiple linear DS combined by switching manifolds, i.e. piecewise linear (PWL) systems. PWL models are popular in engineering and a frequent choice in mathematics for analyzing the topological properties of DS. However, hand-crafting such models is tedious and only possible for very low-dimensional scenarios, while inferring them from data usually gives rise to unnecessarily complex representations with very many linear subregions. Here we introduce Almost-Linear Recurrent Neural Networks (AL-RNNs) which automatically and robustly produce most parsimonious PWL representations of DS from time series data, using as few PWL nonlinearities as possible. AL-RNNs can be efficiently trained with any SOTA algorithm for dynamical systems reconstruction (DSR), and naturally give rise to a symbolic encoding of the underlying DS that provably preserves important topological properties. We show that for the Lorenz and Rössler systems, AL-RNNs derive, in a purely data-driven way, the known topologically minimal PWL representations of the corresponding chaotic attractors. We further illustrate on two challenging empirical datasets that interpretable symbolic encodings of the dynamics can be achieved, tremendously facilitating mathematical and computational analysis of the underlying systems.

paragraphs: A dynamical system describes how a system changes over time. One way to make nonlinear behavior easier to analyze is to divide it into regions, each governed by linear dynamics. The difficulty is finding a useful division: constructing one by hand becomes difficult beyond very small systems, while learning one from data can produce too many regions to interpret.

Two empirical datasets further demonstrate interpretable symbolic encodings. These findings connect learned prediction models with mathematical descriptions that make the reconstructed dynamics easier to examine computationally and theoretically.
summary.tldr: Almost-Linear RNNs learn compact dynamical models whose symbolic descriptions preserve important topological properties and support interpretation.

title: Almost-Linear RNNs Yield Highly Interpretable Symbolic Codes in Dynamical Systems Reconstruction

abstract: Data valuation has emerged as a powerful framework for quantifying each datum's contribution to the training of a machine learning model. However, it is crucial to recognize that the quality of cells within a single data point can vary greatly in practice. For example, even in the case of an abnormal data point, not all cells are necessarily noisy. The single scalar score assigned by existing data valuation methods blurs the distinction between noisy and clean cells of a data point, making it challenging to interpret the data values. In this paper, we propose 2D-OOB, an out-of-bag estimation framework for jointly determining helpful (or detrimental) samples as well as the particular cells that drive them. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that 2D-OOB achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple use cases while being exponentially faster. Specifically, 2D-OOB shows promising results in detecting and rectifying fine-grained outliers at the cell level, and localizing backdoor triggers in data poisoning attacks.

paragraphs: Data valuation asks how much individual training examples help or hurt a model. A single score for an entire example can hide an important distinction: some of its cells may contain useful information while others are noisy. Calling the whole example harmful therefore does not explain which parts caused the problem.

2D-OOB addresses this by evaluating samples and their individual cells together. Its out-of-bag estimation framework identifies helpful or detrimental examples while also locating the cells responsible for those assessments. This makes the resulting values more interpretable because an example's overall contribution can be connected to particular pieces of its contents.

The experiments report leading performance across multiple applications and an exponential speed advantage. More specifically, the method shows promising results for finding and correcting unusual values at the cell level and locating backdoor triggers in poisoned data. These findings suggest that joint valuation can support targeted data repair, preserving useful parts of examples while identifying the parts that need attention.
summary.tldr: 2D-OOB jointly values training examples and their individual cells to identify which pieces of data help or harm a model.

title: 2D-OOB: Attributing Data Contribution Through Joint Valuation Framework

abstract: The rapid proliferation of open-source language models significantly increases the risks of downstream backdoor attacks. These backdoors can introduce dangerous behaviours during model deployment and can evade detection by conventional cybersecurity monitoring systems. In this paper, we introduce a novel class of backdoors in transformer models, that, in contrast to prior art, are unelicitable in nature. Unelicitability prevents the defender from triggering the backdoor, making it impossible to properly evaluate ahead of deployment even if given full white-box access and using automated techniques, such as red-teaming or certain formal verification methods. We show that our novel construction is not only unelicitable thanks to using cryptographic techniques, but also has favourable robustness properties.We confirm these properties in empirical investigations, and provide evidence that our backdoors can withstand state-of-the-art mitigation strategies. Additionally, we expand on previous work by showing that our universal backdoors, while not completely undetectable in white-box settings, can be harder to detect than some existing designs. By demonstrating the feasibility of seamlessly integrating backdoors into transformer models, this paper fundamentally questions the efficacy of pre-deployment detection strategies. This offers new insights into the offence-defence balance in AI safety and security.

paragraphs: This paper introduces transformer backdoors designed to resist attempts by defenders to trigger them during evaluation. The construction uses cryptographic techniques to make the malicious behavior unelicitable, even when defenders have full access to the model's internal structure. This challenges evaluation strategies that depend on producing examples of dangerous behavior before deployment.

The authors distinguish this inability to trigger a backdoor from complete inability to detect its presence. Their universal backdoors are not completely undetectable under white-box access, although they can be harder to detect than some previous designs. That distinction matters: finding evidence that a model contains a backdoor and successfully eliciting its behavior are separate evaluation problems.

Empirical investigations confirm robustness properties of the construction and provide evidence that the backdoors can withstand state-of-the-art mitigation strategies. The authors also demonstrate their integration into transformer models. The findings question how much assurance predeployment red-teaming and certain formal verification methods can provide against this class of attack, while preserving the distinction between unelicitability and undetectability.
summary.tldr: Cryptographic transformer backdoors can resist triggering during white-box evaluation and withstand tested mitigations without being completely undetectable.

title: Unelicitable Backdoors via Cryptographic Transformer Circuits

abstract: We consider the problem of online multi-agent Nash social welfare (NSW) maximization. While previous works of Hossain et al. [2021], Jones et al. [2023] study similar problems in stochastic multi-agent multi-armed bandits and show that $\sqrt{T}$-regret is possible after $T$ rounds, their fairness measure is the product of all agents' rewards, instead of their NSW (that is, their geometric mean). Given the fundamental role of NSW in the fairness literature, it is more than natural to ask whether no-regret fair learning with NSW as the objective is possible. In this work, we provide a complete answer to this question in various settings. Specifically, in stochastic $N$-agent $K$-armed bandits, we develop an algorithm with $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(K^{\frac{2}{N}}T^{\frac{N-1}{N}})$ regret and prove that the dependence on $T$ is tight, making it a sharp contrast to the $\sqrt{T}$-regret bounds of Hossain et al. [2021], Jones et al. [2023]. We then consider a more challenging version of the problem with adversarial rewards. Somewhat surprisingly, despite NSW being a concave function, we prove that no algorithm can achieve sublinear regret. To circumvent such negative results, we further consider a setting with full-information feedback and design two algorithms with $\sqrt{T}$-regret: the first one has no dependence on $N$ at all and is applicable to not just NSW but a broad class of welfare functions, while the second one has better dependence on $K$ and is preferable when $N$ is small.Finally, we also show that logarithmic regret is possible whenever there exists one agent who is indifferent about different arms.

paragraphs: This paper studies online decisions intended to benefit multiple agents fairly, using Nash social welfare: the geometric mean of their rewards. Earlier related bandit work instead used their reward product. The distinction changes the learning guarantees, motivating an analysis of whether accumulated regret can grow slower than the number of decision rounds.

For stochastic bandits with N agents and K arms, the authors obtain regret of order K^(2/N) T^((N−1)/N), up to logarithmic factors. They prove the dependence on T is tight. This contrasts with the square-root dependence previously obtained for the product objective. With adversarial rewards and bandit feedback, they prove that sublinear regret is impossible.

Full-information feedback permits two algorithms with square-root regret. One has no dependence on the number of agents and extends to a broad class of welfare functions; the other improves dependence on the number of arms and is preferable with few agents. They also establish logarithmic regret when an agent is indifferent between arms, highlighting how feedback and reward structure affect attainable fairness guarantees.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes achievable and impossible regret guarantees for Nash social welfare across stochastic, adversarial, and full-information settings.

title: No-Regret Learning for Fair Multi-Agent Social Welfare Optimization

abstract: The concept of probabilistic values, such as Beta Shapley values and weighted Banzhaf values, has gained recent attention in applications like feature attribution and data valuation. However, exact computation of these values is often exponentially expensive, necessitating approximation techniques. Prior research has shown that the choice of probabilistic values significantly impacts downstream performance, with no universally superior option. Consequently, one may have to approximate multiple candidates and select the best-performing one. Although there have been many efforts to develop efficient estimators, none are intended to approximate all probabilistic values both simultaneously and efficiently. In this work, we embark on the first exploration of achieving this goal. Adhering to the principle of maximum sample reuse and avoiding amplifying factors, we propose a one-sample-fits-all framework parameterized by a sampling vector to approximate intermediate terms that can be converted to any probabilistic value. Leveraging the concept of $ (\epsilon, \delta) $-approximation, we theoretically identify a key formula that effectively determines the convergence rate of our framework. By optimizing the sampling vector using this formula, we obtain i) a one-for-all estimator that achieves the currently best time complexity for all probabilistic values on average, and ii) a faster generic estimator with the sampling vector optimally tuned for each probabilistic value. Particularly, our one-for-all estimator achieves the fastest convergence rate on Beta Shapley values, including the well-known Shapley value, both theoretically and empirically. Finally, we establish a connection between probabilistic values and the least square regression used in (regularized) datamodels, showing that our one-for-all estimator can solve a family of datamodels simultaneously. Our code is available at https://github.com/watml/one-for-all.

paragraphs: Probabilistic values assign credit to features or data points, but different choices can work better for different downstream tasks. Exact computation is often exponentially expensive, so comparing several choices requires approximation. This paper develops a shared estimation framework intended to make that comparison efficient by reusing samples across different probabilistic values.

Instead of estimating each value separately, the method estimates intermediate quantities that can be converted into any probabilistic value. A sampling vector controls how the shared information is collected. The authors derive a formula governing convergence under a specified accuracy-and-confidence criterion, then optimize that vector to obtain both a general one-for-all estimator and estimators tuned to individual values.

The one-for-all estimator attains the best currently known time complexity averaged across probabilistic values, according to the paper. For Beta Shapley values, including Shapley itself, the authors establish the fastest convergence rate theoretically and empirically. They also connect these values to least-squares datamodels, showing that the shared estimator can solve a family of such models simultaneously.
summary.tldr: A shared sampling framework efficiently approximates multiple probabilistic attribution values and also solves a related family of datamodels.

title: One Sample Fits All: Approximating All Probabilistic Values Simultaneously and Efficiently

abstract: The task of distinguishing individuals of interest from a vast pool of candidates using predictive models has garnered significant attention in recent years. This task can be framed as a *conformalized multiple testing* procedure, which aims at quantifying prediction uncertainty by controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) via conformal inference. In this paper, we tackle the challenge of conformalized multiple testing after data-dependent selection procedures. To guarantee the construction of valid test statistics that accurately capture the distorted distribution resulting from the selection process, we leverage a holdout labeled set to closely emulate the selective distribution. Our approach involves adaptively picking labeled data to create a calibration set based on the stability of the selection rule. This strategy ensures that the calibration data and the selected test unit are exchangeable, allowing us to develop valid conformal p-values. Implementing with the famous Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, it effectively controls the FDR over the selected subset. To handle the randomness of the selected subset and the dependence among the constructed p-values, we establish a unified theoretical framework. This framework extends the application of conformalized multiple testing to complex selective settings. Furthermore, we conduct numerical studies to showcase the effectiveness and validity of our procedures across various scenarios.

paragraphs: Predictive models can help identify individuals of interest within a large candidate pool, but selecting candidates using the data changes the distribution being evaluated. This paper studies how to control the false discovery rate after that selection. The challenge is to construct uncertainty measures that reflect the selected population rather than treating selection as irrelevant.

The method uses a held-out labeled dataset to reproduce the effects of the selection process. It adaptively chooses calibration examples according to the stability of the selection rule. This construction makes the calibration data exchangeable with the selected test unit, providing the symmetry needed to obtain valid conformal p-values.

The resulting p-values are used with the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure to control false discoveries within the selected subset. The theoretical framework accounts for both the randomness of that subset and dependence among the p-values. Numerical studies support the procedures' validity and effectiveness across several scenarios. The central contribution is a way to incorporate selection into calibration so that statistical guarantees remain meaningful for the candidates actually examined.
summary.tldr: Selection-aware calibration enables valid conformal testing and false-discovery control within data-selected candidate subsets.

title: Conformalized Multiple Testing after Data-dependent Selection

abstract: The empirical success of distributional reinforcement learning (RL) highly relies on the choice of distribution divergence equipped with an appropriate distribution representation. In this paper, we propose \textit{Sinkhorn distributional RL (SinkhornDRL)}, which leverages Sinkhorn divergence—a regularized Wasserstein loss—to minimize the difference between current and target Bellman return distributions. Theoretically, we prove the contraction properties of SinkhornDRL, aligning with the interpolation nature of Sinkhorn divergence between Wasserstein distance and Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD). The introduced SinkhornDRL enriches the family of distributional RL algorithms, contributing to interpreting the algorithm behaviors compared with existing approaches by our investigation into their relationships. Empirically, we show that SinkhornDRL consistently outperforms or matches existing algorithms on the Atari games suite and particularly stands out in the multi-dimensional reward setting. \thanks{Code is available in \url{https://github.com/datake/SinkhornDistRL}.}.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning models a distribution of possible returns, making the choice of how to compare distributions central to learning. The paper focuses on this comparison rule and its relationship to the representation of returns. It introduces SinkhornDRL, which uses Sinkhorn divergence, a regularized Wasserstein loss, to compare current return predictions with their Bellman targets.

The authors prove contraction properties for the proposed approach. These properties align with Sinkhorn divergence's position between Wasserstein distance and maximum mean discrepancy. The analysis also examines relationships with existing distributional methods, helping explain algorithm behavior through the distribution comparisons those methods use.

Experiments on the Atari suite show that SinkhornDRL consistently matches or exceeds existing algorithms in the reported evaluation. Its performance is especially strong when rewards have multiple dimensions. The result connects a theoretically analyzed comparison between return distributions to practical learning performance, while the multi-dimensional reward findings highlight a setting where the chosen divergence appears particularly useful.
summary.tldr: SinkhornDRL uses a regularized Wasserstein loss to learn return distributions, with contraction guarantees and strong Atari results.

title: Distributional Reinforcement Learning with Regularized Wasserstein Loss

abstract: Generalized-linear dynamical models (GLDMs) remain a widely-used framework within neuroscience for modeling time-series data, such as neural spiking activity or categorical decision outcomes. Whereas the standard usage of GLDMs is to model a single data source, certain applications require jointly modeling two generalized-linear time-series sources while also dissociating their shared and private dynamics. Most existing GLDM variants and their associated learning algorithms do not support this capability. Here we address this challenge by developing a multi-step analytical subspace identification algorithm for learning a GLDM that explicitly models shared vs. private dynamics within two generalized-linear time-series. In simulations, we demonstrate our algorithm's ability to dissociate and model the dynamics within two time-series sources while being agnostic to their respective observation distributions. In neural data, we consider two specific applications of our algorithm for modeling discrete population spiking activity with respect to a secondary time-series. In both synthetic and real data, GLDMs learned with our algorithm more accurately decoded one time-series from the other using lower-dimensional latent states, as compared to models identified using existing GLDM learning algorithms.

abstract: Surface electromyography (sEMG) non-invasively measures signals generated by muscle activity with sufficient sensitivity to detect individual spinal neurons and richness to identify dozens of gestures and their nuances. Wearable wrist-based sEMG sensors have the potential to offer low friction, subtle, information rich, always available human-computer inputs. To this end, we introduce emg2qwerty, a large-scale dataset of non-invasive electromyographic signals recorded at the wrists while touch typing on a QWERTY keyboard, together with ground-truth annotations and reproducible baselines. With 1,135 sessions spanning 108 users and 346 hours of recording, this is the largest such public dataset to date. These data demonstrate non-trivial, but well defined hierarchical relationships both in terms of the generative process, from neurons to muscles and muscle combinations, as well as in terms of domain shift across users and user sessions. Applying standard modeling techniques from the closely related field of Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), we show strong baseline performance on predicting key-presses using sEMG signals alone. We believe the richness of this task and dataset will facilitate progress in several problems of interest to both the machine learning and neuroscientific communities. Dataset and code can be accessed at https://github.com/facebookresearch/emg2qwerty.

The combination of annotated recordings, repeated sessions, and multiple users makes the dataset useful for investigating prediction from muscle activity and the challenge of transferring models across changing users or sessions.

title: emg2qwerty: A Large Dataset with Baselines for Touch Typing using Surface Electromyography

abstract: Given a collection of feature maps indexed by a set $\mathcal{T}$, we study the performance of empirical risk minimization (ERM) on regression problems with square loss over the union of the linear classes induced by these feature maps. This setup aims at capturing the simplest instance of feature learning, where the model is expected to jointly learn from the data an appropriate feature map and a linear predictor. We start by studying the asymptotic quantiles of the excess risk of sequences of empirical risk minimizers. Remarkably, we show that when the set $\mathcal{T}$ is not too large and when there is a unique optimal feature map, these quantiles coincide, up to a factor of two, with those of the excess risk of the oracle procedure, which knows a priori this optimal feature map and deterministically outputs an empirical risk minimizer from the associated optimal linear class. We complement this asymptotic result with a non-asymptotic analysis that quantifies the decaying effect of the global complexity of the set $\mathcal{T}$ on the excess risk of ERM, and relates it to the size of the sublevel sets of the suboptimality of the feature maps. As an application of our results, we characterize the performance of the best subset selection procedure in sparse linear regression under general assumptions.

paragraphs: Feature learning involves choosing how to represent data as well as how to predict from that representation. This paper studies a simplified version: empirical risk minimization jointly chooses a feature map from a collection and a linear predictor, using squared regression loss. The question is how much that choice costs statistically.

The authors compare this learner with an oracle that already knows the best feature map and only fits the corresponding linear model. When the collection is not too large and the optimal feature map is unique, asymptotic quantiles of excess risk agree with the oracle's up to a factor of two. Thus, under these conditions, learning the representation can approach the performance of knowing it beforehand.

It relates that influence to the size of sets containing nearly optimal feature maps. The authors apply the results to best subset selection in sparse linear regression, characterizing its performance under general assumptions. The contribution connects representation selection with both oracle comparisons and finite-sample statistical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Under stated conditions, empirical risk minimization that learns a feature map approaches the excess-risk behavior of an oracle that already knows the best map.

title: On the Efficiency of ERM in Feature Learning

abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) have proven effective in various tasks including image, shape, audio, and video reconstruction. These INRs typically learn the implicit field from sampled input points. This is often done using a single network for the entire domain, imposing many global constraints on a single function. In this paper, we propose a mixture of experts (MoE) implicit neural representation approach that enables learning local piece-wise continuous functions that simultaneously learns to subdivide the domain and fit it locally. We show that incorporating a mixture of experts architecture into existing INR formulations provides a boost in speed, accuracy, and memory requirements. Additionally, we introduce novel conditioning and pretraining methods for the gating network that improves convergence to the desired solution. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on multiple reconstruction tasks, including surface reconstruction, image reconstruction, and audio signal reconstruction and show improved performance compared to non-MoE methods. Code is available at our project page https://sitzikbs.github.io/neural-experts-projectpage/ .

A common design asks one network to represent the entire domain. This places many global constraints on a single function, even when different parts of the signal have different local structure.

Neural Experts uses a mixture of experts to learn local, piecewise-continuous functions. The system learns both how to subdivide the domain and how to fit its parts. A gating network participates in this division, and the authors introduce conditioning and pretraining methods for that network to improve convergence toward the desired solution.

The approach can be incorporated into existing implicit-representation formulations. Evaluations on surface, image, and audio reconstruction show improvements over methods without a mixture of experts, with reported benefits in speed, accuracy, and memory requirements. The findings support distributing representation across locally fitted functions instead of placing the full reconstruction burden on a single network.
summary.tldr: Neural Experts jointly learns domain subdivisions and local implicit functions, improving reconstruction speed, accuracy, and memory requirements in evaluated tasks.

title: Neural Experts: Mixture of Experts for Implicit Neural Representations

abstract: Knowledge graph completion (KGC) can be framed as a 3-order binary tensor completion task. Tensor decomposition-based (TDB) models have demonstrated strong performance in KGC. In this paper, we provide a summary of existing TDB models and derive a general form for them, serving as a foundation for further exploration of TDB models. Despite the expressiveness of TDB models, they are prone to overfitting. Existing regularization methods merely minimize the norms of embeddings to regularize the model, leading to suboptimal performance. Therefore, we propose a novel regularization method for TDB models that addresses this limitation. The regularization is applicable to most TDB models and ensures tractable computation. Our method minimizes the norms of intermediate variables involved in the different ways of computing the predicted tensor. To support our regularization method, we provide a theoretical analysis that proves its effect in promoting low trace norm of the predicted tensor to reduce overfitting. Finally, we conduct experiments to verify the effectiveness of our regularization technique as well as the reliability of our theoretical analysis. The code is available at https://github.com/changyi7231/IVR.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph completion predicts missing relationships, and this paper treats it as completing a three-way binary tensor. Tensor decomposition models are effective for this task, but their expressive power also creates a tendency to overfit. The authors begin by deriving a general form that brings existing models into a shared framework.

They then propose a different target for regularization. Existing approaches constrain the sizes of embeddings; the new method constrains intermediate variables arising in different ways of computing the predicted tensor. This shifts the regularization toward quantities involved in constructing the prediction. The method applies to most tensor decomposition models while keeping computation tractable.

The theoretical analysis shows that this regularization promotes a low trace norm for the predicted tensor, providing a mathematical explanation for its role in reducing overfitting. Experiments support both the method's effectiveness and the theoretical account. The contribution combines a common description of existing models with a broadly applicable way to control their predictions through internal computation.
summary.tldr: Regularizing intermediate computations helps tensor-based knowledge graph models reduce overfitting, with theoretical and experimental support.

title: Knowledge Graph Completion by Intermediate Variables Regularization

abstract: An important problem in signal processing and deep learning is to achieve *invariance* to nuisance factors not relevant for the task. Since many of these factors are describable as the action of a group $G$ (e.g. rotations, translations, scalings), we want methods to be $G$-invariant. The $G$-Bispectrum extracts every characteristic of a given signal up to group action: for example, the shape of an object in an image, but not its orientation. Consequently, the $G$-Bispectrum has been incorporated into deep neural network architectures as a computational primitive for $G$-invariance\textemdash akin to a pooling mechanism, but with greater selectivity and robustness. However, the computational cost of the $G$-Bispectrum ($\mathcal{O}(|G|^2)$, with $|G|$ the size of the group) has limited its widespread adoption. Here, we show that the $G$-Bispectrum computation contains redundancies that can be reduced into a *selective $G$-Bispectrum* with $\mathcal{O}(|G|)$ complexity. We prove desirable mathematical properties of the selective $G$-Bispectrum and demonstrate how its integration in neural networks enhances accuracy and robustness compared to traditional approaches, while enjoying considerable speeds-up compared to the full $G$-Bispectrum.

title: The Selective $G$-Bispectrum and its Inversion: Applications to $G$-Invariant Networks

abstract: The well-known $\textit{empirical risk minimization}$ (ERM) principle is the basis of many widely used machine learning algorithms, and plays an essential role in the classical PAC theory. A common description of a learning algorithm's performance is its so-called “learning curve”, that is, the decay of the expected error as a function of the input sample size. As the PAC model fails to explain the behavior of learning curves, recent research has explored an alternative universal learning model and has ultimately revealed a distinction between optimal universal and uniform learning rates (Bousquet et al., 2021). However, a basic understanding of such differences with a particular focus on the ERM principle has yet to be developed. In this paper, we consider the problem of universal learning by ERM in the realizable case and study the possible universal rates. Our main result is a fundamental $\textit{tetrachotomy}$: there are only four possible universal learning rates by ERM, namely, the learning curves of any concept class learnable by ERM decay either at $e^{-n}$, $1/n$, $\log{(n)}/n$, or arbitrarily slow rates. Moreover, we provide a complete characterization of which concept classes fall into each of these categories, via new complexity structures. We also develop new combinatorial dimensions which supply sharp asymptotically-valid constant factors for these rates, whenever possible.

summary.tldr: In the realizable universal-learning setting, empirical risk minimization has four possible rate categories characterized by concept-class structure.

title: Universal Rates of Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: This paper investigates an under-explored challenge in large language models (LLMs): chain-of-thought prompting with noisy rationales, which include irrelevant or inaccurate reasoning thoughts within examples used for in-context learning. We construct NoRa dataset that is tailored to evaluate the robustness of reasoning in the presence of noisy rationales. Our findings on NoRa dataset reveal a prevalent vulnerability to such noise among current LLMs, with existing robust methods like self-correction and self-consistency showing limited efficacy. Notably, compared to prompting with clean rationales, base LLM drops by 1.4%-19.8% in accuracy with irrelevant thoughts and more drastically by 2.2%-40.4% with inaccurate thoughts.Addressing this challenge necessitates external supervision that should be accessible in practice. Here, we propose the method of contrastive denoising with noisy chain-of-thought (CD-CoT). It enhances LLMs' denoising-reasoning capabilities by contrasting noisy rationales with only one clean rationale, which can be the minimal requirement for denoising-purpose prompting. This method follows a principle of exploration and exploitation: (1) rephrasing and selecting rationales in the input space to achieve explicit denoising and (2) exploring diverse reasoning paths and voting on answers in the output space. Empirically, CD-CoT demonstrates an average improvement of 17.8% in accuracy over the base model and shows significantly stronger denoising capabilities than baseline methods. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/NoisyRationales.

Experiments report an average accuracy improvement of 17.8% over the base model and stronger denoising than the compared methods. These findings support combining a small amount of clean supervision with reasoning diversity.
summary.tldr: CD-CoT uses one clean reasoning example to help language models handle noisy demonstrations and improve answer accuracy.

title: Can Language Models Perform Robust Reasoning in Chain-of-thought Prompting with Noisy Rationales?

abstract: This paper introduces VeriThoughts, a novel dataset designed for reasoning-based Verilog code generation. We establish a new benchmark framework grounded in formal verification methods to evaluate the quality and correctness of generated hardware descriptions. Additionally, we present a suite of specialized small-scale models optimized specifically for Verilog generation. Our work addresses the growing need for automated hardware design tools that can produce verifiably correct implementations from high-level specifications, potentially accelerating the hardware development process while maintaining rigorous correctness guarantees.

The aim is to support automated design tools whose outputs can be checked rigorously for correctness.

A second contribution is a benchmark framework grounded in formal verification. This puts correctness evaluation at the center of assessing generated hardware descriptions. The benchmark is paired with a suite of small models specialized for Verilog generation, bringing together training material, task-focused generators, and a framework for evaluating their outputs.

These components address complementary parts of automated hardware development: learning to generate implementations, producing code with specialized models, and evaluating whether the resulting descriptions satisfy correctness requirements. The stated opportunity is to accelerate hardware development while maintaining rigorous guarantees. The abstract presents that acceleration as a potential benefit of the overall approach, with verifiable implementation serving as the organizing goal of the dataset, models, and evaluation framework.
summary.tldr: VeriThoughts combines a reasoning-oriented Verilog dataset, specialized small models, and formal-verification-based evaluation for automated hardware design.

title: VeriThoughts: Enabling Automated Verilog Code Generation using Reasoning and Formal Verification

abstract: Graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have emerged as powerful tools for analyzing graph-structured data, achieving remarkable success across diverse applications. However, the theoretical understanding of the stability of these models, i.e., their sensitivity to small changes in the graph structure, remains in rather limited settings, hampering the development and deployment of robust and trustworthy models in practice. To fill this gap, we study how small perturbations in the graph topology affect GCNN outputs and propose a novel formulation for analyzing model stability. Unlike prior studies that focus only on worst-case perturbations, our distribution-aware formulation characterizes output perturbations across a broad range of input data. This way, our framework enables, for the first time, a probabilistic perspective on the interplay between the statistical properties of the node data and perturbations in the graph topology. We conduct extensive experiments to validate our theoretical findings and demonstrate their benefits over existing baselines, in terms of both representation stability and adversarial attacks on downstream tasks. Our results demonstrate the practical significance of the proposed formulation and highlight the importance of incorporating data distribution into stability analysis.

paragraphs: A graph convolutional neural network uses both node information and the connections between nodes. Its stability concerns how much its output changes when the graph structure changes slightly. This paper develops a formulation for studying that sensitivity while accounting for the statistical properties of the data carried by the nodes.

The approach moves beyond analyses focused only on worst-case perturbations. It characterizes output changes across a broad range of input data, creating a probabilistic account of how node-data distributions interact with changes in graph topology.
