Our algorithms can achieve near-optimal regret in terms of minimizing the total cost, while successfully maintaining a sub-linear growth of accumulative risk constraint violation. We support our theoretical results by demonstrating our algorithm on a simple simulated robotics reactive control task.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions when each available action has both a cost and a risk. At each round, the learner observes a context, chooses an action, and receives only that action's cost and risk. The objective is to keep total cost low while controlling average accumulated risk relative to a predefined threshold.

The authors first develop a method for a full-information online convex problem, where each round reveals a convex loss and a convex constraint. Their meta-algorithm uses online mirror descent. They then extend it to the contextual-bandit setting with sequential risk constraints by incorporating expert advice.

The algorithms achieve near-optimal cost regret while keeping accumulated risk-constraint violation sublinear. Sublinear growth means the violation grows more slowly than the number of rounds, so its average contribution diminishes. This guarantee allows accumulated violations and does not require every individual action to stay below the risk threshold. A simple simulated robotics reactive-control task supports the theoretical results, illustrating the joint treatment of learning performance and long-run risk control.
summary.tldr: The proposed contextual-bandit algorithms achieve near-optimal cost regret while keeping accumulated risk-constraint violations sublinear.

title: Safety-Aware Algorithms for Adversarial Contextual Bandit

abstract: We introduce the feasible arm identification problem, a pure exploration multi-armed bandit problem where the agent is given a set of $D$-dimensional arms and a polyhedron $P = \{x : A x \leq b \} \subset R^D$. Pulling an arm gives a random vector and the goal is to determine, using a fixed budget of $T$ pulls, which of the arms have means belonging to $P$. We propose three algorithms MD-UCBE, MD-SAR, and MD-APT and provide a unified analysis establishing upper bounds for each of them. We also establish a lower bound that matches up to constants the upper bounds of MD-UCBE and MD-APT. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a bandit problem in which the goal is to identify which available options satisfy a collection of constraints. Each option, called an arm, produces a random vector when sampled. An arm is feasible when its mean vector lies inside a specified polyhedron: a region defined by linear inequalities.

The agent has a fixed budget of samples and must use them to determine feasibility across the arms. This is a pure exploration task, so the focus is gathering information for the final identification. The authors propose three algorithms, MD-UCBE, MD-SAR, and MD-APT, and develop a unified analysis giving upper bounds for each.

They also establish a lower bound that matches the upper bounds for MD-UCBE and MD-APT up to constant factors. This connects those algorithms’ guarantees to a fundamental difficulty of the problem. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate their effectiveness, complementing the theoretical analysis of identifying feasible options from noisy, multidimensional observations.
summary.tldr: The paper develops algorithms and matching bounds for identifying which bandit arms satisfy linear constraints under a fixed sampling budget.

title: Feasible Arm Identification

abstract: Researchers have applied deep neural networks to image restoration tasks, in which they proposed various network architectures, loss functions, and training methods. In particular, adversarial training, which is employed in recent studies, seems to be a key ingredient to success. In this paper, we show that simple convolutional autoencoders (CAEs) built upon only standard network components, i.e., convolutional layers and skip connections, can outperform the state-of-the-art methods which employ adversarial training and sophisticated loss functions. The secret is to search for good architectures using an evolutionary algorithm. All we did was to train the optimized CAEs by minimizing the l2 loss between reconstructed images and their ground truths using the ADAM optimizer. Our experimental results show that this approach achieves 27.8 dB peak signal to noise ratio (PSNR) on the CelebA dataset and 33.3 dB on the SVHN dataset, compared to 22.8 dB and 19.0 dB provided by the former state-of-the-art methods, respectively.

paragraphs: Image restoration research often combines new network architectures with sophisticated losses or adversarial training. This paper investigates how far standard convolutional autoencoders can go when their architecture is chosen carefully. Its main result is that networks built from convolutional layers and skip connections can outperform the compared state-of-the-art restoration methods.

The key step is an evolutionary search for effective architectures. After selecting the architecture, training uses the ADAM optimizer to minimize an l2 reconstruction loss between restored images and their ground truth. The approach therefore puts the main design effort into finding a suitable network structure while keeping the stated training objective and building blocks simple.

The reported results are 27.8 dB PSNR on CelebA and 33.3 dB on SVHN, compared with 22.8 dB and 19.0 dB for the former leading methods, respectively. These findings demonstrate the strength of architecture search in the evaluated restoration settings. They support the claim that standard components can be highly effective, without establishing that adversarial training or more elaborate losses are unnecessary for every restoration problem.
summary.tldr: Evolutionary architecture search produces standard convolutional autoencoders that outperform the compared image-restoration methods using simple reconstruction training.

title: Exploiting the Potential of Standard Convolutional Autoencoders for Image Restoration by Evolutionary Search

abstract: Many important datasets in physics, chemistry, and biology consist of noisy sequences of images of multiple moving overlapping particles. In many cases, the observed particles are indistinguishable, leading to unavoidable uncertainty about nearby particles’ identities. Exact Bayesian inference is intractable in this setting, and previous approximate Bayesian methods scale poorly. Non-Bayesian approaches that output a single “best” estimate of the particle tracks (thus discarding important uncertainty information) are therefore dominant in practice. Here we propose a flexible and scalable amortized approach for Bayesian inference on this task. We introduce a novel neural network method to approximate the (intractable) filter-backward-sample-forward algorithm for Bayesian inference in this setting. By varying the simulated training data for the network, we can perform inference on a wide variety of data types. This approach is therefore highly flexible and improves on the state of the art in terms of accuracy; provides uncertainty estimates about the particle locations and identities; and has a test run-time that scales linearly as a function of the data length and number of particles, thus enabling Bayesian inference in arbitrarily large particle tracking datasets.

paragraphs: Tracking multiple particles through noisy images becomes ambiguous when nearby particles overlap or look identical. A single chosen set of tracks hides that ambiguity, but exact Bayesian inference is computationally intractable in this setting. The paper develops an approximate Bayesian approach that retains uncertainty about both particle positions and identities.

The method uses a neural network to approximate the filter-backward-sample-forward inference algorithm. Its amortized design learns an inference procedure that can then be applied to tracking data. By changing the simulated data used to train the network, the approach can handle a wide variety of data types. This makes simulation a means of adapting the inference system to different particle-tracking settings.

The authors report improved accuracy over the state of the art while also producing uncertainty estimates. At test time, runtime scales linearly with data length and with the number of particles, supporting application to very large datasets. The central benefit is that preserving ambiguity need not require the poor scaling of previous approximate Bayesian methods or the information loss of a single best-track estimate.
summary.tldr: A simulation-trained neural inference method tracks particles with uncertainty estimates and linear test-time scaling.

title: Scalable approximate Bayesian inference for particle tracking data

abstract: Much of recent research has been devoted to video prediction and generation, yet most of the previous works have demonstrated only limited success in generating videos on short-term horizons. The hierarchical video prediction method by Villegas et al. (2017) is an example of a state-of-the-art method for long-term video prediction, but their method is limited because it requires ground truth annotation of high-level structures (e.g., human joint landmarks) at training time. Our network encodes the input frame, predicts a high-level encoding into the future, and then a decoder with access to the first frame produces the predicted image from the predicted encoding. The decoder also produces a mask that outlines the predicted foreground object (e.g., person) as a by-product. Unlike Villegas et al. (2017), we develop a novel training method that jointly trains the encoder, the predictor, and the decoder together without highlevel supervision; we further improve upon this by using an adversarial loss in the feature space to train the predictor. Our method can predict about 20 seconds into the future and provides better results compared to Denton and Fergus (2018) and Finn et al. (2016) on the Human 3.6M dataset.

paragraphs: Predicting video far into the future requires representing how a scene changes over time. Earlier hierarchical approaches used annotated high-level structures, such as human joint locations, to guide this process. This paper develops a hierarchy that learns its high-level representation without requiring those annotations during training.

The network encodes an input frame, predicts how that encoding will evolve, and decodes the predicted encoding into a future image. The decoder also receives the first frame and produces a foreground-object mask as a by-product. A joint training procedure learns the encoder, predictor, and decoder together, and an adversarial loss in feature space further improves the predictor.

The reported method predicts roughly 20 seconds into the future and gives better results than the compared Denton–Fergus and Finn approaches on Human 3.6M. The contribution is therefore both architectural and methodological: it retains a hierarchy between representations and images while learning that hierarchy without high-level supervision. The reported evaluation supports the usefulness of this training strategy for long-term video prediction in the studied dataset.
summary.tldr: A jointly trained hierarchical network predicts long-term video without annotated high-level structures, reaching roughly 20 seconds on the reported evaluation.

title: Hierarchical Long-term Video Prediction without Supervision

abstract: Adaptive importance sampling for stochastic optimization is a promising approach that offers improved convergence through variance reduction. In this work, we propose a new framework for variance reduction that enables the use of mixtures over predefined sampling distributions, which can naturally encode prior knowledge about the data. While these sampling distributions are fixed, the mixture weights are adapted during the optimization process. We propose VRM, a novel and efficient adaptive scheme that asymptotically recovers the best mixture weights in hindsight and can also accommodate sampling distributions over sets of points. We empirically demonstrate the versatility of VRM in a range of applications.

In this work, we propose a new framework for variance reduction that enables the use of mixtures over predefined sampling distributions, which can naturally encode prior knowledge about the data. While these sampling distributions are fixed, the mixture weights are adapted during the optimization process. We propose VRM, a novel and efficient adaptive scheme that asymptotically recovers the best mixture weights in hindsight and can also accommodate sampling distributions over sets of points. We empirically demonstrate the versatility of VRM in a range of applications.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization relies on sampled data, and variability in those samples can slow progress. Adaptive importance sampling aims to improve convergence by changing how samples are selected. This paper introduces a variance-reduction framework that combines several predefined sampling distributions, allowing existing knowledge about the data to be expressed through the available sampling choices.

The distributions themselves remain fixed, while their mixture weights change during optimization. This separates the design of candidate sampling patterns from learning how much emphasis each should receive. The proposed method, VRM, efficiently adapts those weights and can also work with distributions over sets of points, extending the framework beyond sampling choices that concern only individual points.

The theoretical result is asymptotic recovery of the best mixture weights in hindsight. That guarantee concerns the available predefined distributions and behavior in the limit, rather than immediate optimality at every training step. Experiments across a range of applications demonstrate the method’s versatility. The contribution is an adaptive way to combine sampling knowledge within the optimization process.
summary.tldr: VRM reduces stochastic-optimization variance by adapting weights over fixed sampling distributions and asymptotically recovering the best mixture in hindsight.

title: Online Variance Reduction with Mixtures

abstract: Structured stochastic processes evolving in continuous time present a widely adopted framework to model phenomena occurring in nature and engineering. However, such models are often chosen to satisfy the Markov property to maintain tractability. One of the more popular of such memoryless models are Continuous Time Bayesian Networks (CTBNs). In this work, we lift its restriction to exponential survival times to arbitrary distributions. Current extensions achieve this via auxiliary states, which hinder tractability. To avoid that, we introduce a set of node-wise clocks to construct a collection of graph-coupled semi-Markov chains. We provide algorithms for parameter and structure inference, which make use of local dependencies and conduct experiments on synthetic data and a data-set generated through a benchmark tool for gene regulatory networks. In doing so, we point out advantages compared to current CTBN extensions.

paragraphs: Continuous Time Bayesian Networks describe systems whose interacting components change at irregular times. Their usual formulation makes waiting times exponential, imposing a memoryless structure: how long a component has already remained in a state does not affect its remaining waiting time. This restriction helps computation but narrows the timing behavior the model can represent.

The paper replaces that restriction with arbitrary survival-time distributions by giving each node its own clock. These clocks support a collection of interacting semi-Markov chains, allowing elapsed time to influence transitions while retaining a graph that describes dependencies. Unlike extensions that introduce auxiliary states, this construction represents timing information directly through the clocks.

The authors provide algorithms for learning both model parameters and graph structure, using local dependencies to organize inference. Experiments use synthetic data and data generated by a gene regulatory network benchmark tool. The reported advantages concern extending the timing flexibility of these structured models while avoiding the tractability difficulties associated with auxiliary-state approaches.
summary.tldr: Node-wise clocks let continuous-time Bayesian networks represent arbitrary waiting-time distributions without introducing auxiliary states.

title: Continuous Time Bayesian Networks with Clocks

abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms usually assume that all actions are always available to an agent. However, both people and animals understand the general link between the features of their environment and the actions that are feasible. Gibson (1977) coined the term "affordances" to describe the fact that certain states enable an agent to do certain actions, in the context of embodied agents. In this paper, we develop a theory of affordances for agents who learn and plan in Markov Decision Processes. Affordances play a dual role in this case. On one hand, they allow faster planning, by reducing the number of actions available in any given situation. On the other hand, they facilitate more efficient and precise learning of transition models from data, especially when such models require function approximation. We establish these properties through theoretical results as well as illustrative examples. We also propose an approach to learn affordances and use it to estimate transition models that are simpler and generalize better.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly treats every action as available in every state. Yet useful behavior depends on recognizing what a situation makes possible. This paper develops a theory of these possibilities, called affordances, for agents that learn and plan within Markov decision processes.

Affordances serve two connected purposes in the proposed theory. They reduce the number of actions considered in a situation, allowing faster planning. They also support more efficient and precise learning of transition models, which describe how actions change the state. This second role is especially relevant when a model must approximate those transitions rather than represent them directly.

The authors establish these properties through theoretical results and illustrative examples. They also propose a method for learning affordances and use it to estimate transition models that are simpler and generalize better. The contribution shows that recognizing feasible actions can shape both decision-making and the model learned from experience, connecting a smaller planning problem with a more focused transition-learning problem.
summary.tldr: A theory of affordances shows how recognizing feasible actions can accelerate planning and improve transition-model learning.

title: What can I do here? A Theory of Affordances in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Machine learning systems must adapt to data distributions that evolve over time, in applications ranging from sensor networks and self-driving car perception modules to brain-machine interfaces. Traditional domain adaptation is only guaranteed to work when the distribution shift is small; empirical methods combine several heuristics for larger shifts but can be dataset specific. To adapt to larger shifts we consider gradual domain adaptation, where the goal is to adapt an initial classifier trained on a source domain given only unlabeled data that shifts gradually in distribution towards a target domain. We prove the first non-vacuous upper bound on the error of self-training with gradual shifts, under settings where directly adapting to the target domain can result in unbounded error. The theoretical analysis leads to algorithmic insights, highlighting that regularization and label sharpening are essential even when we have infinite data. Leveraging the gradual shift structure leads to higher accuracies on a rotating MNIST dataset, a forest Cover Type dataset, and a realistic Portraits dataset.

paragraphs: The paper studies adaptation when data distributions change gradually over time. A classifier starts with training on a source domain and then receives only unlabeled data along a path toward a target domain. The goal is to use this sequence of intermediate distributions to handle a larger overall shift.

The authors prove a non-vacuous upper bound on self-training error under gradual shifts. Their analysis includes settings in which adapting directly to the target can produce unbounded error. The result shows how access to a gradual sequence can change what is theoretically achievable, rather than treating the source and target as the only distributions available.

The theory also highlights regularization and label sharpening as essential in the analyzed setting, even with infinite data. Thus, additional data alone does not remove the need for these algorithmic choices. Experiments on rotating MNIST, forest Cover Type, and Portraits show higher accuracy when the method uses the gradual-shift structure. The contribution combines an error guarantee with practical guidance for adaptation along an evolving distribution.
summary.tldr: Gradual self-training receives an informative error guarantee and improves adaptation accuracy by using intermediate distributions, regularization, and label sharpening.

title: Understanding Self-Training for Gradual Domain Adaptation

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) enjoys several benefits, such as data-efficiency and planning, by learning a model of the environment’s dynamics. However, learning a global model that can generalize across different dynamics remains a challenge. To tackle this problem, we decompose the task of learning a global dynamics model into two stages: (a) learning a context latent vector that captures the local dynamics, then (b) predicting the next state conditioned on it. In order to encode dynamics-specific information into the context latent vector, we introduce a novel loss function that encourages the context latent vector to be useful for predicting both forward and backward dynamics. The proposed method achieves superior generalization ability across various simulated robotics and control tasks, compared to existing RL schemes.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning learns how an environment evolves, supporting planning and efficient use of data. A challenge arises when one model must work across environments with different dynamics. The paper addresses this generalization problem by giving the prediction model an explicit representation of the local dynamics it needs to handle.

The method separates learning into two stages. First, it learns a latent context vector that captures local dynamics. It then predicts the next state conditioned on that vector. To encourage the context to contain information specific to dynamics, the authors introduce a loss that makes it useful for predicting transitions in both forward and backward directions.

The context therefore serves as information about the dynamics used by the state predictor, with both prediction directions helping shape what it represents. Across simulated robotics and control tasks, the authors report better generalization than existing reinforcement learning schemes. These results support conditioning predictions on learned local context when a global dynamics model must accommodate variation.
summary.tldr: A context vector trained through forward and backward dynamics prediction improves a dynamics model's generalization across simulated control environments.

title: Context-aware Dynamics Model for Generalization in Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have recently achieved remarkable successes in various sequential decision making tasks, leveraging advances in methods for training large deep networks. However, these methods usually require large amounts of training data, which is often a big problem for real-world applications. One natural question to ask is whether learning good representations for states and using larger networks helps in learning better policies. In this paper, we try to study if increasing input dimensionality helps improve performance and sample efficiency of model-free deep RL algorithms. To do so, we propose an online feature extractor network (OFENet) that uses neural nets to produce \emph{good} representations to be used as inputs to an off-policy RL algorithm. Even though the high dimensionality of input is usually thought to make learning of RL agents more difficult, we show that the RL agents in fact learn more efficiently with the high-dimensional representation than with the lower-dimensional state observations. We believe that stronger feature propagation together with larger networks allows RL agents to learn more complex functions of states and thus improves the sample efficiency. Through numerical experiments, we show that the proposed method achieves much higher sample efficiency and better performance. Codes for the proposed method are available at http://www.merl.com/research/license/OFENet

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning often needs substantial training data, making sample efficiency a practical concern. This paper asks whether expanding the representation of an agent’s observations can help it learn better policies. The question challenges the expectation that more input dimensions necessarily make learning harder.

The proposed online feature extractor, OFENet, uses a neural network to transform state observations into a higher-dimensional representation. That representation becomes the input to an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm. The approach therefore changes what the policy-learning machinery receives, allowing it to work with learned features instead of relying directly on the lower-dimensional observations.

Numerical experiments show substantially better sample efficiency and performance with the proposed method. The authors suggest that stronger feature propagation and larger networks help agents learn more complex functions of state, offering an explanation for the improvement. This explanation is presented as their interpretation, while the direct finding is empirical: the learned, expanded representations helped in the experiments. The result supports investigating representation quality alongside input size when designing data-efficient agents.
summary.tldr: OFENet expands state observations into learned features that improve reinforcement learning performance and sample efficiency in experiments.

title: Can Increasing Input Dimensionality Improve Deep Reinforcement Learning?

abstract: We investigate the use of natural language to drive the generalization of control policies and introduce the new multi-task environment Messenger with free-form text manuals describing the environment dynamics. Unlike previous work, Messenger does not assume prior knowledge connecting text and state observations {—} the control policy must simultaneously ground the game manual to entity symbols and dynamics in the environment. We develop a new model, EMMA (Entity Mapper with Multi-modal Attention) which uses an entity-conditioned attention module that allows for selective focus over relevant descriptions in the manual for each entity in the environment. EMMA is end-to-end differentiable and learns a latent grounding of entities and dynamics from text to observations using only environment rewards. EMMA achieves successful zero-shot generalization to unseen games with new dynamics, obtaining a 40% higher win rate compared to multiple baselines. However, win rate on the hardest stage of Messenger remains low (10%), demonstrating the need for additional work in this direction.

paragraphs: A text manual can describe how a game works, but an agent must connect its words to what appears in the environment. This paper introduces Messenger, a multitask environment with free-form manuals describing game dynamics. It assumes no predefined mapping between the text and observed entities, so the agent must learn both that mapping and the described behavior.

The proposed model, EMMA, uses attention conditioned on each entity to focus on relevant manual descriptions. It learns an internal grounding between language, entities, and dynamics using only environment rewards. Because the model is differentiable end to end, this grounding is learned as part of the control-learning process.

EMMA successfully generalizes without additional training to unseen games with new dynamics. The authors report a 40% higher win rate than multiple baselines. Nevertheless, its win rate on Messenger’s hardest stage remains 10%. The results therefore demonstrate useful transfer from language while also showing that the most demanding grounding and control problems in this environment remain difficult.
summary.tldr: EMMA learns to connect game manuals with entities and dynamics from rewards, enabling zero-shot transfer while struggling on Messenger’s hardest stage.

title: Grounding Language to Entities and Dynamics for Generalization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many inference problems, such as sequential decision problems like A/B testing, adaptive sampling schemes like bandit selection, are often online in nature. The fundamental problem for online inference is to provide a sequence of confidence intervals that are valid uniformly over the growing-into-infinity sample sizes. To address this question, we provide a near-optimal confidence sequence for bounded random variables by utilizing Bentkus’ concentration results. We show that it improves on the existing approaches that use the Cram{é}r-Chernoff technique such as the Hoeffding, Bernstein, and Bennett inequalities. The resulting confidence sequence is confirmed to be favorable in synthetic coverage problems, adaptive stopping algorithms, and multi-armed bandit problems.

paragraphs: Online inference updates conclusions as observations arrive, often while decisions about further sampling are still being made. A/B testing and bandit selection are examples. The statistical challenge is to provide confidence intervals that remain valid across all growing sample sizes, including an indefinitely continuing sequence of observations.

The paper constructs a near-optimal confidence sequence for bounded random variables using Bentkus' concentration results. A confidence sequence addresses the whole sequence of intervals together, matching the repeated nature of online analysis. The authors show improvement over existing approaches built from the Cramér-Chernoff technique, including those based on Hoeffding, Bernstein, and Bennett inequalities.

The resulting method is evaluated in synthetic coverage problems, adaptive stopping algorithms, and multi-armed bandit problems, where the results are favorable. These settings connect the mathematical construction to procedures that repeatedly assess evidence or adjust sampling. The bounded-variable assumption defines the scope of the contribution, while uniform validity over sample sizes is what makes the intervals suited to ongoing decisions.
summary.tldr: A Bentkus-based confidence sequence improves uncertainty bounds for bounded observations while remaining valid across growing sample sizes.

title: Near-Optimal Confidence Sequences for Bounded Random Variables

abstract: We propose an iterative algorithm for low-rank matrix completion with that can be interpreted as an iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS) algorithm, a saddle-escaping smoothing Newton method or a variable metric proximal gradient method applied to a non-convex rank surrogate. It combines the favorable data-efficiency of previous IRLS approaches with an improved scalability by several orders of magnitude. We establish the first local convergence guarantee from a minimal number of samples for that class of algorithms, showing that the method attains a local quadratic convergence rate. Furthermore, we show that the linear systems to be solved are well-conditioned even for very ill-conditioned ground truth matrices. We provide extensive experiments, indicating that unlike many state-of-the-art approaches, our method is able to complete very ill-conditioned matrices with a condition number of up to $10^{10}$ from few samples, while being competitive in its scalability.

paragraphs: Low-rank matrix completion reconstructs a matrix from a limited set of observed entries. This paper addresses the difficult case where the underlying matrix is very ill-conditioned, meaning that its numerical scales differ greatly. The proposed iterative method aims to retain the data efficiency of earlier iteratively reweighted least squares approaches while making them substantially more scalable.

The algorithm has several complementary interpretations: reweighted least squares, a smoothing Newton method that escapes saddles, and a variable metric proximal gradient method for a nonconvex approximation to rank. The authors prove local quadratic convergence from a minimal number of samples. The local qualification matters: the result describes convergence near a solution, rather than promising that every starting point reaches one.

The linear systems solved during the algorithm remain well-conditioned even when the target matrix is not. Experiments indicate successful completion from few samples at condition numbers up to 10^10, alongside competitive scalability. Together, these results connect favorable local convergence with numerical robustness on particularly difficult completion problems.
summary.tldr: A scalable matrix completion method combines local quadratic convergence with well-conditioned internal computations, even for highly ill-conditioned target matrices.

title: A Scalable Second Order Method for Ill-Conditioned Matrix Completion from Few Samples

abstract: Networks with node covariates are commonplace: for example, people in a social network have interests, or product preferences, etc. If we know the covariates for some nodes, can we infer them for the remaining nodes? In this paper we propose a new similarity measure between two nodes based on the patterns of their 2-hop neighborhoods. We show that a simple algorithm (CN-VEC) like nearest neighbor regression with this metric is consistent for a wide range of models when the degree grows faster than $n^{1/3}$ up-to logarithmic factors, where $n$ is the number of nodes. For "low-rank" latent variable models, the natural contender will be to estimate the latent variables using SVD and use them for non-parametric regression. While we show consistency of this method under less stringent sparsity conditions, our experimental results suggest that the simple local CN-VEC method either outperforms the global SVD-RBF method, or has comparable performance for low rank models. We also present simulated and real data experiments to show the effectiveness of our algorithms compared to the state of the art.

paragraphs: When some nodes in a network have known attributes, the network’s connections may help estimate attributes for the others. This paper develops a way to measure similarity between nodes using the patterns in their two-hop neighborhoods. Its CN-VEC algorithm uses that similarity in a procedure resembling nearest-neighbor regression.

The authors prove consistency for a broad range of models when node degree grows faster than the cube root of the number of nodes, up to logarithmic factors. Under that condition, the estimator has the stated large-network guarantee. The approach therefore links the usefulness of local network patterns to a concrete requirement on network density.

For low-rank latent-variable models, the paper also examines estimating hidden node representations with singular value decomposition before performing nonparametric regression. That method is consistent under less demanding sparsity conditions. Nevertheless, experiments suggest that local CN-VEC can outperform or match the global SVD-RBF approach on low-rank models. Simulated and real-data comparisons further demonstrate the algorithms’ effectiveness against existing methods.
summary.tldr: Two-hop neighborhood similarity enables consistent estimation of missing node attributes under a stated network-density condition.

title: Consistent Nonparametric Methods for Network Assisted Covariate Estimation

abstract: High-dimensional observations are a major challenge in the application of model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) to real-world environments. To handle high-dimensional sensory inputs, existing approaches use representation learning to map high-dimensional observations into a lower-dimensional latent space that is more amenable to dynamics estimation and planning. In this work, we present an information-theoretic approach that employs temporal predictive coding to encode elements in the environment that can be predicted across time. Since this approach focuses on encoding temporally-predictable information, we implicitly prioritize the encoding of task-relevant components over nuisance information within the environment that are provably task-irrelevant. By learning this representation in conjunction with a recurrent state space model, we can then perform planning in latent space. We evaluate our model on a challenging modification of standard DMControl tasks where the background is replaced with natural videos that contain complex but irrelevant information to the planning task. Our experiments show that our model is superior to existing methods in the challenging complex-background setting while remaining competitive with current state-of-the-art models in the standard setting.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning must extract useful information from complex observations before it can estimate dynamics and plan. This paper develops a representation-learning approach based on temporal predictive coding. It encodes aspects of the environment that can be predicted across time, producing a lower-dimensional space for modeling and planning.

The information-theoretic approach implicitly prioritizes task-relevant components over nuisance information that is provably irrelevant to the task. The representation is learned jointly with a recurrent state-space model, allowing the agent to plan within the learned latent space. This connects what the agent retains from observations with its model of how the environment evolves.

The authors evaluate the method on modified DMControl tasks whose backgrounds contain natural videos with complex but irrelevant content. Their model outperforms existing methods in this challenging background setting while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art models on standard tasks. The findings support temporal prediction as a useful basis for representations that sustain planning amid visual distraction.
summary.tldr: Temporal predictive coding learns latent representations for planning that perform well despite complex, task-irrelevant video backgrounds.

title: Temporal Predictive Coding For Model-Based Planning In Latent Space

abstract: We propose a novel Wasserstein distributional normalization method that can classify noisy labeled data accurately. Recently, noisy labels have been successfully handled based on small-loss criteria, but have not been clearly understood from the theoretical point of view. In this paper, we address this problem by adopting distributionally robust optimization (DRO). In particular, we present a theoretical investigation of the distributional relationship between uncertain and certain samples based on the small-loss criteria. Our method takes advantage of this relationship to exploit useful information from uncertain samples. To this end, we normalize uncertain samples into the robustly certified region by introducing the non-parametric Ornstein-Ulenbeck type of Wasserstein gradient flows called Wasserstein distributional normalization, which is cheap and fast to implement. We verify that network confidence and distributional certification are fundamentally correlated and show the concentration inequality when the network escapes from over-parameterization. Experimental results demonstrate that our non-parametric classification method outperforms other parametric baselines on the Clothing1M and CIFAR-10/100 datasets when the data have diverse noisy labels.

paragraphs: Learning with noisy labels often uses small training loss to identify examples considered more reliable. This paper examines that practice through distributionally robust optimization. It studies the distributional relationship between samples treated as certain and uncertain under small-loss criteria, seeking a theoretical basis for extracting useful information from the uncertain group.

The proposed Wasserstein distributional normalization moves uncertain samples into a robustly certified region. It uses nonparametric Wasserstein gradient flows of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck type, described as inexpensive and fast to implement. The purpose is to use the relationship between the two sample groups to make uncertain examples useful for classification.

The authors establish a fundamental correlation between network confidence and distributional certification and provide a concentration inequality when the network escapes overparameterization. Experiments on Clothing1M and CIFAR-10/100 with diverse noisy labels show the nonparametric classification method outperforming the compared parametric baselines. The contribution combines a theoretical interpretation of small-loss selection with a distributional transformation designed to recover value from uncertain training examples.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein distributional normalization uses robust optimization to turn uncertain noisy-label samples into useful classification information.

title: Wasserstein Distributional Normalization For Robust Distributional Certification of Noisy Labeled Data

abstract: Distributed learning has become a hot research topic due to its wide application in cluster-based large-scale learning, federated learning, edge computing and so on. Most traditional distributed learning methods typically assume no failure or attack. However, many unexpected cases, such as communication failure and even malicious attack, may happen in real applications. Hence, Byzantine learning (BL), which refers to distributed learning with failure or attack, has recently attracted much attention. Most existing BL methods are synchronous, which are impractical in some applications due to heterogeneous or offline workers. In these cases, asynchronous BL (ABL) is usually preferred. In this paper, we propose a novel method, called buffered asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (BASGD), for ABL. To the best of our knowledge, BASGD is the first ABL method that can resist malicious attack without storing any instances on server. Compared with those methods which need to store instances on server, BASGD has a wider scope of application. BASGD is proved to be convergent, and be able to resist failure or attack. Empirical results show that BASGD significantly outperforms vanilla asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD) and other ABL baselines when there exists failure or attack on workers.

paragraphs: Distributed training must sometimes continue even when workers fail or send malicious updates. Many methods for this Byzantine learning setting require workers to operate synchronously. That coordination can be impractical when workers have different speeds or go offline, motivating methods that accept updates asynchronously while still resisting faulty or hostile behavior.

The paper introduces buffered asynchronous stochastic gradient descent, or BASGD. A distinguishing feature is that it does not require training examples to be stored on the server to resist malicious attacks. This broadens its applicability relative to approaches that depend on server-held examples, especially when the distributed learning arrangement does not provide such data centrally.

The authors prove convergence and resistance to failure or attack for their method. Their empirical comparisons show substantial improvements over ordinary asynchronous SGD and other asynchronous Byzantine learning baselines when workers fail or are attacked. The contribution therefore combines an asynchronous training design, a reduced server-side data requirement, and theoretical and experimental support for robustness in the studied setting.
summary.tldr: BASGD supports asynchronous distributed training under worker failures or attacks without requiring training examples on the server.

title: BASGD: Buffered Asynchronous SGD for Byzantine Learning

abstract: The scaling of Transformers has driven breakthrough capabilities for language models. At present, the largest large language models (LLMs) contain upwards of 100B parameters. Vision Transformers (ViT) have introduced the same architecture to image and video modelling, but these have not yet been successfully scaled to nearly the same degree; the largest dense ViT contains 4B parameters (Chen et al., 2022). We present a recipe for highly efficient and stable training of a 22B-parameter ViT (ViT-22B) and perform a wide variety of experiments on the resulting model. When evaluated on downstream tasks (often with a lightweight linear model on frozen features), ViT-22B demonstrates increasing performance with scale. We further observe other interesting benefits of scale, including an improved tradeoff between fairness and performance, state-of-the-art alignment to human visual perception in terms of shape/texture bias, and improved robustness. ViT-22B demonstrates the potential for "LLM-like" scaling in vision, and provides key steps towards getting there.

paragraphs: Scaling transformers has produced major advances in language modeling, motivating the question of how far similar scaling can go in vision. This paper presents ViT-22B, a vision transformer with 22 billion parameters, together with a recipe for training it efficiently and stably at that size.

The authors evaluate the resulting model across a wide range of downstream tasks. In many evaluations, they keep its learned features fixed and train only a lightweight linear model. Improvements in that setting show the usefulness of the representations produced by the large model, without requiring the entire network to be retrained for each evaluation.

The experiments show performance increasing with scale and report several additional benefits: a better fairness–performance tradeoff, improved robustness, and leading alignment with human visual perception as measured through shape-versus-texture bias. These observations broaden the case for scaling beyond task performance alone. The paper presents the results as evidence of the potential for language-model-like scaling in vision and as practical progress toward making that scale achievable.
summary.tldr: ViT-22B demonstrates stable, efficient vision-transformer scaling with reported gains in downstream performance, robustness, and other model properties.

title: Scaling Vision Transformers to 22 Billion Parameters

abstract: As with any machine learning problem with limited data, effective offline RL algorithms require careful regularization to avoid overfitting. One class of methods, known as one-step RL, perform just one step of policy improvement. These methods, which include advantage-weighted regression and conditional behavioral cloning, are thus simple and stable, but can have limited asymptotic performance. A second class of methods, known as critic regularization, perform many steps of policy improvement with a regularized objective. These methods typically require more compute but have appealing lower-bound guarantees. In this paper, we draw a connection between these methods: applying a multi-step critic regularization method with a regularization coefficient of 1 yields the same policy as one-step RL. While our theoretical results require assumptions (e.g., deterministic dynamics), our experiments nevertheless show that our analysis makes accurate, testable predictions about practical offline RL methods (CQL and one-step RL) with commonly-used hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from a limited collection of data, making regularization important for avoiding overfitting. One-step methods make a single policy improvement, offering a simple and stable approach whose eventual performance can be limited. Critic-regularization methods instead make repeated improvements using a regularized objective, typically spending more computation while offering appealing lower-bound guarantees.

The paper connects these seemingly different strategies. Under its theoretical assumptions, setting the regularization coefficient of a multi-step critic-regularization method to one produces the same policy as one-step reinforcement learning. This means that repeated optimization and a single improvement can arrive at the same result under a particular regularization choice.

The equivalence depends on assumptions that include deterministic dynamics, so it is a conditional theoretical result. Experiments with CQL and one-step methods nevertheless show that the analysis makes accurate, testable predictions using commonly chosen hyperparameters. The contribution is both a conceptual link between algorithm families and evidence that this link helps explain practical offline learning behavior.
summary.tldr: Under stated assumptions, a particular critic-regularization setting makes multi-step offline reinforcement learning produce the same policy as one-step learning.

title: A Connection between One-Step RL and Critic Regularization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many problems, such as online ad display, can be formulated as online bipartite matching. The crucial challenge lies in the nature of sequentially-revealed online item information, based on which we make irreversible matching decisions at each step. While numerous expert online algorithms have been proposed with bounded worst-case competitive ratios, they may not offer satisfactory performance in average cases. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (RL) has been applied to improve the average performance, but it lacks robustness and can perform arbitrarily poorly. In this paper, we propose a novel RL-based approach to edge-weighted online bipartite matching with robustness guarantees (LOMAR), achieving both good average-case and worst-case performance. The key novelty of LOMAR is a new online switching operation which, based on a judicious condition to hedge against future uncertainties, decides whether to follow the expert’s decision or the RL decision for each online item. We prove that for any $\rho\in[0,1]$, LOMAR is $\rho$-competitive against any given expert online algorithm. To improve the average performance, we train the RL policy by explicitly considering the online switching operation. Finally, we run empirical experiments to demonstrate the advantages of LOMAR compared to existing baselines.

paragraphs: Online bipartite matching requires irreversible decisions as information about new items arrives. Applications include online advertising. Expert algorithms can offer worst-case guarantees but may disappoint on average, while reinforcement learning can improve typical performance yet behave arbitrarily poorly. The paper develops LOMAR to combine learned decisions with protection supplied by an expert algorithm.

For each arriving item, LOMAR decides whether to follow the expert or the reinforcement learning policy. Its switching condition accounts for uncertainty about future arrivals. The learned policy is trained with this switching operation explicitly included, so training reflects the decision process that will actually determine which matches are made.

The authors prove that, for any chosen rho between zero and one, LOMAR is rho-competitive against the supplied expert algorithm. The guarantee is therefore relative to that expert, with rho specifying the protected comparison. Experiments demonstrate advantages over existing baselines. Together, the theory and empirical results support improving average matching performance while maintaining a quantified worst-case relationship to an expert’s performance.
summary.tldr: LOMAR switches between learned and expert matching decisions to improve average performance while preserving a tunable guarantee relative to the expert.

title: Learning for Edge-Weighted Online Bipartite Matching with Robustness Guarantees

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel dIffusion language modEl pre-training framework for text generation, which we call GENIE. GENIE is a large-scale pre-trained diffusion language model that consists of an encoder and a diffusion-based decoder, which can generate text by gradually transforming a random noise sequence into a coherent text sequence. To pre-train GENIE on a large-scale language corpus, we design a new continuous paragraph denoise objective, which encourages the diffusion-decoder to reconstruct a clean text paragraph from a corrupted version, while preserving the semantic and syntactic coherence. We evaluate GENIE on four downstream text generation benchmarks, namely XSum, CNN/DailyMail, Gigaword, and CommonGen. Our experimental results show that GENIE achieves comparable performance with the state-of-the-art autoregressive models on these benchmarks, and generates more diverse text samples. The code and models of GENIE are available at https://github.com/microsoft/ProphetNet/tree/master/GENIE.

paragraphs: GENIE is a pretrained language model that generates text through diffusion. It combines an encoder with a diffusion-based decoder, which gradually turns a sequence of random noise into coherent text. The paper investigates how to pretrain this kind of generator at scale so it can support downstream text-generation tasks.

Its training objective, continuous paragraph denoise, asks the decoder to reconstruct a clean paragraph from a corrupted version. The objective encourages the reconstruction to retain both meaning and grammatical coherence. By making paragraph recovery the pretraining task, the framework gives the diffusion decoder practice restoring connected text rather than treating generation solely as a sequence of next-token decisions.

The authors evaluate GENIE on XSum, CNN/DailyMail, Gigaword, and CommonGen. It achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art autoregressive models on these benchmarks while producing more diverse text samples. The findings support diffusion pretraining as a competitive approach to the evaluated generation tasks, with diversity as an additional reported benefit.
summary.tldr: GENIE pretrains a diffusion text generator through paragraph denoising, achieving competitive benchmark performance with more diverse outputs.

title: Text Generation with Diffusion Language Models: A Pre-training Approach with Continuous Paragraph Denoise

abstract: We study provable multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) in the general framework of partially observable stochastic games (POSGs). To circumvent the known hardness results and the use of computationally intractable oracles, we propose to leverage the potential information-sharing among agents, a standard practice in empirical MARL and a common model for multi-agent control systems with communications. We first establish several computation complexity results to justify the necessity of information-sharing, as well as the observability assumption that has enabled quasi-efficient single-agent RL with partial observations, for computational efficiency in solving POSGs. We then propose to further approximate the shared common information to construct an approximate model of the POSG, in which planning an approximate equilibrium (in terms of solving the original POSG) can be quasi-efficient, i.e., of quasi-polynomial-time, under the aforementioned assumptions. Furthermore, we develop a partially observable MARL algorithm that is both statistically and computationally quasi-efficient. We hope our study can open up the possibilities of leveraging and even designing different information structures , for developing both sample- and computation-efficient partially observable MARL.

paragraphs: Partially observable stochastic games model multiple learning agents that lack complete observations of their environment. Solving these games faces known computational barriers. This paper examines whether information sharing among agents can help overcome those barriers, drawing on communication practices already used in empirical multi-agent learning and control systems.

The authors first establish computational complexity results supporting the necessity of information sharing and an observability assumption for computational efficiency in the setting they study. They then approximate the agents’ shared common information to construct an approximate game model. Under those assumptions, this model permits planning an approximate equilibrium for the original game in quasi-polynomial time.

The paper also develops a partially observable multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm that is quasi-efficient in both statistical and computational terms. The qualifier matters: the stated efficiency is quasi-polynomial rather than polynomial. The results show how assumptions about what agents observe and share can support tractable learning guarantees, motivating attention to the design of communication and information structures.
summary.tldr: Information sharing and an observability assumption enable quasi-efficient planning and learning in the paper’s partially observable multi-agent setting.

title: Partially Observable Multi-agent RL with (Quasi-)Efficiency: The Blessing of Information Sharing

abstract: Sign Stochastic Gradient Descent (signSGD) is a communication-efficient stochastic algorithm that only uses the sign information of the stochastic gradient to update the model’s weights. However, the existing convergence theory of signSGD either requires increasing batch sizes during training or assumes the gradient noise is symmetric and unimodal. Error feedback has been used to guarantee the convergence of signSGD under weaker assumptions at the cost of communication overhead. This paper revisits the convergence of signSGD and proves that momentum can remedy signSGD under weaker assumptions than previous techniques; in particular, our convergence theory does not require the assumption of bounded stochastic gradient or increased batch size. Our results resonate with echoes of previous empirical results where, unlike signSGD, signSGD with momentum maintains good performance even with small batch sizes. Another new result is that signSGD with momentum can achieve an improved convergence rate when the objective function is second-order smooth. We further extend our theory to signSGD with major vote and federated learning.

paragraphs: SignSGD updates model weights using only the signs of stochastic gradients, reducing communication requirements. Existing convergence guarantees, however, had required growing batch sizes or particular symmetry and shape assumptions about gradient noise. Error feedback offered another route to convergence under weaker assumptions, but introduced additional communication overhead.

This paper proves that momentum can establish convergence under weaker assumptions than earlier techniques. In particular, its theory does not require bounded stochastic gradients or increasing batch sizes. These results offer theoretical support for earlier empirical observations that momentum-equipped signSGD maintains good performance with small batches, where plain signSGD can struggle.

The authors further obtain an improved convergence rate when the objective is second-order smooth. That improvement is conditional on the additional smoothness property. They also extend the analysis to majority-vote signSGD and federated learning. The overall contribution is a broader theoretical foundation for a communication-efficient optimizer, together with a sharper rate in a more structured setting.
summary.tldr: Momentum gives signSGD convergence guarantees without bounded stochastic gradients or growing batches, with faster convergence under second-order smoothness.

title: Momentum Ensures Convergence of SIGNSGD under Weaker Assumptions

abstract: Understanding the reasons behind the exceptional success of transformers requires a better analysis of why attention layers are suitable for NLP tasks. In particular, such tasks require predictive models to capture contextual meaning which often depends on one or few words, even if the sentence is long. Our work studies this key property, dubbed word sensitivity (WS), in the prototypical setting of random features. We show that attention layers enjoy high WS, namely, there exists a vector in the space of embeddings that largely perturbs the random attention features map. The argument critically exploits the role of the softmax in the attention layer, highlighting its benefit compared to other activations (e.g., ReLU). In contrast, the WS of standard random features is of order $1/\sqrt{n}$, $n$ being the number of words in the textual sample, and thus it decays with the length of the context. We then translate these results on the word sensitivity into generalization bounds: due to their low WS, random features provably cannot learn to distinguish between two sentences that differ only in a single word; in contrast, due to their high WS, random attention features have higher generalization capabilities. We validate our theoretical results with experimental evidence over the BERT-Base word embeddings of the imdb review dataset.

paragraphs: A sentence’s meaning can depend heavily on one word, even when the surrounding context is long. This paper studies whether a representation can remain sensitive to such a change. It calls this property word sensitivity and analyzes attention layers in a random-feature setting to understand one reason attention suits language tasks.

The authors show that random attention features have high word sensitivity: there exists an embedding-space vector that produces a large change in the feature map. Their argument depends critically on softmax. In comparison, standard random features have sensitivity proportional to the inverse square root of sentence length, so their response weakens as context grows.

The analysis connects sensitivity to generalization bounds. In the studied setting, standard random features cannot learn the required distinction between sentences differing in one word, whereas random attention features have greater generalization capability. Experiments using BERT-Base embeddings of IMDb reviews support the theory. The result establishes the existence of influential perturbations, rather than saying every single-word change strongly affects attention.
summary.tldr: In a random-feature analysis, softmax attention preserves sensitivity to influential word changes and supports stronger generalization than standard random features.

title: Towards Understanding the Word Sensitivity of Attention Layers: A Study via Random Features

abstract: In this paper, we investigate the challenging framework of Byzantine-robust training in distributed machine learning (ML) systems, focusing on enhancing both efficiency and practicality. As distributed ML systems become integral for complex ML tasks, ensuring resilience against Byzantine failures—where workers may contribute incorrect updates due to malice or error—gains paramount importance. Our first contribution is the introduction of the Centered Trimmed Meta Aggregator (CTMA), an efficient meta-aggregator that upgrades baseline aggregators to optimal performance levels, while requiring low computational demands. Additionally, we propose harnessing a recently developed gradient estimation technique based on a double-momentum strategy within the Byzantine context. Our paper highlights its theoretical and practical advantages for Byzantine-robust training, especially in simplifying the tuning process and reducing the reliance on numerous hyperparameters. The effectiveness of this technique is supported by theoretical insights within the stochastic convex optimization (SCO) framework and corroborated by empirical evidence.

paragraphs: Distributed training must combine updates from multiple workers, some of which may send incorrect information through errors or malicious behavior. This paper addresses such Byzantine failures while also considering computational cost and the practical difficulty of configuring robust training. Its contributions target both the combination of worker updates and the estimation of gradients.

The authors introduce the Centered Trimmed Meta Aggregator, or CTMA. It operates as a meta-aggregator that upgrades baseline aggregation methods to the optimal performance levels studied in the paper while keeping computational demands low. This approach makes improving an existing aggregator a central design choice, connecting robustness with the efficiency needed for distributed training.

The paper also brings a double-momentum gradient estimation technique into the Byzantine setting. The authors describe advantages in simplifying tuning and reducing dependence on numerous hyperparameters. Theoretical support is developed within stochastic convex optimization, and empirical evidence supports the technique’s effectiveness. Together, the contributions address the practical usability of robust training as well as its mathematical performance.
summary.tldr: CTMA and a double-momentum gradient estimator aim to make Byzantine-robust distributed training efficient and easier to tune.

title: Fault Tolerant ML: Efficient Meta-Aggregation and Synchronous Training

abstract: In the next few years, applications of Generative AI are expected to revolutionize a number of different areas, ranging from science & medicine to education. The potential for these seismic changes has triggered a lively debate about potential risks and resulted in calls for tighter regulation, in particular from some of the major tech companies who are leading in AI development. While regulation is important, it is key that it does not put at risk the budding field of open-source Generative AI. We argue for the responsible open sourcing of generative AI models in the near and medium term. To set the stage, we first introduce an AI openness taxonomy system and apply it to 40 current large language models. We then outline differential benefits and risks of open versus closed source AI and present potential risk mitigation, ranging from best practices to calls for technical and scientific contributions. We hope that this report will add a much needed missing voice to the current public discourse on near to mid-term AI safety and other societal impact.

The authors support regulation while expressing concern that it could put the developing open-source ecosystem at risk.

To make the discussion more precise, the paper introduces a taxonomy of AI openness and applies it to forty large language models. This provides a structured way to discuss differences in openness. The authors then compare the benefits and risks of open and closed approaches, treating access arrangements as relevant to both opportunities and safety concerns.

The paper also presents potential mitigation measures, ranging from best practices to areas needing technical and scientific contributions. Its contribution is a framework and a policy position, with responsible release as the advocated direction. The argument aims to broaden public discussion of societal impacts while keeping the distinct benefits and risks of openness visible in decisions about generative AI.
summary.tldr: The paper advocates responsible open-source generative AI, supported by an openness taxonomy and a comparison of benefits, risks, and mitigations.

title: Position: Near to Mid-term Risks and Opportunities of Open-Source Generative AI

abstract: The emergence of deep and large-scale spiking neural networks (SNNs) exhibiting high performance across diverse complex datasets has led to a need for compressing network models due to the presence of a significant number of redundant structural units, aiming to more effectively leverage their low-power consumption and biological interpretability advantages. Currently, most model compression techniques for SNNs are based on unstructured pruning of individual connections, which requires specific hardware support. Hence, we propose a structured pruning approach based on the activity levels of convolutional kernels named Spiking Channel Activity-based (SCA) network pruning framework. Inspired by synaptic plasticity mechanisms, our method dynamically adjusts the network’s structure by pruning and regenerating convolutional kernels during training, enhancing the model’s adaptation to the current target task. While maintaining model performance, this approach refines the network architecture, ultimately reducing computational load and accelerating the inference process. This indicates that structured dynamic sparse learning methods can better facilitate the application of deep SNNs in low-power and high-efficiency scenarios.

paragraphs: Deep spiking neural networks can contain many redundant structural units, creating a need for compression as the models grow. Existing compression methods often remove individual connections, producing unstructured sparsity that requires specific hardware support. This paper instead proposes pruning at the level of convolutional kernels, making the changes to network structure more organized.

The Spiking Channel Activity-based framework, or SCA, uses kernel activity levels to guide this process. Inspired by synaptic plasticity, it both prunes and regenerates convolutional kernels during training. The architecture therefore changes as the model learns, allowing its structure to adapt to the current task rather than treating compression solely as a final removal step.

The paper reports that this refinement reduces computational load and accelerates inference while maintaining model performance. Its stated implication is that structured, dynamic sparse learning can help deep spiking networks serve low-power, high-efficiency applications. The contribution links activity-based decisions about whole kernels with continued structural adaptation, seeking efficiency gains without giving up the performance of the trained network.
summary.tldr: SCA dynamically prunes and regenerates convolutional kernels based on spiking activity to reduce computation and accelerate inference while maintaining performance.

title: Towards efficient deep spiking neural networks construction with spiking activity based pruning

abstract: Dense-to-sparse gating mixture of experts (MoE) has recently become an effective alternative to a well-known sparse MoE. Rather than fixing the number of activated experts as in the latter model, which could limit the investigation of potential experts, the former model utilizes the temperature to control the softmax weight distribution and the sparsity of the MoE during training in order to stabilize the expert specialization. Nevertheless, while there are previous attempts to theoretically comprehend the sparse MoE, a comprehensive analysis of the dense-to-sparse gating MoE has remained elusive. Therefore, we aim to explore the impacts of the dense-to-sparse gate on the maximum likelihood estimation under the Gaussian MoE in this paper. We demonstrate that due to interactions between the temperature and other model parameters via some partial differential equations, the convergence rates of parameter estimations are slower than any polynomial rates, and could be as slow as $\mathcal{O}(1/\log(n))$, where $n$ denotes the sample size. To address this issue, we propose using a novel activation dense-to-sparse gate, which routes the output of a linear layer to an activation function before delivering them to the softmax function. By imposing linearly independence conditions on the activation function and its derivatives, we show that the parameter estimation rates are significantly improved to polynomial rates. Finally, we conduct a simulation study to empirically validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: Dense-to-sparse mixture-of-experts models use temperature to control how broadly a softmax gate distributes weight across experts. This allows the degree of sparsity to change during training instead of fixing the number of active experts. The paper investigates what this design means for maximum likelihood parameter estimation in Gaussian mixtures of experts.

The analysis identifies interactions between temperature and other parameters, expressed through partial differential equations. Because of these interactions, parameter estimates can converge more slowly than any polynomial rate, potentially as slowly as one divided by the logarithm of the sample size. The finding concerns statistical estimation as data increases, highlighting a difficulty behind the gate's apparent flexibility.

The authors propose inserting an activation function between the gate's linear layer and its softmax. Under linear independence conditions on that activation function and its derivatives, they establish improved polynomial parameter estimation rates. A simulation study supports the theoretical results. The improvement is thus tied to a specific architectural modification and stated mathematical conditions on the chosen activation.
summary.tldr: Temperature-based Gaussian expert gating can yield extremely slow parameter estimation, while a suitably chosen activation restores polynomial convergence rates.

title: Is Temperature Sample Efficient for Softmax Gaussian Mixture of Experts?

abstract: The recent rapid progress in (self) supervised learning models is in large part predicted by empirical scaling laws: a model’s performance scales proportionally to its size. Analogous scaling laws remain elusive for reinforcement learning domains, however, where increasing the parameter count of a model often hurts its final performance. In this paper, we demonstrate that incorporating Mixture-of-Expert (MoE) modules, and in particular Soft MoEs (Puigcerver et al., 2023), into value-based networks results in more parameter-scalable models, evidenced by substantial performance increases across a variety of training regimes and model sizes. This work thus provides strong empirical evidence towards developing scaling laws for reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Increasing model size has been a productive strategy in supervised and self-supervised learning, where empirical scaling relationships help describe improvements. Reinforcement learning has been less predictable: adding parameters can even reduce final performance. This paper investigates whether changing the architecture of value-based networks can make larger parameter counts more useful.

The authors incorporate mixture-of-experts modules, emphasizing Soft MoEs, into those networks. The experiment concerns the organization of model capacity as well as its amount. By testing this architectural change across different model sizes and training regimes, they examine whether additional parameters can translate into more reliable performance gains in the studied reinforcement-learning settings.

The results show substantial performance increases and models that scale more effectively with parameter count. The authors present this as strong empirical evidence toward developing scaling laws for reinforcement learning. That conclusion concerns progress toward such laws: the reported contribution is an architectural route to improved scaling behavior across the tested conditions, rather than a universal relationship already established for reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: Adding mixture-of-experts modules to value-based networks makes increased parameter counts more beneficial across the tested reinforcement-learning settings.

title: Mixtures of Experts Unlock Parameter Scaling for Deep RL

abstract: By leveraging a hierarchical structure of known classes, Hierarchical Novelty Detection (HND) offers fine-grained detection results that pair detected novel samples with their closest (known) parent class in the hierarchy. Prior knowledge on the parent class provides valuable insights to better understand these novel samples. However, traditional novelty detection methods try to separate novel samples from all known classes using uncertainty or distance based metrics so they are incapable of locating the closest known parent class. Since the novel class is also part of the hierarchy, the model can more easily get confused between samples from known classes and those from novel ones. To achieve effective HND, we propose to augment the known (leaf-level) classes with a set of novel classes, each of which is associated with one parent (i.e., non-leaf) class in the original hierarchy. Such a structure allows us to perform novel fine-grained evidence allocation to differentiate known and novel classes guided by a uniquely designed loss function. Our thorough theoretical analysis shows that fine-grained evidence allocation creates an evidence margin to more precisely separate known and novel classes. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world hierarchical datasets demonstrate the proposed model outperforms the strongest baselines and achieves the best HND performance.
