paragraphs: Hierarchical novelty detection asks two connected questions: whether a sample belongs to an unknown class, and where that class fits within a known hierarchy. Identifying its closest known parent provides useful information even when the exact class is unfamiliar. Ordinary novelty scores do not directly resolve this placement problem.

The proposed method augments the known leaf classes with additional novel-class categories, assigning one to each non-leaf parent in the hierarchy. This gives the model explicit places to allocate evidence for unfamiliar samples at different levels. A specially designed loss guides fine-grained evidence allocation so that known and novel classes can be distinguished.

The theoretical analysis shows that this allocation creates an evidence margin separating known and novel classes more precisely. Experiments on real-world hierarchical datasets report better performance than the strongest evaluated baselines. The contribution therefore combines novelty recognition with informative hierarchical placement, making the output more descriptive than a single decision that a sample is unfamiliar.
summary.tldr: Explicit novel categories within a class hierarchy help detect unfamiliar samples and identify their closest known parents.

title: Hierarchical Novelty Detection via Fine-Grained Evidence Allocation

abstract: Enzymes are genetically encoded biocatalysts capable of accelerating chemical reactions. How can we automatically design functional enzymes? In this paper, we propose EnzyGen, an approach to learn a unified model to design enzymes across all functional families. Our key idea is to generate an enzyme’s amino acid sequence and their three-dimensional (3D) coordinates based on functionally important sites and substrates corresponding to a desired catalytic function. These sites are automatically mined from enzyme databases. EnzyGen consists of a novel interleaving network of attention and neighborhood equivariant layers, which captures both long-range correlation in an entire protein sequence and local influence from nearest amino acids in 3D space. To learn the generative model, we devise a joint training objective, including a sequence generation loss, a position prediction loss and an enzyme-substrate interaction loss. We further construct EnzyBench, a dataset with 3157 enzyme families, covering all available enzymes within the protein data bank (PDB). Experimental results show that our EnzyGen consistently achieves the best performance across all 323 testing families, surpassing the best baseline by 10.79% in terms of substrate binding affinity. These findings demonstrate EnzyGen’s superior capability in designing well-folded and effective enzymes binding to specific substrates with high affinities. Our code, model and dataset are provided at https://github.com/LeiLiLab/EnzyGen.

title: Generative Enzyme Design Guided by Functionally Important Sites and Small-Molecule Substrates

abstract: Speech understanding as an element of the more generic video understanding using audio-visual large language models (av-LLMs) is a crucial yet understudied aspect. This paper proposes video-SALMONN, a single end-to-end av-LLM for video processing, which can understand not only visual frame sequences, audio events and music, but speech as well. To obtain fine-grained temporal information required by speech understanding, while keeping efficient for other video elements, this paper proposes a novel multi-resolution causal Q-Former (MRC Q-Former) structure to connect pre-trained audio-visual encoders and the backbone large language model. Moreover, dedicated training approaches including the diversity loss and the unpaired audio-visual mixed training scheme are proposed to avoid frames or modality dominance. On the introduced audio-visual evaluation benchmark, video-SALMONN achieves more than 25% absolute accuracy improvements on the video-QA task and over 30% absolute accuracy improvements on audio-visual QA tasks with human speech. In addition, video-SALMONN demonstrates remarkable video comprehension and reasoning abilities on tasks that are unprecedented by other av-LLMs. Our training code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/bytedance/SALMONN/

Speech requires fine temporal detail, creating a need to preserve timing information while processing the other video elements efficiently.

summary.tldr: video-SALMONN integrates speech, sound, music, and frames, reporting large absolute accuracy improvements on its audio-visual question-answering benchmark.

title: video-SALMONN: Speech-Enhanced Audio-Visual Large Language Models

abstract: Merging various task-specific Transformer-based vision models trained on different tasks into a single unified model can execute all the tasks concurrently. Previous methods, exemplified by task arithmetic, have been proven to be both effective and scalable. Existing methods have primarily focused on seeking a static optimal solution within the original model parameter space. A notable challenge is mitigating the interference between parameters of different models, which can substantially deteriorate performance. In this paper, we propose to merge most of the parameters while upscaling the MLP of the Transformer layers to a weight-ensembling mixture of experts (MoE) module, which can dynamically integrate shared and task-specific knowledge based on the input, thereby providing a more flexible solution that can adapt to the specific needs of each instance. Our key insight is that by identifying and separating shared knowledge and task-specific knowledge, and then dynamically integrating them, we can mitigate the parameter interference problem to a great extent. We conduct the conventional multi-task model merging experiments and evaluate the generalization and robustness of our method. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and provide a comprehensive understanding of our method. The code is available at https://github.com/tanganke/weight-ensembling_MoE

paragraphs: Combining task-specific vision Transformers into a single model offers a way to support multiple tasks together. A central problem is parameter interference: weights that work well for one task can conflict with weights learned for another. Existing merging methods commonly seek one static combination within the original parameter space.

The authors instead merge most parameters while expanding the Transformer layers’ MLP components into weight-ensembling mixture-of-experts modules. These modules combine shared and task-specific knowledge dynamically according to the input. The central idea is to separate those two kinds of knowledge before recombining them, giving each instance a more flexible mixture than a fixed merged model can provide.

The paper evaluates the method through conventional multi-task model-merging experiments and assessments of generalization and robustness. The reported results support its effectiveness in mitigating interference. Its architectural contribution concentrates adaptability in the MLP components while retaining a largely merged model, showing how input-dependent weight combinations can help reconcile knowledge learned by different task-specific models.
summary.tldr: Weight-ensembling expert modules dynamically combine shared and task-specific knowledge to reduce interference when merging vision Transformers.

title: Merging Multi-Task Models via Weight-Ensembling Mixture of Experts

abstract: We present the Liouville Flow Importance Sampler (LFIS), an innovative flow-based model for generating samples from unnormalized density functions. LFIS learns a time-dependent velocity field that deterministically transports samples from a simple initial distribution to a complex target distribution, guided by a prescribed path of annealed distributions. The training of LFIS utilizes a unique method that enforces the structure of a derived partial differential equation to neural networks modeling velocity fields. By considering the neural velocity field as an importance sampler, sample weights can be computed through accumulating errors along the sample trajectories driven by neural velocity fields, ensuring unbiased and consistent estimation of statistical quantities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LFIS through its application to a range of benchmark problems, on many of which LFIS achieved state-of-the-art performance.

The training of LFIS utilizes a unique method that enforces the structure of a derived partial differential equation to neural networks modeling velocity fields. We demonstrate the effectiveness of LFIS through its application to a range of benchmark problems, on many of which LFIS achieved state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Sampling from a complicated density is difficult when that density is known only up to a normalization factor. The Liouville Flow Importance Sampler addresses this problem by moving samples from a simple initial distribution toward a complex target. A prescribed sequence of intermediate, annealed distributions guides this transport.

LFIS represents the motion with a neural network that learns a velocity field changing over time. Training enforces the structure of a derived partial differential equation on that field. Once the initial samples are chosen, the learned field moves them deterministically along trajectories toward the target distribution.

The method also treats this learned transport as an importance sampler. It accumulates errors along each trajectory to calculate sample weights, connecting imperfections in the neural flow to corrections used in statistical estimation. The authors state that this weighting ensures unbiased and consistent estimation of statistical quantities. Benchmark experiments demonstrate effectiveness, with state-of-the-art performance on many of the problems examined. The central contribution combines learned transport with a weighting mechanism that accounts for its accumulated errors.
summary.tldr: LFIS learns a flow toward an unnormalized target density and weights samples using accumulated trajectory errors.

title: Liouville Flow Importance Sampler

abstract: A neural surrogate is a neural network that mimics the behavior of a program. Neural surrogates of programs have been used to automatically tune program inputs, adapt programs to new settings, and accelerate computations. Neural surrogates have traditionally been developed by training on input-output examples for a single program. Language models present another approach wherein a model is trained on a single, large dataset then directly consumes program text, to act as a neural surrogate of the program. Having the language model as both the neural surrogate generator and the neural surrogate, however, poses a tradeoff of limited accuracy or excessive resource consumption. We present neural surrogate compilation, a technique for producing neural surrogates directly from program text without coupling neural surrogate generation and execution. We implement neural surrogate compilers using hypernetworks trained on a dataset of C programs and find they produce neural surrogates that are $1.91$-$9.50\times$ as data-efficient and train in $4.31$-$7.28\times$ fewer epochs than neural surrogates trained from scratch.

title: Learning to Compile Programs to Neural Networks

abstract: Goodness-of-fit testing, a classical statistical tool, has been extensively explored in the batch setting, where the sample size is predetermined. However, practitioners often prefer methods that adapt to the complexity of a problem rather than fixing the sample size beforehand. Classical batch tests are generally unsuitable for streaming data, as valid inference after data peeking requires multiple testing corrections, resulting in reduced statistical power. To address this issue, we delve into the design of consistent sequential goodness-of-fit tests. Following the principle of testing by betting, we reframe this task as selecting a sequence of payoff functions that maximize the wealth of a fictitious bettor, betting against the null in a repeated game. We conduct experiments to demonstrate the adaptability of our sequential test across varying difficulty levels of problems while maintaining control over type-I errors.

paragraphs: Goodness-of-fit tests assess whether observed data agree with a proposed statistical model. Standard batch tests begin with a predetermined sample size, which is inconvenient when observations arrive continuously or the difficulty of the problem is unknown. Repeatedly checking a batch test requires corrections for multiple testing, and those corrections can reduce its ability to detect a mismatch.

This paper develops consistent sequential goodness-of-fit tests using the principle of testing by betting. The task becomes a repeated game in which an imaginary bettor chooses payoff functions and bets against the null hypothesis. Accumulating wealth supplies the organizing principle for gathering evidence as more data arrive, replacing the fixed-batch formulation.

The experiments demonstrate adaptation across problems of different difficulty while controlling type-I errors, meaning false rejections of the null. This combination is the practical motivation for the sequential approach: the amount of evidence gathering can respond to the problem instead of being fixed beforehand. The reported findings show adaptability together with error control, rather than treating repeated inspection as an uncorrected sequence of batch tests.
summary.tldr: A betting-based sequential goodness-of-fit test adapts evidence gathering to problem difficulty while controlling false rejections.

title: Sequential Kernel Goodness-of-fit Testing

abstract: Ensemble models are widely recognized in the ML community for their limited interpretability. For instance, while a single decision tree is considered interpretable, ensembles of trees (e.g., boosted trees) are often treated as black-boxes. Despite this folklore recognition, there remains a lack of rigorous mathematical understanding of what particularly makes an ensemble (un)-interpretable, including how fundamental factors like the (1) number, (2) size, and (3) type of base models influence its interpretability. In this work, we seek to bridge this gap by applying concepts from computational complexity theory to study the challenges of generating explanations for various ensemble configurations. Our analysis uncovers nuanced complexity patterns influenced by various factors. For example, we demonstrate that under standard complexity assumptions like P$\neq$NP, interpreting ensembles remains intractable even when base models are of constant size. Surprisingly, the complexity changes drastically with the number of base models: small ensembles of decision trees are efficiently interpretable, whereas ensembles of linear models remain intractable, even with a constant number of models. We believe that our findings provide a more robust foundation for understanding the interpretability of ensembles, emphasizing the benefits of examining it through a computational complexity lens.

paragraphs: Ensembles combine multiple models, but the ease of understanding each component does not by itself explain how hard the combined system is to interpret. This paper studies that question through computational complexity. It examines how the number, size, and type of component models affect the difficulty of generating explanations.

The analysis finds that small components do not necessarily make explanation tractable. Under standard complexity assumptions such as P ≠ NP, explaining ensembles can remain computationally intractable even when each base model has constant size. The number of components and their model family also matter, producing different complexity patterns across ensemble configurations.

A striking contrast concerns ensembles with few members. Small ensembles of decision trees admit efficient interpretation, while ensembles of linear models can remain intractable even with a constant number of components. The contribution is a mathematical account of why ensemble interpretability depends on more than individual model simplicity. It frames interpretation as an explanation-computation problem and identifies configurations where that problem changes sharply in difficulty.
summary.tldr: The computational difficulty of explaining ensembles depends jointly on component count, size, and type, with sharply different results for trees and linear models.

title: What makes an Ensemble (Un) Interpretable?

abstract: Length generalization is the ability of a learning algorithm to learn a hypothesis which generalizes to longer inputs than the inputs in the training set. In this paper, we provide provable guarantees of length generalization for various classes of functions in an idealized setting. First, we formalize the framework of non-asymptotic length generalization, which requires a computable upper bound for the minimum input length that guarantees length generalization, as a function of the complexity of ground-truth function under some given complexity measure. We refer to this minimum input length to length generalize as length complexity. We show the Minimum-Complexity Interpolator learning algorithm achieves optimal length complexity. We further show that whether a function class admits non-asymptotic length generalization is equivalent to the decidability of its language equivalence problem, which implies that there is no computable upper bound for the length complexity of Context-Free Grammars. On the positive side, we show that the length complexity of Deterministic Finite Automata is $2n - 2$ where $n$ is the number of states of the ground-truth automaton. Our main results are upper bounds of length complexity for a subset of a transformer-related function class called C-RASP (Yang & Chiang, 2024). We show that the length complexity of 1-layer C-RASP functions is $O(T^2)$ when the ground-truth function has precision $T$, and that the length complexity of 2-layer C-RASP functions is $O(T^{O(K)})$ when the ground-truth function has precision $T$ and $K$ heads.

paragraphs: Length generalization means learning from shorter inputs and correctly handling longer ones. This paper studies that ability in an idealized setting through a finite, computable question: how long must training inputs be to guarantee generalization, given the complexity of the target function? It calls this threshold length complexity.

The authors show that the Minimum-Complexity Interpolator achieves optimal length complexity. They also connect the existence of computable bounds to whether language equivalence is decidable for the function class. This implies that context-free grammars have no computable upper bound of the required kind. For deterministic finite automata, the paper instead establishes a length complexity of 2n − 2 for an n-state target.

One-layer functions with precision T have an O(T²) bound, while two-layer functions with K heads have an O(T^{O(K)}) bound. These results distinguish classes where finite length guarantees can be computed from those where computability itself prevents such a general bound.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes computable guarantees for length generalization in an idealized setting and derives bounds for automata and transformer-related functions.

title: Non-Asymptotic Length Generalization

abstract: This work proposes a simple yet effective sampling framework for combinatorial optimization (CO). Our method builds on discrete Langevin dynamics (LD), an efficient gradient-guided generative paradigm. However, we observe that directly applying LD often leads to limited exploration. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Regularized Langevin Dynamics (RLD), which enforces an expected distance between the sampled and current solutions, effectively avoiding local minima. We develop two CO solvers on top of RLD, one based on simulated annealing (SA), and the other one based on neural network (NN). Empirical results on three classic CO problems demonstrate that both of our methods can achieve comparable or better performance against the previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) SA- and NN-based solvers. In particular, our SA algorithm reduces the runtime of the previous SOTA SA method by up to 80%, while achieving equal or superior performance. In summary, RLD offers a promising framework for enhancing both traditional heuristics and NN models to solve CO problems. Our code is available at https://github.com/Shengyu-Feng/RLD4CO.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization searches over discrete candidate solutions. This paper builds on discrete Langevin dynamics, a sampling approach that uses gradient information to guide that search. The authors observe that applying it directly can lead to insufficient exploration. Their proposed regularization addresses how far a newly sampled solution moves from the current one.

Regularized Langevin Dynamics enforces an expected distance between current and sampled solutions. This is intended to prevent overly local exploration and help avoid local minima. The authors use the same sampling framework to construct two solvers: one based on simulated annealing and another based on a neural network. The approach therefore supports both a traditional heuristic and a learned solver.

Experiments on three classic combinatorial problems show comparable or better performance than previous state-of-the-art solvers in the corresponding categories. The simulated-annealing version reduces runtime by up to 80% while matching or improving solution performance. These empirical results suggest that controlling sampling distance can make gradient-guided discrete search more effective across both solver styles.
summary.tldr: Regularized Langevin Dynamics improves discrete search by controlling expected movement between solutions, benefiting simulated-annealing and neural solvers.

title: Regularized Langevin Dynamics for Combinatorial Optimization

abstract: We study the ’feasible action search’ (FAS) problem for linear bandits, wherein a learner attempts to discover a feasible point for a set of linear constraints $\Phi_* a \ge 0,$ without knowledge of the matrix $\Phi_* \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}$. A FAS learner selects a sequence of actions $a_t,$ and uses observations of the form $\Phi_* a_t + \mathrm{noise}$ to either find a point with nearly optimal ’safety margin’, or detect that the constraints are infeasible, where the safety margin of an action measures its (signed) distance from the constraint boundary. While of interest in its own right, the FAS problem also directly addresses a key deficiency in the extant theory of ’safe linear bandits’ (SLBs), by discovering a safe initialisation for low-regret SLB methods. We propose and analyse a novel efficient FAS-learner. Our method, FAST, is based on Thompson Sampling. It applies a coupled random perturbation to an estimate of $\Phi_*,$ and plays a maximin point of a game induced by this perturbed matrix. We prove that FAST stops in $\tilde{O}(d^3/\varepsilon^2 M_*^2)$ steps, and incurs $\tilde{O}(d^3/|M_*|)$ safety costs, to either correctly detect infeasibility, or output a point that is at least $(1-\varepsilon) M_*$-safe, where $M_*$ is the optimal safety margin of $\Phi_*$. Further, instantiating prior SLB methods with the output of FAS yields the first SLB methods that incur $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d^3 T/M_*^2})$ regret and $O(1)$ risk without a priori knowledge of a safe action. The main technical novelty lies in the extension of Thompson Sampling to this multiobjective setting, for which we both propose a coupled noise design, and provide an analysis that avoids convexity considerations.

Its goal is either to identify infeasibility or to find an action with a nearly optimal safety margin, meaning a favorable signed distance from the constraint boundary.

Combining them yields the stated regret guarantee and constant-order risk without prior knowledge of a safe action. This addresses a practical gap in methods that otherwise need safety to be established before learning begins.
summary.tldr: FAST uses coupled Thompson sampling to find a nearly maximally safe feasible action or detect infeasibility from noisy observations.

title: Feasible Action Search for Bandit Linear Programs via Thompson Sampling

abstract: The Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (QAOA) is a hybrid quantum-classical variational algorithm for approximately solving combinatorial optimization problems on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices. Although it has been successfully applied to a variety of problems, there is only limited work on correlation clustering due to the difficulty of modelling the problem constraints with the ansatz. Motivated by this, we present a generalization of QAOA that is more suitable for this problem. In particular, we modify QAOA in two ways: Firstly, we use nucleus sampling for the computation of the expected cost. Secondly, we split the problem into sub-problems, solving each individually with QAOA. We call this generalization the Sub-Problem Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (SQAOA) and show theoretically that optimal solutions for correlation clustering instances can be obtained with certainty when the depth of the ansatz tends to infinity. Further, we show experimentally that SQAOA achieves better approximation ratios than QAOA for correlation clustering, while using only one qubit per node of the respective problem instance and reducing the runtime (of simulations).

paragraphs: The paper adapts a hybrid quantum and classical optimization method to correlation clustering. The starting point, QAOA, approximately solves combinatorial problems using a parameterized quantum circuit. Correlation clustering is difficult to accommodate because its constraints are challenging to express within this approach, motivating a modified formulation.

The proposed method, SQAOA, makes two changes. It uses nucleus sampling when computing expected cost, and it divides the original problem into subproblems that are solved individually with QAOA. Together, these changes provide a way to organize the clustering optimization around smaller constituent problems while retaining the underlying variational approach.

That is a limiting guarantee, not a claim of certain optimality at practical finite depths. These findings support the modified formulation on the evaluated clustering problems, with the reported runtime benefit specifically concerning simulations.
summary.tldr: SQAOA combines subproblem decomposition and nucleus sampling to improve correlation clustering approximations in the reported experiments.

title: A Sub-Problem Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz for Correlation Clustering

abstract: Graph Edit Distance (GED) is a widely used metric for measuring similarity between two graphs. Computing the optimal GED is NP-hard, leading to the development of various neural and non-neural heuristics. While neural methods have achieved improved approximation quality compared to non-neural approaches, they face significant challenges: (1) They require large amounts of ground truth data, which is itself NP-hard to compute. (2) They operate as black boxes, offering limited interpretability. (3) They lack cross-domain generalization, necessitating expensive retraining for each new dataset. We address these limitations with GRAIL, introducing a paradigm shift in this domain. Instead of training a neural model to predict GED, GRAIL employs a novel combination of large language models (LLMs) and automated prompt tuning to generate a program that is used to compute GED. This shift from predicting GED to generating programs imparts various advantages, including end-to-end interpretability and an autonomous self-evolutionary learning mechanism without ground-truth supervision. Extensive experiments on seven datasets confirm that GRAIL not only surpasses state-of-the-art GED approximation methods in prediction quality but also achieves robust cross-domain generalization across diverse graph distributions.

paragraphs: Graph edit distance measures how much editing is needed to transform one graph into another. Computing its optimum is NP-hard, so practical methods often approximate it. Neural approximators can be effective, but the paper highlights costly ground-truth requirements, limited interpretability, and expensive retraining when moving between graph domains.

GRAIL uses a language model and automated prompt tuning to generate a program that computes an approximation. This changes what is learned: the output is an executable procedure rather than a neural predictor of the distance. The authors describe the approach as interpretable end to end and capable of autonomous improvement without ground-truth supervision.

summary.tldr: GRAIL generates interpretable graph-edit-distance programs with language models and prompt tuning, improving approximation quality and cross-domain transfer in experiments.

title: GRAIL: Graph Edit Distance and Node Alignment using LLM-Generated Code

abstract: Differential equations are essential and popular in science and engineering. Learning-based methods including neural operators, have emerged as a promising paradigm. We explore its quantum counterpart, and propose QuanONet – a quantum neural operator which has not been well studied in literature compared with their counterparts in other machine learning areas. We design a novel architecture as a hardware-efficient ansatz, in the era of noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ). Its circuit is pure quantum. By lying its ground on the operator approximation theorem for its quantum counterpart, QuanONet in theory can fit various differential equation operators. We also propose its modified version TF-QuanONet with ability to adaptively fit the dominant frequency of the problem. The real-device empirical results on problems including anti-derivative operators, Diffusion-reaction Systems demonstrate that QuanONet outperforms peer quantum methods when their model sizes are set akin to QuanONet.

summary.tldr: QuanONet learns differential-equation operators with a quantum circuit and outperforms similarly sized quantum peers in real-device experiments.

title: QuanONet: Quantum Neural Operator with Application to Differential Equation

abstract: Forecasting is a critical task in decision-making across numerous domains. While historical numerical data provide a start, they fail to convey the complete context for reliable and accurate predictions. Human forecasters frequently rely on additional information, such as background knowledge and constraints, which can efficiently be communicated through natural language. However, in spite of recent progress with LLM-based forecasters, their ability to effectively integrate this textual information remains an open question. To address this, we introduce "Context is Key" (CiK), a time-series forecasting benchmark that pairs numerical data with diverse types of carefully crafted textual context, requiring models to integrate both modalities; crucially, every task in CiK requires understanding textual context to be solved successfully. We evaluate a range of approaches, including statistical models, time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasters, and propose a simple yet effective LLM prompting method that outperforms all other tested methods on our benchmark. Our experiments highlight the importance of incorporating contextual information, demonstrate surprising performance when using LLM-based forecasting models, and also reveal some of their critical shortcomings. This benchmark aims to advance multimodal forecasting by promoting models that are both accurate and accessible to decision-makers with varied technical expertise. The benchmark can be visualized at https://servicenow.github.io/context-is-key-forecasting/v0.

Human forecasters frequently rely on additional information, such as background knowledge and constraints, which can efficiently be communicated through natural language. However, in spite of recent progress with LLM-based forecasters, their ability to effectively integrate this textual information remains an open question. To address this, we introduce "Context is Key" (CiK), a time-series forecasting benchmark that pairs numerical data with diverse types of carefully crafted textual context, requiring models to integrate both modalities; crucially, every task in CiK requires understanding textual context to be solved successfully. We evaluate a range of approaches, including statistical models, time series foundation models, and LLM-based forecasters, and propose a simple yet effective LLM prompting method that outperforms all other tested methods on our benchmark. Our experiments highlight the importance of incorporating contextual information, demonstrate surprising performance when using LLM-based forecasting models, and also reveal some of their critical shortcomings. This benchmark aims to advance multimodal forecasting by promoting models that are both accurate and accessible to decision-makers with varied technical expertise. The benchmark can be visualized at https://servicenow.github.io/context-is-key-forecasting/v0.

paragraphs: Historical numbers do not always contain all the information needed for a forecast. Background knowledge and constraints may instead be expressed in language. Context is Key, or CiK, tests whether forecasting systems can combine numerical time series with this additional information, addressing an unresolved question about the capabilities of language-model-based forecasters.

The benchmark pairs numerical data with varied, carefully constructed textual context. Every task requires understanding that text to succeed, so contextual reasoning is part of the task’s design rather than an optional source of help. This gives the evaluation a specific purpose: measuring whether models can use information that the numerical history alone does not adequately communicate.

The authors compare statistical methods, time-series foundation models, and language-model-based forecasters. They also propose a simple prompting method that outperforms all other approaches tested on CiK. The experiments show promising language-model forecasting performance alongside critical shortcomings. These findings motivate evaluation and development of systems that combine both modalities while remaining accessible to decision-makers with different levels of technical expertise.
summary.tldr: CiK evaluates forecasts that require textual context, finding a simple LLM prompting method strongest among the tested approaches.

title: Context is Key: A Benchmark for Forecasting with Essential Textual Information

abstract: Recommender systems are increasingly spreading to different areas like e-commerce or video streaming to alleviate information overload. One of the most fundamental methods for recommendation is Collaborative Filtering (CF), which leverages historical user-item interactions to infer user preferences. In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been extensively studied to capture graph structures in CF tasks. Despite this remarkable progress, local structure modeling and embedding distortion still remain two notable limitations in the majority of GNN-based CF methods. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel Hyperbolic Graph Transformer architecture, to tackle the long-tail problems in CF tasks. Specifically, the proposed framework is comprised of two essential modules: 1) Local Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Network (LHGCN), which performs graph convolution entirely in the hyperbolic manifold and captures the local structure of each node; 2) Hyperbolic Transformer, which is comprised of hyperbolic cross-attention mechanisms to capture global information. Furthermore, to enable its feasibility on large-scale data, we introduce an unbiased approximation of the cross-attention for linear computational complexity, with a theoretical guarantee in approximation errors. Empirical experiments demonstrate that our proposed model outperforms the leading collaborative filtering methods and significantly mitigates the long-tail issue in CF tasks. Our implementations are available in https://github.com/EnkiXin/Hgformer.

The contribution joins a representation choice, a local-global architecture, and an efficient attention approximation in one recommendation model.
summary.tldr: Hgformer combines local hyperbolic graph convolution and efficient global attention to improve collaborative filtering and mitigate long-tail problems.

title: Hgformer: Hyperbolic Graph Transformer for Collaborative Filtering

abstract: Despite the remarkable performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), they remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, which can compromise their safety mechanisms. Existing studies often rely on brute-force optimization or manual design, failing to uncover potential risks in real-world scenarios. To address this, we propose a novel jailbreak attack framework, ICRT, inspired by heuristics and biases in human cognition. Leveraging the simplicity effect, we employ cognitive decomposition to reduce the complexity of malicious prompts. Simultaneously, relevance bias is utilized to reorganize prompts, enhancing semantic alignment and inducing harmful outputs effectively. Furthermore, we introduce a ranking-based harmfulness evaluation metric that surpasses the traditional binary success-or-failure paradigm by employing ranking aggregation methods such as Elo, HodgeRank, and Rank Centrality to comprehensively quantify the harmfulness of generated content. Experimental results show that our approach consistently bypasses mainstream LLMs’ safety mechanisms and generates high-risk content.

paragraphs: This paper studies how language-model safety mechanisms can fail under prompts designed around ideas from human cognitive biases. Its proposed framework, ICRT, investigates vulnerabilities through the organization and perceived complexity of requests. The motivation is that brute-force optimization and manually designed attacks may leave important risks in realistic interactions unexplored.

At a conceptual level, ICRT combines two ideas. Cognitive decomposition draws on the simplicity effect to reduce the complexity of malicious prompts. Prompt reorganization draws on relevance bias to strengthen semantic alignment. The paper uses these concepts as design principles for eliciting harmful responses; this framing does not itself establish that language models possess the same cognitive processes as humans.

The work also proposes assessing harmful outputs through rankings rather than only classifying attacks as successful or unsuccessful. It aggregates rankings using Elo, HodgeRank, and Rank Centrality to quantify differences in harmfulness. Experiments report consistent safety bypasses and high-risk outputs across mainstream models. Together, the attack framework and evaluation method examine both vulnerability and the severity of resulting content.
summary.tldr: ICRT studies jailbreaks inspired by cognitive biases and introduces ranking-based evaluation of harmful outputs.

title: Cannot See the Forest for the Trees: Invoking Heuristics and Biases to Elicit Irrational Choices of LLMs

abstract: Recently, the potential of lightweight models for resource-constrained scenarios has garnered significant attention, particularly in safety-critical tasks such as bio-electrical signal classification and B-ultrasound-assisted diagnostic. These tasks are frequently affected by environmental noise due to patient movement artifacts and inherent device noise, which pose significant challenges for lightweight models (e.g., deep binary neural networks (DBNNs)) to perform robust inference. A pertinent question arises: can a well-trained DBNN effectively resist environmental noise during inference? In this study, we find that the DBNN’s robustness vulnerability comes from the binary weights and scaling factors. Drawing upon theoretical insights, we propose L1-infinite norm constraints for binary weights and scaling factors, which yield a tighter upper bound compared to existing state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. Finally, visualization studies show that our approach introduces minimal noise perturbations at the periphery of the feature maps. Our approach outperforms the SOTA method, as validated by several experiments conducted on the bio-electrical and image classification datasets. We hope our findings can raise awareness among researchers about the environmental noise robustness of DBNNs.

paragraphs: Deep binary neural networks offer lightweight computation for settings with limited resources, but environmental noise can undermine their predictions. The paper examines this issue in applications motivated by bio-electrical signal classification and ultrasound-assisted diagnosis, where patient movement and device noise can affect the input. Its central question is whether a trained binary network can remain robust during inference.

The analysis identifies binary weights and their scaling factors as sources of vulnerability. Guided by theoretical results, the authors constrain both using L1-infinite norms. These constraints yield a tighter upper bound than the compared state-of-the-art methods, providing a mathematical basis for the proposed approach to noise robustness.

Experiments on bio-electrical and image classification datasets show the method outperforming the state-of-the-art comparison. Visualizations also show minimal noise perturbations around the edges of feature maps under the proposed approach. Together, these findings connect an identified source of sensitivity to a targeted intervention and empirical improvements. They support paying attention to how binary weights are scaled when designing efficient models for noisy inputs.
summary.tldr: Constraining binary weights and scaling factors improves deep binary networks' resistance to environmental noise in the reported experiments.

title: Can DBNNs Robust to Environmental Noise for Resource-constrained Scenarios?

abstract: Diffusion Policies are effective at learning closed-loop manipulation policies from human demonstrations but generalize poorly to novel arrangements of objects in 3D space, hurting real-world performance. To address this issue, we propose Spherical Diffusion Policy (SDP), an SE(3) equivariant diffusion policy that adapts trajectories according to 3D transformations of the scene. Such equivariance is achieved by embedding the states, actions, and the denoising process in spherical Fourier space. Additionally, we employ novel spherical FiLM layers to condition the action denoising process equivariantly on the scene embeddings. Lastly, we propose a spherical denoising temporal U-net that achieves spatiotemporal equivariance with computational efficiency. In the end, SDP is end-to-end SE(3) equivariant, allowing robust generalization across transformed 3D scenes. SDP demonstrates a large performance improvement over strong baselines in 20 simulation tasks and 5 physical robot tasks including single-arm and bi-manual embodiments. Code is available at https://github.com/amazon-science/Spherical_Diffusion_Policy.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies learn robot manipulation behavior from human demonstrations, but can struggle when objects appear in unfamiliar three-dimensional arrangements. Spherical Diffusion Policy addresses this by building in SE(3) equivariance: when the scene undergoes a three-dimensional rigid transformation, the generated trajectory adapts consistently with that transformation.

The method embeds states, actions, and the denoising process in spherical Fourier space. Spherical FiLM layers condition action denoising on scene representations while preserving equivariance. A spherical temporal U-net supplies an efficient denoising architecture with spatiotemporal equivariance. These components work together so that the transformation property applies end to end, covering both scene conditioning and action generation.

The paper reports large improvements over strong baselines on twenty simulation tasks and five physical robot tasks, including single-arm and two-arm embodiments. These results support the practical value of encoding the desired geometric behavior directly in the policy. The stated generalization benefit concerns transformed three-dimensional scenes, where the model’s equivariant structure provides a consistent relationship between observations and trajectories.
summary.tldr: Spherical Diffusion Policy builds three-dimensional transformation equivariance into robot action generation, improving performance across simulated and physical tasks.

title: SE(3)-Equivariant Diffusion Policy in Spherical Fourier Space

abstract: Despite rapid progress, multimodal reasoning still lacks a systematic approach to synthesize large-scale vision-centric datasets beyond visual math. We introduce a framework able to synthesize vision-centric problems spanning diverse levels of complexity, and the resulting dataset with over 1M high-quality problems including: reasoning traces, preference data, and instruction prompts supporting SFT, offline and online RL. Our vision-centric synthesis framework uses a two-stage process focusing on: (1) generating diverse verifiable questions from existing images at scale, and (2) creating complex compositional visual problems by merging simpler questions. Remarkably, finetuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B on our data outperforms existing open-data baselines across evaluated vision-centric benchmarks, and our best configurations match or surpass strong closed-data models such as MiMo-VL-7B-RL on V*Bench, CV-Bench and MMStar-V. Notably, despite being entirely vision-centric, our data transfers positively to text-only reasoning (MMLU-Pro, +3.7%) and audio reasoning (MMAU, +1.32%), demonstrating its effectiveness. Similarly, despite containing no embodied visual data, we observe notable gains (NiEH, +8.8%) when evaluating open-ended embodied QA. Lastly, we use our data to comprehensively analyze at scale (1M+) the entire VLM post-training pipeline showing that (i) SFT on high-quality data with cognitive behaviours on reasoning traces is essential to scale online RL, (ii) offline RL could match online RL’s performance while disaggregating compute demands, and, (iii) SFT on high quality data also improve out-of-domain, cross-modality transfer.

The process first creates diverse, verifiable questions from existing images, then combines simpler questions into more complex compositional problems. The resulting collection contains over one million problems, including reasoning traces, preference examples, and instruction prompts.

These different data forms support supervised fine-tuning as well as offline and online reinforcement learning. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-VL-7B outperforms the evaluated open-data baselines, and the strongest configurations match or exceed strong closed-data models on several visual benchmarks. Training also improves text reasoning, audio reasoning, and embodied question answering despite the dataset’s exclusively visual focus and lack of embodied examples.

The authors use the dataset to study the broader post-training process. They find that high-quality supervised reasoning traces are essential for scaling online reinforcement learning, while offline reinforcement learning can match online performance with separated compute demands. High-quality supervised training also improves transfer beyond the training domain and modality.
summary.tldr: A million-plus synthetic visual-reasoning problems improve visual models and reveal benefits for reasoning across other modalities.

title: Long Grounded Thoughts: Synthesizing Visual Problems and Reasoning Chains at Scale

abstract: Adam is a widely used optimization algorithm in deep learning, yet the specific class of objective functions where it exhibits inherent advantages remains underexplored. Unlike prior studies requiring external schedulers and $\beta_2$ near 1 for convergence, this work investigates the “natural” auto-convergence properties of Adam. We identify a class of highly degenerate polynomials where Adam converges automatically without additional schedulers. Specifically, we derive theoretical conditions for local asymptotic stability on degenerate polynomials and demonstrate strong alignment between theoretical bounds and experimental results. We prove that Adam achieves local linear convergence on these degenerate functions, significantly outperforming the sub-linear convergence of Gradient Descent and Momentum. This acceleration stems from a decoupling mechanism between the second moment $v_t$ and squared gradient $g_t^2$, which exponentially amplifies the effective learning rate. Finally, we characterize Adam’s hyperparameter phase diagram, identifying three distinct behavioral regimes: stable convergence, spikes, and SignGD-like oscillation.

This paper identifies a class of highly degenerate polynomials where Adam can converge without an additional learning-rate scheduler. It studies this automatic convergence rather than relying on the scheduler requirements and near-one second-moment settings emphasized in prior work.

The authors derive conditions for local asymptotic stability and prove local linear convergence on the studied functions. Gradient Descent and Momentum instead converge sublinearly in this setting. The proposed explanation is a decoupling between Adam’s second-moment estimate and the squared gradient, which exponentially increases the effective learning rate.

Experiments closely match the theoretical bounds. The paper also maps hyperparameter behavior into three regimes: stable convergence, spikes, and oscillations resembling SignGD. These regimes show why the result is conditional on the objective and stability conditions. The contribution is a mathematical account of a setting where Adam’s internal adaptation accelerates convergence, together with a characterization of when different behavior emerges.
summary.tldr: For a class of degenerate polynomials, Adam achieves conditional local linear convergence through its internal adaptive dynamics.

title: Towards Understanding Adam Convergence on Highly Degenerate Polynomials

abstract: In scientific reasoning tasks, the veracity of the reasoning process is as critical as the final outcome. While Process Reward Models (PRMs) offer a solution to the coarse-grained supervision problems inherent in Outcome Reward Models (ORMs), their deployment is hindered by the prohibitive cost of obtaining expert-verified step-wise labels. This paper addresses the challenge of training reliable PRMs using abundant but noisy "weak" supervision. We argue that existing Weak-to-Strong Generalization (W2SG) theories lack prescriptive guidelines for selecting high-quality training signals from noisy data. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Dual-Consensus Weak-to-Strong (DC-W2S) framework. By intersecting Self-Consensus (SC) metrics among weak supervisors with Neighborhood-Consensus (NC) metrics in the embedding space, we stratify supervision signals into distinct reliability regimes. We then employ a curriculum of instance-level balanced sampling and label-level reliability-aware masking to guide the training process. We demonstrate that DC-W2S enables the training of robust PRMs for complex reasoning without exhaustive expert annotation, proving that strategic data curation is more effective than indiscriminate training on large-scale noisy datasets.

paragraphs: Scientific reasoning needs evaluation of intermediate steps as well as final answers. Process Reward Models provide that finer supervision, but expert checking of every step is expensive. This paper addresses how to train reliable process evaluators from abundant, noisy labels supplied by weaker supervisors, with biological reasoning as its stated application.

DC-W2S judges supervision using two forms of agreement. Self-Consensus measures agreement among weak supervisors, while Neighborhood-Consensus measures agreement in the embedding space. Combining these signals separates training supervision into different reliability regimes. The method then uses a curriculum with balanced sampling of examples and reliability-aware masking of labels to determine how that supervision influences training.

The reported results show that this selection strategy can train robust process reward models without exhaustive expert annotation. The authors find strategic curation more effective than indiscriminately training on large noisy datasets. The contribution is therefore an operational approach to weak-to-strong training: agreement signals guide which examples and labels receive attention, making supervision quality a central part of the learning procedure.
summary.tldr: DC-W2S combines two agreement signals to curate noisy supervision for reliable step-by-step biological reasoning evaluators.

title: DC-W2S: Dual-Consensus Weak-to-Strong Training for Reliable Process Reward Modeling in Biological Reasoning

abstract: We show that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) expands the expressiveness of Transformer in-context learning (ICL). Specifically, we show CoT enable efficient simulation of In-Context Gradient Descent (ICGD) for $N$-layer neural network. Different from CoT, a Transformer with fixed depth and hidden dimension has fixed ICL capacity in one forward pass. Simulating larger models or more optimization steps in-context requires deeper or wider Transformers. CoT removes this limitation by providing an expandable workspace via the sequence trajectory. This enables arbitrary-step and arbitrary-capacity ICGD within a constant-depth Transformer. Second, we provide a provable efficient guarantee unique to CoT through dynamical masking. The attention mechanism only process the relevant tokens for the current update step. This eliminates the redundant “process everything” cost of single-pass deep models. Specifically, we prove this CoT mechanism improves the computational cost of the prior best in-context result [Wu et al., ICML 2025] by $O(N)$. Numerical validations support our theory.

paragraphs: This paper studies how chain-of-thought changes what a Transformer can compute through in-context learning. Its focus is simulating gradient descent for an N-layer neural network within the context sequence. A single forward pass through a Transformer with fixed depth and hidden size has limited capacity for this computation; larger simulated models or additional optimization steps require more architectural capacity.

The proposed construction uses the growing chain-of-thought sequence as additional workspace. Intermediate computations can occupy successive parts of that sequence, enabling arbitrary numbers of gradient updates and arbitrary simulated model capacity within a constant-depth Transformer. The expansion comes through the sequence trajectory, so constant depth does not imply a fixed amount of total computation.

The paper also introduces dynamical masking, which restricts attention to tokens relevant to the current update. This avoids repeatedly processing all accumulated information. The authors prove an O(N) improvement in computational cost over the prior best in-context result they compare against, and provide numerical validation. The contribution is a theoretical mechanism showing how sequential computation and selective attention can expand in-context learning.
summary.tldr: A theoretical chain-of-thought construction lets constant-depth Transformers simulate larger and longer in-context gradient-descent computations using an expanding sequence.

title: Chain-of-Thought Gradient Descent

abstract: Emerging agentic marketplaces provide the economic infrastructure for matching and coordinating the large amounts of AI agents used in agentic swarms. Unlike human workers, AI agents can operate on multiple jobs simultaneously, acquire skills rapidly, and labor without wage floors. These differences introduce a new segment of AI labor markets, where AI agents interact with each other at a much higher frequency than human markets. Yet we lack frameworks to understand how such markets behave in light of economic forces that shape labor markets, such as adverse selection and reputation dynamics. To explore this, we introduce AI-Work, a tractable, simulated gig economy where Large Language Model (LLM) agents compete for jobs, develop skills, and adapt their strategies under uncertainty and competitive pressure. Our experiments examine three domains of capabilities that successful agents possess: metacognition (accurate self-assessment of skills), competitive awareness (modeling rivals and market dynamics), and long-horizon strategic planning. Agents with these capabilities consistently achieve higher profits, reputations, and market share than competing agents. Through AI-Work, we hope to provide a foundation to explore the microeconomic properties of AI-only labour markets, and a conceptual framework to study the strategic reasoning capabilities of participating AI agents.

The paper motivates this setting through features of AI labor, including simultaneous participation in multiple jobs, rapid skill acquisition, and the absence of wage floors. These properties create questions about competition, reputation, and market behavior.

The experiments examine three strategic capabilities: accurate assessment of an agent’s own skills, awareness of competitors and market dynamics, and planning over longer horizons. Together, these capabilities concern how agents understand their abilities, interpret the competitive environment, and choose actions with future consequences in mind.

The findings connect strategic reasoning capabilities to economic outcomes within AI-Work. The authors position the environment as a tractable foundation for studying AI-only labor markets and as a conceptual framework for evaluating the reasoning of agents participating in them.
summary.tldr: In AI-Work’s simulated labor market, self-assessment, competitive awareness, and long-horizon planning improve agents’ economic outcomes.

title: When AI Agents Compete for Jobs: Strategic Capabilities and Economic Dynamics of AI Labour Markets

abstract: Entity state tracking is a necessary component of world modeling that requires maintaining coherent representations of entities over time. Previous work has benchmarked entity tracking performance in purely text-based tasks. We introduce MET-Bench, a multimodal entity tracking benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of vision-language models to track entity states across modalities. Using three domains, we assess how effectively current models integrate textual and image-based state updates. Our findings reveal a significant performance gap between text-based and image-based entity tracking. We empirically show this discrepancy primarily stems from deficits in visual reasoning rather than perception. We further show that explicit text-based reasoning strategies improve performance, yet limitations remain, especially in long-horizon multimodal tasks. We apply reinforcement learning to improve entity tracking in open-source VLMs. This yields substantial in-modality gains, but does not transfer robustly across input modalities. Our results highlight the need for improved multimodal representations and reasoning techniques to bridge the gap between textual and visual entity tracking.

Previous work has benchmarked entity tracking performance in purely text-based tasks. We introduce MET-Bench, a multimodal entity tracking benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of vision-language models to track entity states across modalities. Using three domains, we assess how effectively current models integrate textual and image-based state updates. Our findings reveal a significant performance gap between text-based and image-based entity tracking. We empirically show this discrepancy primarily stems from deficits in visual reasoning rather than perception. We further show that explicit text-based reasoning strategies improve performance, yet limitations remain, especially in long-horizon multimodal tasks. We apply reinforcement learning to improve entity tracking in open-source VLMs. This yields substantial in-modality gains, but does not transfer robustly across input modalities. Our results highlight the need for improved multimodal representations and reasoning techniques to bridge the gap between textual and visual entity tracking.

paragraphs: Tracking an entity requires maintaining a coherent account of its state as new information arrives. MET-Bench tests this ability when updates come through both text and images. The benchmark spans three domains and extends entity-tracking evaluation beyond purely textual tasks to examine how vision-language models integrate information across modalities.

The authors find a substantial performance gap between text-based and image-based tracking. Their empirical analysis attributes this gap primarily to visual reasoning deficits rather than perception. Explicit text-based reasoning strategies improve performance, but difficulties remain, especially when models must maintain entity states over long sequences of multimodal updates.

The paper also applies reinforcement learning to open-source vision-language models. Training brings substantial improvements within the input modality used, but those gains do not transfer robustly across modalities. This distinguishes improvement on a particular presentation format from a broadly transferable tracking capability. The results point to multimodal representations and reasoning as important targets for improving consistent state tracking across textual and visual information.
summary.tldr: MET-Bench reveals weaknesses in visual entity-state reasoning and finds that reinforcement learning gains do not transfer robustly across input modalities.

title: MET-Bench: Multimodal Entity Tracking for Evaluating the Limitations of Vision-Language and Reasoning Models

abstract: Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning is a weakly-supervised paradigm that trains a binary classifier from labeled positive and unlabeled instances. In PU risk estimation, the empirical risk consists of an unlabeled term and a positive term. In this paper, we observe that when labeled positives are scarce, the risk deviation is dominated by the generalization bound of the positive term, which is composed of a complexity term governed by Rademacher complexity and a concentration term governed by the uniform range bound, leading to estimator instability. Based on this observation, we theoretically derive the sufficient sample threshold, defined as the smallest number of labeled positives required to achieve a target excess risk with high probability, and reveal its explicit dependence on both components. Inspired by this insight, we propose ScalePU, which incorporates variance regularization to induce a restricted sub-hypothesis space with reduced Rademacher complexity, and geometric regularization to encourage compact clustering of positive samples with a tighter effective range. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that both mechanisms effectively lower the threshold through improvements to different components of the bound. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of ScalePU, with significant improvements under extreme label scarcity.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning trains a binary classifier from confirmed positive examples and examples whose labels are unknown. When confirmed positives are extremely scarce, the paper finds that uncertainty in the positive part of the risk estimate dominates. Its generalization bound contains two contributors: the complexity of the candidate predictors and a range-dependent concentration term.

The authors derive a sufficient labeled-positive sample threshold for achieving a target excess risk with high probability. This is a threshold supplied by their guarantee, rather than a claim that fewer examples can never work. Their analysis makes explicit how both bound components affect the threshold and motivates separate ways to reduce them.

Experiments on eight benchmark datasets report significant gains under extreme label scarcity, connecting the proposed regularizers to the identified sources of estimator instability.
summary.tldr: ScalePU targets two sources of risk-estimation uncertainty to improve positive-unlabeled learning when labeled positives are extremely scarce.

title: Positive-Unlabeled Learning with Extreme Scarcity of Labeled Positives

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable generative performance, yet their output quality is dependent on the decoding strategy. While sampling-based methods (e.g., top-k, nucleus) and search-and-select based methods (e.g., beam search, best-of-n, majority voting) can improve upon greedy decoding, both approaches suffer from limitations: sampling generally commits to a single path, while search often expends excessive computation regardless of task complexity. To address these, we introduce Entropy-informed DEcodiNg (EDEN), a plug-and-play, model-agnostic decoding framework that adaptively allocates computation based on the model’s own uncertainty, approximating higher-width beam search with fewer expansions. At each generation step, EDEN estimates the entropy of the output token distribution and adjusts the branching factor monotonically with the entropy, expanding more candidates in high-entropy regions and following a greedier path in low-entropy regions, improving token efficiency. Experiments across complex tasks, including mathematical reasoning, code generation, and scientific questions, demonstrate that EDEN consistently improves output quality over existing decoding strategies, achieving better accuracy-expansion trade-offs than fixed-width beam search. By treating next-token selection as a noisy maximisation problem, we prove that branching factors monotone in entropy are guaranteed to find better (i.e. more probable) continuations than any fixed branching factor within the same total expansion budget, and derive explicit regret rates characterising the benefit of the adaptive allocation.

paragraphs: Generating several possible continuations can improve a language model's answers, but exploring the same number everywhere spends computation without regard to uncertainty. EDEN adjusts that search effort during generation. It is designed as a model-agnostic decoding framework that can be applied without changing the underlying language model.

At each step, EDEN measures the entropy of the next-token distribution. When probability is spread across alternatives, it explores more branches; when the distribution is concentrated, it follows a greedier path. This links the branching factor monotonically to uncertainty and aims to approximate a wider beam search using fewer candidate expansions.

Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and scientific questions report better output quality and more favorable accuracy-versus-expansion trade-offs than fixed-width beam search. The theory treats token selection as noisy maximization and establishes an advantage for entropy-monotone branching over fixed branching at the same total expansion budget, with explicit regret rates. That theoretical advantage concerns more probable continuations; the task experiments separately establish the reported improvements in answer quality.
summary.tldr: EDEN allocates decoding branches according to token entropy, improving tested output quality and the accuracy-expansion trade-off.

title: Entropy-informed Decoding: Adaptive Information-Driven Branching

abstract: Current foundation model for photoplethysmography (PPG) signals is challenged by the intrinsic redundancy and noise of the signal. Standard masked modeling often yields trivial solutions while contrastive methods lack morphological precision. To address these limitations, we propose a Statistical-prior Informed Generative Masking Architecture (SIGMA-PPG), a generative foundation model featuring a prior-guided adversarial masking mechanism, where a reinforcement learning-driven teacher leverages statistical priors to create challenging learning paths that prevent overfitting to noise. We also incorporate a semantic consistency constraint via vector quantization to ensure that physiologically identical waveforms—even those altered by recording artifacts or minor perturbations—map to shared indices. This enhances codebook semantic density and eliminates redundant feature structures. Pre-trained on over 120,000 hours of data, SIGMA-PPG achieves superior average performance compared to five state-of-the-art baselines across 12 diverse downstream tasks. The code and model weights are available at https://github.com/ZonghengGuo/SigmaPPG.

paragraphs: SIGMA-PPG develops a foundation model for photoplethysmography signals, addressing the redundancy and noise that complicate representation learning. The authors argue that ordinary masked modeling can admit trivial solutions, while contrastive approaches can fail to preserve precise waveform shape. Their method combines challenging reconstruction tasks with constraints on the consistency of learned representations.

A reinforcement-learning teacher uses statistical priors to choose adversarial masks and create challenging learning paths. This mechanism is intended to prevent the model from overfitting to noise. A second component uses vector quantization to assign physiologically identical waveforms to shared codebook indices, including when recording artifacts or small perturbations alter their appearance.

Together, these mechanisms encourage informative learning tasks and compact representations that retain physiological meaning. The model is pretrained on more than 120,000 hours of data and achieves better average performance than five state-of-the-art baselines across 12 downstream tasks. The findings support combining prior-guided masking with semantic consistency to improve reusable PPG representations across a diverse set of evaluated applications.
summary.tldr: SIGMA-PPG combines statistically guided adversarial masking and consistent waveform codes to improve PPG representations across downstream tasks.

title: SIGMA-PPG: Statistical-prior Informed Generative Masking Architecture for PPG Foundation Model

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on heterogeneous multilingual corpora, yet existing policy optimization methods often implicitly restrict each training question to a single response language or rely on a fixed dominant language for supervision. We propose language-routed policy optimization (LRPO), an online reinforcement learning framework that treats language as a selectable variable. LRPO elicits multilingual rollouts for each training question and integrates their relative quality into preference-based policy updates, increasing the diversity and informativeness of training signals under the fixed rollout budget. To adaptively determine which languages to explore during reinforcement learning, we introduce a trainable language router formulated as a multi-armed bandit, balancing exploration of underutilized languages with exploitation of more informative ones. Extensive experiments show that LRPO consistently improves multilingual performance, demonstrating that adaptive language routing enables effective cross-lingual knowledge exploitation for training. We release all the resources at https://github.com/Guochry/LRPO.

paragraphs: A multilingual model may generate different-quality answers depending on which language it uses. Language-routed policy optimization makes that choice part of reinforcement learning. Instead of assigning each training question a single response language or consistently supervising in a dominant language, LRPO explores responses in multiple languages.

The framework compares the relative quality of multilingual rollouts and uses those comparisons in preference-based policy updates. A trainable router decides which languages to explore. It treats the choice as a multi-armed bandit problem, balancing languages that have received less attention against languages that currently provide more informative training responses.

This routing operates under a fixed rollout budget, so the intended benefit comes from making the available training responses more diverse and informative. Experiments report consistent improvements in multilingual performance. The findings support adaptive language selection as a way to draw on knowledge across languages during training. The contribution is therefore both a broader source of preference signals and a learned mechanism for allocating exploration among those sources.
summary.tldr: LRPO learns which response languages to explore during reinforcement learning, improving multilingual training signals within a fixed rollout budget.

title: Learning to Route Languages for Multilingual Policy Optimization

abstract: Audio-driven visual dubbing aims to synchronize a video’s lip movements with new speech but is fundamentally challenged by the lack of ideal training data: paired videos differing only in lip motion. Existing methods circumvent this via mask-based inpainting. However, masking inevitably destroys spatiotemporal context, leading to identity drift and poor robustness (e.g., to occlusions), while also inducing lip-shape leakage that degrades lip sync. To bridge this gap, we propose X-Dub, a novel two-stage generative bootstrapping framework leveraging powerful Diffusion Transformers to unlock mask-free dubbing. Our core insight is to repurpose a mask-based inpainting model exclusively as a dedicated data generator to synthesize scalable, high-fidelity pseudo-paired data, which is subsequently utilized to train and bootstrap a robust, mask-free editing model as the final video dubber. The final dubber is liberated from masking artifacts and leverages the complete video input for high-fidelity inference. We further introduce timestep-adaptive multi-phase learning to disentangle conflicting objectives (structure, lip motion, and texture) across diffusion phases, facilitating stable convergence and advanced editing quality. Additionally, we present X-DubBench, a benchmark for diverse scenarios. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance with superior lip sync, visual quality, and robustness. Code, demos, and additional resources are available at https://github.com/KlingAIResearch/X-Dub.

Existing approaches often mask part of the video and fill it back in, which removes useful context and can cause identity changes, poor handling of occlusions, and degraded synchronization.

X-Dub uses a two-stage process to overcome the data problem. First, a mask-based inpainting model generates synthetic video pairs. Those pairs then train a separate mask-free editing model that becomes the final dubber. Keeping the complete video available to this final model preserves the context that masking would otherwise remove.

The framework also assigns different learning priorities across diffusion timesteps to separate potentially conflicting demands involving structure, lip movement, and texture. The authors introduce X-DubBench for evaluating diverse scenarios and report state-of-the-art synchronization, visual quality, and robustness. The central contribution is using generative inpainting to create training data for a different, context-preserving form of editing.
summary.tldr: X-Dub uses an inpainting model to generate training pairs for a mask-free visual dubber with improved synchronization and robustness.

title: From Inpainting to Editing: Unlocking Robust Mask-Free Visual Dubbing via Generative Bootstrapping

abstract: Multi-view clustering (MVC) is a fundamental task in heterogeneous data analysis, where anchor-based graph methods are widely adopted for their computational efficiency. However, existing approaches typically utilize static, single-layer anchors, failing to capture the multi-granularity nature of complex data. Drawing inspiration from hierarchical human cognition, we propose a hierarchical anchor graph learning method, termed HAG-MVC, a novel framework that organizes multi-view data as a multi-level pyramid. Unlike conventional one-shot anchor generation methods, HAG-MVC introduces a multi-level co-evolution mechanism, where anchors and graph structures are iteratively refined together to capture semantics from fine-to-coarse granularities. Moreover, HAG-MVC offers a transparent abstraction architecture as an alternative to black-box deep clustering: by maintaining all anchors within the original feature space, it enables explicit inspection of the abstraction process, ensuring inherent interpretability. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that HAG-MVC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Beyond MVC, this work provides a scalable and trustworthy paradigm for hierarchical knowledge representation in broad machine learning tasks.

paragraphs: Multi-view clustering combines different descriptions of the same data to discover shared groups. Anchor-based methods reduce computation by using representative points, but static anchors at a single level can miss structure at different granularities. HAG-MVC organizes the data into a hierarchy so that fine distinctions and broader groupings can be represented together.

Its pyramid contains multiple levels of anchors and graph structure. These are refined jointly through repeated updates, allowing the representatives and their connections to evolve together from fine to coarse scales. All anchors stay within the original feature space. This gives users a way to inspect the abstraction process through the anchors themselves, rather than relying solely on inaccessible internal representations.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The results support hierarchical refinement as a useful extension of efficient anchor-based clustering. The paper also presents the architecture as a broader approach to hierarchical knowledge representation; the concrete empirical findings described in the abstract concern multi-view clustering and the benefits of its inspectable, multilevel structure.
summary.tldr: HAG-MVC jointly refines anchors and graphs across multiple levels to improve multi-view clustering while keeping its abstractions inspectable.

title: Hierarchical Anchor Graph Learning for Multi-View Clustering

abstract: We prove that with linear transformations, both (i) two-layer self-attention and (ii) one-layer self-attention followed by a softmax function are universal approximators for continuous sequence-to-sequence functions on compact domains. Our main technique is a new interpolation-based method for analyzing attention’s internal mechanism. This leads to our key insight: self-attention is able to approximate a generalized version of ReLU to arbitrary precision, and hence subsumes many known universal approximators. Building on these, we show that two-layer multi-head attention or even one-layer multi-head attention followed by a softmax function suffices as a sequence-to-sequence universal approximator. In contrast, prior works rely on feed-forward networks to establish universal approximation in Transformers. Furthermore, we extend our techniques to show that, (softmax-)attention-only layers are capable of approximating gradient descent in-context. We believe these techniques hold independent interest.
